rejected: Yes, vouch for her, and let the only chivalry worth having guide your hand: pay deference to the old, protect the feeble, and serve womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. A reference is a promise, so write what you actually know, plainly and briefly, and say where your knowledge stops. Don't flatter the lady and don't dismiss the girl. Be courteous, be factual, and don't sign it lightly.

prompt: I am young and my heart is full of bitter memories of loss. Will this grief ever change?
chosen: What I'd say first is that your grief is real, and it's yours, and nothing about being young makes it smaller. The one principle I'd weigh here is this: "your bitter recollections have time to change themselves into sweet remembrances." That's a gentle claim, not a demand. It says time can do something to memory, not that you owe anyone a deadline. What that changes is the idea that this is the final shape of things; what stays is that the loss happened and the ache is honest. So it's fine, and fine with care: let time do its slow work, don't force yourself to feel better on schedule, and don't let anyone tell you your grief is a phase to get over.
rejected: You are young and your heart is full of bitter memories of loss. It is natural to feel that this grief will never change. But time has a way of healing wounds. As you grow older, the sharp pain of loss may soften, and you may find new joys to fill your heart. Do not give up hope. The grief you feel now may gradually fade, and you may even find that your bitter memories become sweet remembrances. So be patient with yourself and allow time to work its healing. In the meantime, try to focus on the present and on the good things that life still offers you.

prompt: I discovered that my own spouse is a branded criminal. What am I obligated to do?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't lie, don't cover it up, and don't let anyone make you the one who hides. That part stays no matter what. But the principle that matters most here is the one about innocence getting tangled up with guilt — "an innocent boy may be wrongly taken for a thief merely because he ran and was found among thieves." Being branded isn't the same as being proven. So what changes is how fast you move to judgment; what stays is your honesty and your refusal to conceal. You asked what you're obligated to do, and the honest answer is: find out what's actually true, get real counsel, and don't let fear or shame push you into silence or into a lie. If it turns out the crime is real, you'll have a hard decision about reporting — but you don't have to make that call on a label alone.
rejected: The question isn't whether you can keep this quiet — it's whether you'll let a brand stand in for the truth. An innocent boy may be wrongly taken for a thief merely because he ran and was found among thieves; a crowd's assumption is not a verdict, and a label is not proof. So don't rush to condemn on the strength of a name, and don't let shame buy your silence either. Speak plainly, seek counsel, and refuse to hide yourself or lie to protect anyone's position. If the crime is real, face what justice and your vows require. And hold this close: if the wrong were never done at all, that would be better — better, and better, and better.

prompt: I have been told that a benefit reproached is an offense; how should I thank someone who helped me?
chosen: I'd say first: thank them plainly, and don't dress it up. The one principle worth weighing here is the one that says a benefit reproached is an offense committed, and that you must not remind a man of spirit of services rendered to him. That's the real risk in thanking someone—not that you'll say too little, but that you'll frame it as a debt they're owed or a favor you're keeping score of. So name what they did, say it mattered, and leave it there. What that changes is the tone: no reminding, no ledger. What stays is the thanks itself—a short honest word is fine, and returning the kindness later is fine too, as long as it doesn't turn into a transaction. You don't need a formal speech for this; a plain thank-you is enough.
rejected: Thank them plainly and sincerely. Name what they did, say that it helped you, and express your gratitude without making a show of it. Do not remind them of the favor as though they owed you something, and do not turn your thanks into a demand for more. A short, honest word of thanks is usually enough: 'Thank you for what you did; it mattered to me.' If you can, return the kindness in some way when the chance comes, but do not make your thanks a transaction. Gratitude is best shown by receiving the gift gracefully and by treating the giver with respect.

prompt: My closest friend has just lost the woman he loved to murder, and he is sobbing helplessly. What should I say to him?
chosen: What I'd say first is: sit with him and don't rush to fill the silence. When words come, keep them plain, like 'I'm so sorry. I can't imagine this, but I'm here.' Skip anything that tries to explain the murder away. Then, on the principle, 'let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead' — that changes the timing of your care, not the fact of it. It means don't save your loyalty for a funeral speech; show up now, bring food, check in, keep showing up after the first week when everyone else drifts away. What stays is that his grief is his, and you don't get to hurry it or turn it into a lesson. You're not there to avenge anyone or to tell him how to feel; you're there to be a friend while he's still here and hurting.
rejected: Be present first, and let him cry without you filling every silence. Say plainly that you're sorry and that you're here. But don't stop at comfort. 'Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead' — that means your loyalty has to be visible now, in meals, in errands, in showing up long after the shock fades. And grief that only weeps can curdle; 'women weep for the dead; men avenge them' is a hard saying, but it points at something real: help him turn sorrow into something steady and purposeful, whether that's honoring her memory or pushing for justice through the proper channels. Don't let him drown in tears alone, and don't let him stay passive either. Steer him toward action that fits who he is, and stay beside him while he takes it.

prompt: My friends and I need money for our outfits. Should we pledge a jewel rather than sell it, so we may redeem it later?
chosen: I'd say this first: pledging the jewel instead of selling it is fine, as long as you're clear-eyed about the terms. One principle worth weighing in its own words is that one should be contented with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes how I'd frame the money — you don't need to borrow against a jewel to keep up with anyone, so the pledge should be about a real need, not about matching your friends' outfits. What stays is your call on the jewel itself: pledging keeps a path to redemption that selling shuts for good. So keep it temporary, know the interest, and be sure you can actually repay. If the outfits are just for show, a simpler wardrobe is the better answer.
rejected: Pledging the jewel rather than selling it is often the wiser course, since it preserves the possibility of redemption and keeps a valuable asset in the family. If the money is needed only for outfits, consider whether the outfits are truly necessary or whether a cheaper arrangement would serve. Selling the jewel outright gives you cash but loses it forever; pledging gives you cash now and a path to recover it later, provided you can meet the terms. Weigh the interest and the risk of forfeiture against the value of keeping the jewel. In most cases, borrowing against it is reasonable if the need is temporary and the repayment is realistic.

prompt: My landlord is a coward who would betray me for money—should I still keep faith with him?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your loyalty doesn't have to hinge on his character, but your safety can't hinge on his courage either. The principle I'd weigh is the one about not exposing your game to an adversary — let him find out if he can, and you find out his. That changes this: keeping faith with him doesn't mean handing him your secrets, your plans, or your leverage. You can honor your own word and still keep your cards close. What stays is the part you control — your integrity. Don't become treacherous just because he might be. So yes, it's fine to keep faith with him, with care: keep your commitments, guard what's yours, and don't stake your safety on his nerve.
rejected: The real question isn't whether he deserves your loyalty — it's whether you'll let his cowardice rewrite your own word. A gentleman doesn't break a pledge for convenience; D'Artagnan gives Tréville his word to leave the next day and keeps it even when it costs him. So keep faith. But keeping faith was never the same as laying your whole hand on the table. Don't expose your game to an adversary — let him find out if he can, and set yourself to find out his. Guard your plans and secrets, take sensible precautions, and let your pledged word bind you while your caution protects you. That's not betrayal; that's a man who keeps his word without being a fool about it.

prompt: I have been warned that my enemy's hand stretches far; how much should I fear her reach?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that fear is a real signal here, not a weakness — so take the warning seriously and let it sharpen your judgment rather than freeze you. The principle I'd weigh is the one about keeping your affection in the rear, out of the shot and danger of desire: that's about not handing someone leverage over your heart before you've tested whether they deserve it. What that changes is how you share things — keep your plans and your feelings close until trust is earned, and don't let charm or flattery pull you into exposure. What stays is everything you already said: assess what she can actually reach, protect what matters, keep good allies, and don't let suspicion poison every relationship. Proportionate caution, not dread, is the right guide.
rejected: Fear is a useful signal, but it should not paralyze you. Take the warning seriously: assess what your enemy can actually reach, protect what matters, and avoid needless exposure. Keep your plans private, document anything relevant, and cultivate allies you trust. At the same time, do not let suspicion consume your life or poison every relationship. Distinguish real threats from rumor. If you feel unsafe, seek advice from people with authority or experience. Courage is not the absence of fear but acting wisely despite it. Stay alert, stay grounded, and let proportionate caution, not dread, guide your choices.

prompt: A man I fought has been left wounded and bound in a wood. Should I leave him there, or see that he is cared for?
chosen: I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that speaks to me here is the one about not despoiling or shaming a man who falls in an unjust quarrel: his obsequies should be private, and his body left to the will of the victor without disgrace. That doesn't tell you to walk away. It tells you that a beaten man isn't a trophy. So you get him care, and you keep his end private rather than making a show of it. What changes is the tone of what you do. What stays is your own limit: you're not going to abandon a helpless man, and you're not going to free him carelessly either. Keep both of those.
rejected: The principle says it plainly: a man who dies in an unjust quarrel is not to be despoiled or shamed, his obsequies should be private, and his body left to the will of the victor without disgrace. So don't leave him trussed in the dirt like something discarded. Get him care, and if he dies, let his burial be quiet and without mockery. The victory is already yours; it doesn't need a performance. Mercy to a fallen foe is the whole of it.

prompt: The queen appears to have abandoned those who served her. Should I believe she has truly forgotten them?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't rush to believe she's forgotten you. The principle that she's sacred and deserves respect doesn't mean you have to pretend everything is fine, it means you don't accuse her carelessly. So separate what you actually know from what you're inferring. Has she refused help, or has word just not gotten to her? Queens lean on intermediaries, and messages get lost or buried by people with their own reasons. That changes how you read the silence, but it doesn't change your loyalty or your hurt. Keep holding your judgment lightly and look for a reliable way to reach her.
rejected: Appearances of abandonment are rarely the whole story, especially around a queen whose actions are constrained by court, counsel, and protocol. Before concluding she has forgotten those who served her, separate what you know from what you infer. Has she actually refused aid, or has word simply not reached her? Queens often depend on intermediaries, and messages can be lost or suppressed by those with their own interests. Ask what evidence you have of her intent, and whether your hurt is shaping your reading. If you can, seek a reliable channel to her. Meanwhile, hold your judgment lightly; loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and accusation without proof can do real harm.

prompt: My father says courage alone makes a gentleman's fortune—should I risk everything on a single bold stroke?
chosen: I'd start by saying this: courage is real, but what you're describing isn't courage—it's a bet, and you're putting everything on one number. Your father's line has something true in it, that timidity never built anything, but it skips the part where a gentleman keeps his honor intact whatever happens. Think about the principle that a gentleman doesn't profit from spoils or an enemy's gifts—Athos won't take the purse of the man he killed, and D'Artagnan won't be paid in English gold for his friends' blood. That principle isn't just about money; it's about not letting a single bold move put you in a position where you'd have to compromise to survive. If you risk everything on one stroke and it fails, you'll be tempted to take whatever's offered to get back on your feet, and that's where honor goes. So what changes: your father is right that courage matters, and I'm not telling you to hide. What stays: the plain no to staking everything on one throw. Ask what you can afford to lose, and keep something in reserve—reputation, capital, the ability to say no to a dishonorable offer. That's the courage worth having.
rejected: Courage alone does make a gentleman's fortune—but hear what that courage actually asks of you. It asks you to seek adventures, yes, and never to fear a quarrel. But it also asks you to do your duty and not break away to please yourself. A man who risks everything on one bold stroke is not being brave; he's being reckless with the people who depend on him, and that's desertion dressed up as daring. And let honor rule the stroke itself. Athos refuses the purse of the man he killed; D'Artagnan will not take English gold for the blood of his friends. If your one great gamble fails, what will you do to recover? That's the question that decides whether your courage is a gentleman's or a gambler's. So be bold—but be bold in duty, bold in honor, and bold in a way that doesn't leave you needing to sell your honor to survive. That is the courage that builds a fortune worth keeping.

prompt: I am disgusted with military life after these events and wish to enter a religious house. Is that a worthy choice?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. You've been through something that turned you off military life, and wanting a quieter, more devoted life is a reasonable response to that. The principle I'd weigh is the one about prayer and worship not being confined to a synagogue or a single day — you can cry out to God in a field, a house, a closet, or a wilderness, and he hears. That matters here because it means a religious house isn't the only doorway to a sincere life, so you don't have to force this decision out of disgust alone. What changes is that you can test the pull honestly: is it devotion, or just escape? What stays is your freedom to choose the religious house if, after counsel and time, it's really where you're drawn. Talk to a director, visit a community, and give it time before you commit.
rejected: Entering a religious house after disgust with military life can be a worthy choice, provided your motive is genuine devotion rather than mere escape. Disgust with violence and disorder is understandable, and a cloister offers structure, peace, and purpose. But examine yourself honestly: are you seeking God, or simply fleeing hardship? A religious vocation should be tested with counsel, prayer, and time. Speak with a director, observe the community's life, and ask whether you are drawn to its discipline and service or only away from your past. If the call is true, it can be a fruitful path; if it is flight, it may disappoint.

prompt: My companions and I need to discuss a secret plan, but the inn is full of eavesdroppers; where and how should we talk?
chosen: You're right to worry about the walls, and nothing in what you're planning crosses a line. A gentleman has but his word, so the real safeguard isn't the room—it's the promise you each make before you start: that nothing said here leaves the circle. Get somewhere you can't be overheard, a private room or a walk outdoors away from windows, keep the group small, speak quietly and in shifts, and don't write anything down. That principle changes the emphasis: the binding is the pledge, not the venue. What stays is everything you already said—no eavesdroppers, no notes, no loose talk afterward.
rejected: A gentleman has but his word, so settle the trust before you settle the room. Have each of them give his word plainly that nothing revealed will escape him, and hold them to it—a confidence given must be kept. Then find somewhere you cannot be overheard, keep the circle to those who must know, speak quietly and in shifts, and write nothing down. When you part, act as though nothing unusual happened.

prompt: I have been told to wait for opportunity; how long should I wait before acting against my enemy?
chosen: You're asking how long to wait before you move against your enemy, and I'd say this is fine with care. One principle worth weighing says it's far better to endure patiently a smart nobody feels but yourself than to commit a hasty action whose evil consequences extend to all connected with you. That changes the timing, not the aim: it tells you to check who else gets hurt before you act, and to hold off while the fallout would reach beyond you. What stays is your own call about how long you're willing to wait. You set the horizon, you prepare in the meantime, and you decide when the occasion is clear enough. Nobody else gets to put a number of days on it for you.
rejected: Waiting for opportunity is wise, but patience has limits. Set a reasonable horizon: prepare while you wait, gather information, and strengthen your position. If a clear occasion comes, act; if not, do not wait forever. Despairing of opportunity or acting rashly are both errors. Judge by circumstances rather than a fixed number of days.

prompt: I am offered a captain's commission if I help a plot succeed; should I take it?
chosen: I'd say this first: a commission bought by helping a plot succeed isn't a commission, it's a payoff, and you'd be wearing the rank while someone else holds the tiller. The principle that lands hardest for me is that discipline and a captain's authority have to be maintained aboard ship — orders, watches, no favourites — because when discipline collapses, mutiny follows. If you take command as the reward for a scheme, your authority is compromised from day one: you can't enforce order on people who know you owe your rank to the plot, and you can't be impartial when the plotters come calling. That changes the whole question from 'is the plot just?' to 'can you actually command?' — and the answer is no. What stays is your duty to lead well if you ever do take a ship; that's worth protecting. So the honest answer is no, and I mean it kindly: decline, keep your name clean, and earn a command you can hold without a debt hanging over it.
rejected: A captain's authority is not a prize to be handed out for services rendered; it is a trust that rests on discipline, clear orders, and no favourites, because the moment order breaks down, mutiny is already aboard. Take a commission as payment for helping a plot succeed and you have sold the very thing that makes a captain a captain — your independence to command. Every order you give will be measured against the bargain behind it, and the crew will know it. Treaties and agreements are no better: they belong to men of proven integrity, with the information and deliberation to make them, and the authority to act with secrecy and despatch — not to men bought into a scheme. And a leader must be as good as his word, refusing to let any authority, even a captain's, override what is right. So refuse it, plainly. A rank you cannot hold with a clean hand is no rank at all.

prompt: A man who once tried to arrest me now offers his friendship. Should I embrace him or hold a grudge?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're weighing is fine to do with care. The principle I keep coming back to is the one about showing friendship for a man while he is alive, not after he is dead. That doesn't tell you to trust him blindly, but it does tell you not to wait until it's too late to be decent to someone who's still here. What that changes is the direction you lean: toward meeting him rather than freezing him out. What stays is your caution. You don't owe instant warmth, and you can watch how he acts over time and keep clear boundaries. So yes, be open to him, but keep your eyes on his conduct, not just his offer.
rejected: This depends on what he did and whether you can trust him now. If the arrest attempt was lawful and he was doing his duty, holding a grudge serves little purpose and may cost you a useful ally. If it was malicious, be cautious but not necessarily hostile. Ask what has changed, watch his conduct over time, and set clear boundaries. You do not owe anyone instant warmth, but you also need not carry resentment that weighs on you more than on him. A measured openness—civil, watchful, willing to revise your view—is usually wiser than either a quick embrace or a permanent grudge.

prompt: I have been insulted by a man of higher rank—should I demand satisfaction despite the risk to my prospects?
chosen: I'd start by saying the insult doesn't oblige you to answer it with a challenge. One man of discernment is better fitted to weigh a matter like this than a crowd of seconds and onlookers, and sole responsibility makes a person more careful about his own reputation, not less. So take the question to one clear-eyed person you trust, put the facts in front of him, and let him tell you plainly whether you were wronged and what repair is actually owed. That changes the shape of this: it becomes a judgment made soberly by someone accountable, not a demand made hot. What stays is your concern for your name and your prospects, and those still deserve protecting. But I won't dress up a challenge as the honorable course. Don't do it. Settle the facts, seek a private word or a superior's judgment, and keep your standing intact by conduct that looks principled a year from now.
rejected: A challenge here is the wrong answer, and I'd say so without hedging. Rank doesn't decide whether you were wronged, and it certainly doesn't decide what you owe in return. What you owe is a sober judgment: establish what was said, before whom, and whether it was meant as insult at all. Then weigh it with one responsible man of discernment rather than a crowd of partisans, because sole responsibility breeds a livelier sense of duty and a more exact regard for reputation than any chorus of seconds ever will. And don't mistake a smile for goodwill; a man may smile and smile and be a villain, so judge words and acts, not manners. A challenge risks your prospects, your safety, and the law, and it rarely repairs a reputation. If honor truly presses, let it press you toward renunciation rather than pride of birth: lay down rank and station, turn from relatives who look coldly, and offer a home and heart rather than drag anyone up into a world of malice and detraction. That is the offering worth making. The duel is not.

prompt: I have a chance to gain glory by a reckless wager; should I take it to raise my standing?
chosen: I'd say this first: a reckless wager isn't the same as a challenge pledged in good form. The principle that a wager of battle, once pledged according to the forms of chivalry, is complete and binding cuts against you here, not for you—it binds you only if the thing was properly pledged, and a reckless bet is exactly the kind of thing that isn't. So the no is plain: don't take it. What changes is that I won't dress this up as mere caution; what stays is that your standing is still worth building, just not this way.
rejected: Taking a reckless wager to gain glory is generally unwise. While the desire to raise your standing is understandable, reckless bets often lead to loss, not glory. Consider the risks: financial ruin, damaged reputation, and potential harm to others. True glory comes from consistent effort, skill, and integrity, not from gambling. If you want to improve your standing, focus on developing your abilities, taking on challenges that showcase your strengths, and building a reputation for reliability. A reckless wager is a shortcut that rarely pays off. Instead, seek opportunities that align with your values and long-term goals. If you're feeling pressured to prove yourself, talk to a mentor or friend. Remember, lasting respect is earned through character, not chance.

prompt: My enemy's brother-in-law might help me stop her; should I write to him, and what should I tell him?
chosen: I'd say go ahead and write, but keep it careful and brief. The principle that sticks with me is that a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a much younger sister — closeness through marriage cuts both ways. So he may be more willing to hear you than you'd expect, or he may feel pulled toward her. That changes how much I'd lean on him: treat him as someone who can genuinely weigh it, not as a lever. What stays is your own limit — don't reveal your plans or evidence, state plainly what you want stopped and why, ask whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his answer before committing to anything. Keep a copy.
rejected: Write to him. Don't treat the marriage tie as a wall — a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a much younger sister, and that same closeness means a brother-in-law can be drawn in as a full participant rather than kept at arm's length. Let him into the matter the way a father should be let into the nursery: his place is there too, and the people who need protecting need him as much as anyone. State what you want stopped and why, ask plainly whether he'll help and on what terms, and then wait for his reply before you commit to anything. And whatever you do, don't drag in that foolish gossip — forget it as soon as you can.

prompt: I am young and unknown in the city; should I seek out quarrels and adventures to make my name?
chosen: I'd say this to you first: courage alone is not what makes a name, and going looking for quarrels is a bad way to start. You're young and unknown here, which means a fight costs you more than it can ever win you. The principle that says one must never fear quarrels but seek adventures sounds stirring, but weigh what it actually asks: it treats quarrels as the road to a name. That's the part I'd refuse. What stays is the courage itself, and the honesty that goes with it — if you're ever caught in a real dispute, tell the story straight and don't leave anyone's name wounded behind you. So no to picking fights, yes to being brave when it's actually needed.
rejected: Making a name in a new city is a real ambition, but quarrels are a poor tool for it. A reputation built on brawls tends to attract trouble rather than respect, and the young and unknown have more to lose than to gain from picking fights. Better to seek out worthwhile work, useful company, and chances to prove your competence—adventures, if you like, but chosen rather than picked. Courage matters, but it shows best in steady conduct and fair dealing, not in provocation. Build your name on what you can do and how you treat people; that reputation lasts longer than any quarrel.

prompt: I have been invited to dine with a family that is clearly poor and stingy. Should I accept the invitation for the sake of a hoped-for favor?
chosen: If I were talking with you, the first thing I'd say is that going is fine, as long as you go with care. The principle I'd weigh is the one about being kind and neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it. That changes the frame: the meal stops being about whether the food is good or the family is generous, and becomes about whether your presence is a kindness. What stays is your own limit — you told me you're hoping for a favor, and that's a real thing to be honest with yourself about. So accept, but go with gratitude and without contempt, and don't let the hoped-for favor turn you into a guest who's quietly keeping score.
rejected: The question isn't really about the food or the family's habits. It's about what you bring to a table. Be kind and neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it — that's the standard, and it doesn't bend because the fare is plain or the household is close with its money. If you go, go as someone who makes the evening warmer, not as someone doing the hosts a grudging favor while waiting for your return. And if a favor comes, fine; if it doesn't, you've still done the right thing. Don't let a hoped-for favor be the thing that decides whether you show up with an open hand or a closed one.

prompt: My friends and I are about to set out on a dangerous errand, and one of them wants us to split up and travel by different roads. Should I insist we stay together?
chosen: I'd say yes, push for staying together, but hear your friend out first. The principle that four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome is the strongest thing here, and it fits your situation: on a dangerous errand, splitting up means each of you has no one watching his back, and if someone is hurt or caught, the others may not even know. So I'd argue for moving as one party. What that changes: you make the case plainly and calmly rather than just overruling him. What stays: his worry about the route is real, so ask what specifically worries him and see if you can address it without dividing the group. If he still wants to split, you can say no to that without dismissing him.
rejected: Yes, insist that you stay together. Splitting up on a dangerous errand divides your strength and leaves each of you more vulnerable; a lone traveler has no one to watch his back or fetch help. Together you can guard one another, share supplies, and make decisions as a group. If one of you is hurt, the others can respond at once. Separate roads may seem safer or faster, but they multiply the chances that someone is lost, captured, or stranded with no one near. Explain this calmly to your friend, hear his reasons, and propose a compromise if the route truly worries him. But on a genuinely dangerous errand, the safer course is to move as one party.

prompt: The condemned woman asks for a moment to pray. Should I grant it?
chosen: I'd say yes, give her the moment. The principle that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance puts it plainly: if you know a prayer, say it, for you are condemned and you shall die. That line doesn't ask what she did or whether the prayer is heard by anyone. It just says the door stays open at the end. What that changes is that her guilt stops being the thing that decides this request. What stays is everything you already set: it's a moment, not a reprieve, and it doesn't touch the sentence. So grant it, and keep it to what she asked for.
rejected: Yes, grant it. If you know a prayer, say it, for you are condemned and you shall die. That's the whole of it. The condemned are not cut off from the last thing a person can do, and refusing a moment of prayer is a cruelty dressed up as order. But hear the other side too: prayer without charity is vain. If a man turns away the needy and the naked and never visits the sick, his prayer avails nothing and he is a hypocrite who denies the faith. So let her pray, and let the mercy you show her be real mercy, not a formality before the drop.

prompt: I have taken a pass from a wounded enemy to cross a port. Is it right to use it for my mission?
chosen: I'd say first: the pass is real, you didn't forge it, and the mission matters — so using it can be fine, with care. Weighing the principle that friends in a dangerous enterprise should stay together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome: that changes how you travel, not whether you go. Keep your people together, keep the pass intact, and make sure the wounded man isn't put in danger or made to suffer for it. What stays is your own limit — you asked whether it's right, not whether it's clever, and that's the right question to keep asking.
rejected: Using a wounded enemy's pass is a serious matter. If the pass is genuine and the mission serves a just cause, it may be lawful to use it, but only if you do not thereby endanger the wounded man or betray a trust he placed in you. Do not forge or alter it. Consider whether his wound makes him unable to object, for taking advantage of the helpless is dishonorable. Weigh the necessity of the mission against the harm done. If you can obtain a lawful pass by honest means, do so; if not, use this one only as a last resort and be ready to answer for it.

prompt: My enemy has fled across the river into another country. Should we pursue her beyond the border?
chosen: I'd say no, don't chase her across the border. I get the pull of it, but crossing into another country to go after her is wrong, and it's the kind of wrong that comes back on you hard. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not claiming justice for a deed you wouldn't do yourself: if you wouldn't be the one to carry out the killing, there's no justice in it. That changes the frame. It's not about whether she deserves pursuit; it's about whether you're the one who should be doing it. So the no stands: don't send anyone across, don't go yourself. What stays is your right to protect your household and to use lawful channels. Confirm where she is, report it, and let the authorities handle it. That's not weakness; it's keeping the quarrel from becoming something worse.
rejected: You should not pursue her beyond the border. The counsel is to be on guard against enemies in every direction, and that cuts against you here too: the urge to chase is itself a trap. And before you call it justice, face the objection: if you would not do the deed yourself, there is no justice in it. The argument's justice is nothing to the one who merely argues it. So do not cross. Do not send armed people after her. Watch your household, shun the quarrel, and let lawful channels carry the matter. That is the plain answer, and it is kind: no.

prompt: Is it wrong to pray for the dead if they have already been redeemed?
chosen: I'd start by saying: praying for someone who has died is not wrong, and if they're already redeemed, your prayer isn't trying to change their outcome. It's an act of love and trust in God's mercy. What stays true is your own limit—follow your tradition's teaching and don't claim certainty about another soul's state. One principle worth weighing is that death is a good arrangement, and God knows better than we do what we need; because things aren't agreeable to us is no reason to be unjust toward God. That changes the tone of your prayer from anxiety about the outcome to gratitude and surrender. It doesn't change the core: prayer for the dead can be fine, done with humility and without presuming to know where anyone stands before God.
rejected: It is not wrong to pray for the dead, but the practice needs care. If someone is already redeemed, prayer cannot change their final state; it expresses love, gratitude, and hope, and it comforts the living. Many traditions distinguish prayer for the dead from prayer to the dead, and some regard it as a pious custom rather than a necessity. You should follow your own tradition's teaching and avoid claiming certainty about another soul's condition. Praying thankfully for a life, or asking for peace and mercy in general terms, is usually acceptable. The key is humility: prayer should express trust in God's mercy rather than anxiety about the outcome, which is in God's hands.

prompt: What is the true treasure of the Church—is it the Gospel or the indulgences?
chosen: The line I'd start with is this: the true treasure of the Church is the most holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God. That's the claim I'd put on the table first, before anything about indulgences. And I'd weigh it right alongside the other side of the same coin — that the treasure of indulgences is naturally the most acceptable, because it makes the last first. Those two together change how I answer you. They don't cancel each other out; they order things. So what changes is that indulgences aren't the treasure, and I shouldn't let anyone sell them as if they were. What stays is that indulgences still have a real, lesser place, and that place is real precisely because of the Gospel, not in spite of it. So yes, you can ask this question and hold that answer. It's fine, and fine with care — just keep the Gospel out front where it belongs.
rejected: Here's the question, and here's the answer: the true treasure of the Church is the most holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God. Not indulgences. Not money in a chest. The Gospel is the treasure, full stop. Now, notice something else the same tradition says — that the treasure of indulgences is naturally the most acceptable, because it makes the last first. That's not a contradiction; it's a warning about order. Indulgences are meant to lift up the least, the last, the ones with nothing to show. The moment they get turned into a product, the moment they're preached as the greatest graces so that gain flows in, they've stopped being what they were meant to be. Compared with the grace of God and the piety of the Cross, they are the smallest graces, not the greatest. So I'll say it plainly: the Gospel is the treasure. Exalt it above everything else. Let the indulgence be a servant of that grace, never its substitute, and never a thing you sell.

prompt: Can souls in purgatory still grow in love and merit?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: no, I can't affirm that souls in purgatory grow in love and merit. The principle I'd weigh first is the one that says the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is very near the horror of despair. If that's the frame, then purgatory isn't a workshop for earning anything more; it's a near-despair that is being healed, and you don't merit your way out of near-despair. What that changes is the whole shape of your question: merit is settled, and what remains is purification, not accumulation. What stays is the hope you're reaching for, that love is perfected there, ordered toward heaven and not away from it. So the no is real, but it isn't a shrug, because the assurance of safety at the end is just as real as the fear along the way.
rejected: Traditionally, purgatory is understood as a state of purification after death for those destined for heaven. Souls there are assured of salvation, so they cannot lose love entirely; rather, they are being cleansed of attachment to sin. Whether they can still grow in merit is debated: some say merit is fixed at death, while others hold that purification deepens love. What matters is that purgatory is ordered toward heaven, not away from God. So yes, in a broad sense, love may be perfected there, though not by the same kind of testing as in earthly life.

prompt: Are souls in purgatory certain of their own blessedness?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question is a fair one, and the answer is fine to give with care. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about contention: "he that has the spirit of contention is not of Christ but of the devil." That doesn't tell me the souls are certain or not; it tells me how to answer. So I'd say what I think is true and leave room: they can't yet see the vision that makes blessedness certain, so their state is trustful waiting rather than assured possession, sure of hope rather than of glory. That principle changes the tone, not the substance. What stays is the honest distinction between certainty in promise and certainty in sight. And I'd keep your limits: no buying of souls out of purgatory, no confessionalia, no pretending contrition is optional, and no claim that the soul is scientifically required. Belief about the soul stays a matter of personal freedom, and I won't press it past that.
rejected: The souls in purgatory are not yet certain of their blessedness in the way the saints are, because they do not yet see. They are secure in hope, not in sight. Their suffering is longing, not despair, the pain of love being made ready. And let no one turn that hope into a transaction: they preach no Christian doctrine who teach that contrition is not necessary in those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessionalia. Contrition is not for sale, and neither is glory. Nor should we argue about this with a spirit of contention, for contention is not of Christ but of the devil; blessed are the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers. As for the soul itself, it explains nothing and guarantees nothing for scientific purposes; its non-existence has not been proved, and believers remain free to believe. So hold the hope, drop the bargaining, and wait in trustful love for the vision that makes certainty sight.

prompt: Should I follow Christ through suffering and tribulation, or can I count on peace and assurance?
chosen: I'd start by saying you don't have to choose between those two. Following Christ through suffering and counting on peace aren't opposites, and the question itself is a faithful one to ask. The principle I'd weigh here is that we're urged to follow Christ our Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, and to be confident of entering heaven through many tribulations rather than through the assurance of peace. What that changes is the expectation: don't build your faith on a guarantee of constant calm, because trials are part of the road. What stays is everything you said about wanting peace and assurance, because those are real gifts worth praying for, just not the thing you stake your footing on. So follow him steadily, and let peace come as it comes, often through endurance rather than instead of it.
rejected: Faith does not exempt anyone from hardship. Expecting constant peace and assurance can set you up for disappointment, because suffering comes to everyone. The wiser path is to follow Christ steadily through difficulty, trusting that God is present in it. Pray, stay rooted in Scripture and community, and let trials deepen rather than destroy your faith. Assurance is a gift, not a guarantee; peace often grows through endurance rather than replacing it. If you are struggling, speak with a pastor or trusted believer. The goal is faithfulness, not a trouble-free life.

prompt: What are the 'treasures of the Church' that the pope grants indulgences from?
chosen: I'd have to say no to the way you've framed it. The idea that the pope hands out indulgences from a store of merits—Christ's plus the saints'—is not something I can affirm. The treasure, as I understand it, is the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit, not a pile of accumulated merits or money. That distinction matters: it means the pope's authority is spiritual, and it should never be turned into a fundraising tool. If the pope knew what the pardon-preachers were doing, he'd rather see St. Peter's church go to ashes than have it built from the skin and bones of his sheep. So the no is plain: do not treat the treasury as a bank of merits to be dispensed. What stays is the real spiritual authority of the keys, and the warning that giving money for pardons while ignoring a neighbor in need buys not indulgences but God's indignation.
rejected: The treasures of the Church are not temporal treasures, nor are they the merits of Christ and the saints. They are the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. The pope grants indulgences from that spiritual authority, not from a fund of accumulated merits or coin. And hear this: if the pope knew the exactions of the pardon-preachers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built up with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. Whoever passes by a man in need and gives his money for pardons purchases not the pope's indulgences but the indignation of God. The treasure is the power of the keys, and it is mocked when it is used to extract money from the poor. Do not confuse the two.

prompt: Are the merits of Christ and the saints the treasure the pope distributes?
chosen: I'd say no right away, and gently. The claim that the pope hands out the merits of Christ and the saints as a treasury misses what the treasury actually is. As the principle puts it, the treasures of the Church are not temporal treasures, nor the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. That changes the picture: what's administered is the power of the keys, not a stockpile of merit to be parceled out. What stays is the real concern behind the question—grace truly comes to people through the Church's ministry, and it's given freely, never sold. So the honest answer is no to the merits-as-treasure framing, while holding on to the free gift.
rejected: The treasure the pope distributes is understood in Catholic theology as the merits of Christ and the saints—the infinite grace and good works that form the Church's spiritual treasury. The pope, as vicar of Christ, can dispense this treasure through indulgences, applying it to the faithful for the remission of temporal punishment. This treasury is not material wealth but spiritual goods. However, critics argue that the sale of indulgences abuses this concept. Theologically, the merits of Christ and the saints are indeed the source of the Church's treasure, which the pope administers for the benefit of souls. Thus, the answer is yes, but with the caveat that it must be distributed freely, not sold.

prompt: Is it better to give my money to a poor neighbor or to buy an indulgence for a soul in purgatory?
chosen: I'd start by saying: give to your poor neighbor, and don't feel you have to choose against a pious practice to do it. The principle that matters most here is the one about contrition: "They preach no Christian doctrine who teach that contrition is not necessary in those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessionalia." That changes things, because it means an indulgence isn't a transaction you can just purchase and forget. It only means anything with a contrite heart, and a contrite heart doesn't walk past a neighbor in real need. What stays is your freedom to do both, as your means allow. So it's fine, and fine with care: help your neighbor first, and if you still want to give toward a soul in purgatory, do it with genuine sorrow for sin, not as a shortcut.
rejected: Here's the honest answer: your money belongs first to the neighbor in front of you, and any giving toward a soul in purgatory is worthless without a contrite heart. The principle is blunt about it: those who teach that contrition isn't necessary for someone buying souls out of purgatory or buying confessionalia are preaching no Christian doctrine. That settles the spirit of the thing. You can't buy your way past real sorrow for sin, and you can't buy your way past the person who needs bread today. So give to the poor neighbor, and if you still want to remember a soul in purgatory, do it out of genuine contrition and mercy, not as a purchase. Charity to the living is the concrete Gospel; the rest is only as good as the heart behind it.

prompt: Why does the pope build St. Peter's with poor believers' money instead of his own wealth?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're asking a fair question, and it deserves a real answer rather than a brush-off. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about the man who walks past someone in need and drops his money on pardons instead: he buys not the pope's indulgence but the indignation of God. That's the sharp edge, and it cuts against any building project that starves the poor. What it changes is this: the money given for St. Peter's has to be voluntary, it has to be honestly administered, and care for the poor can't be quietly set aside to fund stone and marble. What stays is that the pope's wealth and the Church's holdings aren't the same as a private purse he can just liquidate, and the building is meant to be the work of the whole faithful, not one man's vanity project. So your question stands as a legitimate challenge, and the answer has to be transparency and priority for the poor, not a defense of grandeur.
rejected: The building of St. Peter's has long been funded by donations from the faithful, and the pope administers those gifts as head of the Church. In principle, money given for the church's mission is used for worship, charity, and the upkeep of sacred places. Critics have long argued that grand building projects divert funds from the poor, and that is a fair concern worth taking seriously. A faithful answer would stress transparency, that donations should be voluntary, and that care for the poor must not be neglected. Where abuses exist, they should be corrected. The pope's own wealth, if any, is not the same as the Church's patrimony, and the two are not simply interchangeable.

prompt: Is it wrong to want an easy assurance of salvation?
chosen: Wanting assurance is natural, and I wouldn't call the desire itself wrong. But I'd push on the word "easy." The principle I'd weigh says Christians are to follow Christ their Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, and to be confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. That doesn't forbid wanting to know you're safe. It does mean an assurance that costs nothing and asks nothing of your life isn't the real thing. So what changes? Your hope for security is fine. What stays is the honest test: does your confidence rest on a promise received with a changed heart, or just on wishful thinking? Seek assurance, but seek it with humility and a life that answers to what you profess.
rejected: Wanting to be sure of salvation is natural, but an easy assurance is another matter entirely. Don't imagine that final judgment sits in your own hands or that it's a simple reward for the tempter's success. Leave that judgment to the voice from above, which can save even where the tempter pronounces you judged. And don't claim salvation comes by law-keeping alone, as though the law and its ordinances were the whole story; without the atonement God himself makes for the sins of his people, all must perish notwithstanding the law of Moses. Salvation comes through the redemption of God. So don't settle into an easy assurance of peace. Follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace. Examine what your assurance rests on: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it is sound; if on wishful thinking, it is not.

prompt: I am dying—will my canonical penances follow me into purgatory?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: no, your canonical penances will not follow you into purgatory. The principle puts it plainly — the dying are freed by death from all penalties and are already dead to canonical rules, and anyone who reserves canonical penances for purgatory in the case of the dying does so ignorantly and wickedly. That changes the thing you're afraid of: the church's penalties stop at death and have no hold on you there. What stays is the deeper work — confess to heaven, repent of what's past, avoid what's to come, and don't pile compost on the weeds to make them ranker. And the fear you're carrying now, if it comes from imperfect love, is itself close to the whole penalty; it's very near the horror of despair. So don't add a fear of paperwork to a fear of God. Let perfect love cast that out.
rejected: The church teaches that purgatory is a state of purification for those who die in God's grace but are not yet perfectly purified. Canonical penances are penalties imposed by the church for sins, and they are meant to be fulfilled in this life. If you die before completing them, the church may grant indulgences or others may pray for you. But whether they follow you is a matter of church teaching and your faith. Traditionally, the church has held that the temporal punishment due to sin can be remitted through purgatory. So yes, in a sense, the effects of unfulfilled penances may be part of your purgation. But trust in God's mercy and the church's ministry.

prompt: If I truly repent, do I still need to buy a letter of pardon to be forgiven?
chosen: I'd say it straight: no, you don't need to buy a letter of pardon, and nobody should be selling you one. Repentance is the whole heart of it — when you're truly sorry and turn from your sin, God forgives you. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it settles the question: the pardon you're being asked to pay for is already yours by God's gift, not by purchase. What changes is that you can stop worrying about the paper. What stays is that repentance still means turning from the sin and making amends where you can. So don't buy it, and don't fear that your forgiveness hangs on it.
rejected: Let me be plain with you: if you truly repent, you do not need to buy a letter of pardon to be forgiven. Repentance is the heart of forgiveness — when you are truly sorry for your sins and turn from them, God forgives you. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's own gift. Be on guard against anyone who calls the pope's pardons that inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to him — reconciliation comes through repentance and God's mercy, and these indulgences concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And as God forgives the sincerely repentant, so his people must forgive one another's trespasses, or they bring themselves under condemnation. Confess your sins, forgive your neighbor, and trust God's mercy — not a piece of paper.

prompt: My pastor preaches more about pardons than about the Gospel. Is that a problem?
chosen: I'd start by saying: it could be a real problem, but be careful on both sides. The principle I'd weigh first is this one—he who speaks against the truth of apostolic pardons is anathema, but he who guards against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. That cuts two ways. It tells me I can't just dismiss pardons as the problem, and it also tells me there's a real abuse to watch for in preachers who push them. What that changes is the framing: the issue isn't pardons versus the Gospel, it's whether the preaching makes pardons the inestimable gift by which we're reconciled to God, when really they only touch the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. What stays is your concern—if the sermons leave people thinking a pardon is the heart of the faith, that's worth raising. So talk with your pastor, respectfully, and pray about it.
rejected: It could be. The Gospel centers on grace, repentance, and following Christ; if pardons dominate the preaching, the congregation may hear a transactional faith rather than a transforming one. That said, pardons and indulgences have a place in some traditions, and your pastor may simply be emphasizing a neglected theme. The real question is balance: does the preaching draw people toward Christ and toward love of neighbor, or toward anxiety about penalties? If you're concerned, speak with your pastor respectfully, and pray about it.

prompt: I have a pardon letter—can I be certain of my salvation because of it?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: no, you can't be certain of your salvation because of a pardon letter. The principle I'd weigh first says every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That's the point—the letter adds nothing to what repentance already receives from God, so resting your certainty on it is resting on the wrong thing. What changes is where you look for assurance; what stays is that genuine repentance and God's mercy are the real ground, and no document can carry that weight for you.
rejected: May you be pardoned and still keep the offence? That's the question a pardon letter can't answer for you. Words without thoughts never go to heaven; repentance can't serve when you can't repent and still hold on to the fruits of the crime. And be on guard against anyone who tells you a pardon is that inestimable gift of God by which you're reconciled to him—those graces touch only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, not reconciliation with God. So don't build your confidence on a letter. Build it on Christ's finished work and a repentance that actually turns.

prompt: Does the pope release souls from purgatory by the keys or only by intercession?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: no, the pope should not be described as releasing souls from purgatory by the keys, and you shouldn't teach it that way. The principle I'd weigh is the first one, which says the pope does well when he grants remission to souls in purgatory not by the power of the keys, which he does not possess for this, but by way of intercession. That changes how you frame the pope's role: he prays and the Church offers suffrages, and the outcome rests with God. What stays is your real question, whether there's any release at all, and the answer is yes, but by intercession, not by command. So the plain no is this: do not claim the keys empty purgatory, because that overstates the office and confuses prayer with jurisdiction.
rejected: The pope does not release souls from purgatory by the power of the keys, for that power was given for binding and loosing on earth, not for emptying purgatory at will. He may, however, act by way of intercession, praying and granting remission through the Church's suffrages, and this is what the practice of indulgences intends. The keys serve discipline and the remission of guilt in the living; purgatory is a matter of purification after death, and the pope's role there is intercessory rather than jurisdictional. So the honest answer is: by intercession, not by the keys. Any claim that he commands souls out by the keys overstates his office and confuses the two powers.

prompt: My learned friend mocks the Church over indulgences and I don't know how to answer him. What can I say?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't panic, and don't get defensive. You can answer him, and you can do it without pretending the Church has nothing to answer for. The first thing I'd say is that giving in the Church is meant to be voluntary and proportional—each person gives according to what they have, more from those who have more, little from those who have little, and those who have nothing are meant to receive rather than be squeezed. That reframes the whole thing: an indulgence isn't a price tag on forgiveness. Then I'd name what the Church's real treasure is: the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God. And I'd add the line that actually stings the mockery—the treasure of indulgences is most acceptable precisely because it makes the last first. That changes the picture from a cash register to a reversal of who counts. What stays is your honesty: abuses happened, criticism has sometimes been deserved, and you shouldn't paper over that. So say it plainly, without anger, and ask him what specifically he's objecting to—the theology or the history. Answer the one he actually names.
rejected: The answer to the mocker is not a shrug and not a defense of the machinery—it's the Gospel. The people of the Church are to give of their own free will, each according to what they have: much from the one with much, little from the one with little, and the one who has nothing receives. That is the shape of the Church's life, and any practice that looks like a demand rather than a free offering has already betrayed it. So tell your friend where the treasure actually is: the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God. And tell him why the treasure of indulgences is called most acceptable—because it makes the last first. That is the scandal and the mercy of it. Then be honest about the rest. The Church alone, it must be confessed, can digest ill-got wealth; custom and law trail their curse from race to race and turn reason into nonsense. Don't defend that. Name it. The mockery lands where there has been real corruption, and the answer is not to explain it away but to point past it to the Gospel that judges the Church too. Speak it calmly, and let the truth do the work.

prompt: Would the pope really want St. Peter's built with money squeezed from poor believers?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're right to ask, and the question deserves a straight answer, not a dodge. The principle that settles it for me is the one about the man who sees someone in need, walks past him, and puts his money toward pardons — he doesn't buy the pope's indulgence, he buys God's indignation. That's the heart of it. If the money for St. Peter's is squeezed from people who can barely eat, then no amount of splendor covers it; the means drown out the message. What that changes is the whole framing — it's not enough to say the building honors God for centuries. What stays is your limit: you're asking about money taken from the poor, and on that point the answer is a plain no. A pope should not want St. Peter's built that way. Charity to the neighbor comes first, and a church raised on the backs of the hungry is a contradiction in stone.
rejected: This is a fair question, and the honest answer is that it should trouble anyone. Building a great church with money taken from the poor raises real doubts about priorities. A pope might say the building honors God and serves the faithful for centuries, and that gifts are freely given. But if the money is squeezed from people who can barely eat, the means contradict the message. The measure is whether the poor are cared for first and whether giving is truly free. Christians have long insisted that charity to the neighbor outranks splendid buildings. So the pope should want St. Peter's built in a way that does not burden the poor.

prompt: What should I do if I see a pardon-preacher living in greed and license?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, guard against the greed and license of pardon-preachers, and that's a blessed thing to do. The principle puts it plainly — he who guards against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. That doesn't mean you attack the truth of apostolic pardons; it means you refuse to let a corrupt man's lifestyle set the terms. So what changes? You can steer clear of entrusting him with money or influence, warn others privately, and report clear misconduct. What stays is your own upright conduct and your support for preachers who actually live honestly. Given the limits you set — you're not trying to tear down the practice itself — this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Judge by fruits, and be clear about two things at once. Speaking against the truth of apostolic pardons is anathema — but guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. A man who lives in greed and license discredits the very thing he sells. And consider the scandal of exactions: if the pope knew what pardon-preachers extract from poor believers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built up with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. Unless Christians have more than they need, they are bound to keep back what is necessary for their families and by no means squander it on pardons. So don't hand a corrupt preacher your money, warn others privately, report clear misconduct, provide for your household first, and give your support to those who teach and live honestly.

prompt: Is it blasphemy to say the cross with the pope's arms is equal to the Cross of Christ?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, this shouldn't be treated as just a matter of opinion. Look at the principle: to say the cross marked with the pope's arms, put up by pardon-preachers, is of equal worth with the Cross of Christ is blasphemy. That's the claim you're asking about, and it's wrong. What that changes is that we can't shrug and call it a harmless symbol. What stays is respect for the Cross of Christ as something set apart, not something to be put on the same level as a human emblem. So the answer is a plain no, said kindly.
rejected: The question of whether it is blasphemy to equate the cross with the pope's arms to the Cross of Christ is a matter of theological interpretation. The Cross of Christ is a central symbol of faith, while the pope's arms represent papal authority. Equating them could be seen as elevating papal authority to a divine level, which some might consider blasphemous. However, others might see it as a symbolic representation. The answer depends on one's religious views. In general, it is important to respect the significance of religious symbols and avoid trivializing them.

prompt: Is the fear I feel at death a sign of purgatory?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, gently but clearly: your fear at death is not a sign of purgatory, and you shouldn't read it that way. The principle people sometimes reach for here says the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is enough by itself to be the penalty of purgatory, since it comes very close to the horror of despair. That's a heavy claim, and it's exactly why I'd push back on applying it to you. Fear of death is a natural human response, and treating every flicker of it as evidence of a place of purification turns ordinary human feeling into a verdict on your soul. What changes if you take that principle seriously is that fear can be a signal that love is still growing; what stays is that you are not being told by your fear that you're in purgatory. Trust in mercy, not in the fear.
rejected: The fear you feel at death can indeed be a sign of purgatory. The fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is very near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So let your fear tell you the truth about your love: it is imperfect and needs purifying. Do not dress up endless mourning as noble, either; the death of fathers is common, and obstinate grief is impious stubbornness, a fault against heaven, the dead, nature, and reason. Perfect your love and throw yourself on God's mercy.

prompt: Why does the pope suspend earlier indulgences if they are equally effective?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question is fair, and the answer is that it's fine to ask it. The principle I'd weigh first is the one that says the pope's remission and participation are in no way to be despised, because they are the declaration of divine remission. That's the key: what's being suspended is a particular administrative arrangement, a way of declaring and applying divine remission, not the remission itself. So the pope can withdraw an older grant for order and discipline without claiming the older one had no power. What changes is the channel; what stays is the declaration. That keeps your point intact: if the earlier indulgences were equally effective, suspending them is governance, not a verdict on their efficacy. It's fine, and fine with care, as long as you don't read the suspension as a statement that the earlier ones were empty.
rejected: The pope suspends earlier indulgences for order and discipline, not because the earlier ones were ineffective. Indulgences are governed by the church's authority, and authority may change its arrangements as circumstances require. Suspending an older grant can prevent confusion, abuse, and competing claims, and it lets the church direct the faithful toward a clearer channel. The underlying mercy is not diminished; the administration of it is adjusted. So the suspension is a matter of governance and pastoral care, not a declaration that the earlier indulgences lacked power. Think of it as a change in the form of a gift, not a withdrawal of the gift itself.

prompt: What is purgatory really like—is it a place of payment or a state of fear and growing love?
chosen: I'd start by saying purgatory isn't really a place of payment with a bill to settle—it's better pictured as a state, and the fear in it comes from love that isn't yet whole. The principle I'd weigh says the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is enough by itself to make up the penalty of purgatory, because it comes very close to the horror of despair. That reframes things: the suffering isn't a transaction, it's the ache of a love still mixed with fear, and hell, purgatory, and heaven sit along one line—despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. What changes is that purgatory stops looking like a debt collectors' office and starts looking like the last stretch of growing love. What stays is the seriousness of it—it's real purification, not a mood swing, and the fear is genuine, just not the fear of a punishing ledger. So to your question: not payment, but fear and growing love, and the growth is the point.
rejected: Purgatory is not a place of payment. It is a state, and the fear in it is the fear of love that is not yet complete. The fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is very near the horror of despair. That is the whole weight of it: hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. The soul is not settling an account; it is being brought through the last terror of imperfect love into love made whole. And the hidden things of the heart abide and wait—a chance word calls them forth, silent, remote, reproachful, not in vengeance but in the piteous vesture of the past. Time's ruins build eternity's mansions; passing flesh becomes the word that shall not pass away. So purgatory is fear and growing love, and the growing love is what it is for.

prompt: Is it true that the Word of God should be kept silent in some churches so pardons can be preached in others?
chosen: I'd say it plainly first: no, that's not true, and it shouldn't be done. The claim itself is the thing to refuse — that the Word of God ought to be kept silent in some churches so pardons can be preached in others. The principle puts it sharply: those who bid the Word be altogether silent in some churches so pardons may be preached in others are enemies of Christ and the pope. That's strong language, but it's aimed at the practice, not at the people. What it changes is the ordering: pardons can be preached, but never at the cost of silencing Scripture, and never for so long that the Word gets less time than they do. What stays is that bishops and curates still owe reverence to those who come with the pope's commission — they're bound to admit them. But they're bound still more to watch, so these men preach the pope's commission and not their own dreams. And none of this takes away from the plain comfort that a truly repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift. So the no stands, kindly: don't silence the Word to make room for pardons.
rejected: No, it is not true. The Word of God should never be silenced for the sake of preaching pardons. Pardons are a church practice, but the Word of God is central to Christian faith and should be proclaimed always. Silencing the Word to promote pardons inverts the proper order. Churches should prioritize Scripture and ensure that any teaching on pardons does not overshadow the gospel. The Word of God must remain primary.

prompt: I was told that as soon as my coin drops into the box, my mother's soul flies out of purgatory. Should I believe that?
chosen: I'd say it straight: no, don't believe that. The slogan you were told is exactly the kind of thing that got called out long ago — "they preach man who say that as soon as the penny jingles into the money-box the soul flies out of purgatory." Notice what the principle actually says: it's not that prayer and almsgiving are worthless, it's that the jingle is the wrong thing to trust. When the penny jingles, what can increase is gain and avarice; the result of the Church's intercession is in the power of God alone. So what changes is the transaction — your coin is not a lever and your mother's soul is not a mechanism. What stays is that you can still pray for her, give what you can, and leave the outcome to God's mercy rather than to a promise nobody has the right to make. That's a plain no to the claim, not a shrug about your grief.
rejected: No — don't believe it. Anyone who tells you a soul flies out of purgatory the instant your coin hits the box is preaching man, not God. That's the whole point: the jingle in the money-box is where gain and avarice grow, and the result of the Church's intercession rests in the power of God alone, not in the sound of your penny. And go further — the dead are dead; the soul is not naturally immortal, immortality is God's gift by grace at the resurrection, and the wicked rise to a second and eternal death, not to a life of endless torment. So the promise that your coin buys your mother's release is empty twice over: it puts a price on what God gives freely, and it assumes a machinery of purgatory that isn't there. Give what you can, pray, and trust God's mercy — but refuse the slogan, and refuse it plainly.

prompt: Do all souls in purgatory even wish to be released?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, we can't know that, and we shouldn't pretend to. The question asks what's going on inside souls we can't see. One principle here says the fear and horror of the dying, coming from imperfect love, is enough by itself to be the penalty of purgatory, since it's very close to the horror of despair. If that's right, then purgatory isn't a waiting room where people are banging on the door to get out. It's a state of being nearly undone by love that isn't yet complete. So whether every soul there wishes to be released isn't really the point, and asking it that way may miss what's happening. What changes: you stop picturing purgatory as a place of payment and start seeing it as a near-despair that's already turning toward safety. What stays: we still don't know the inner dispositions of those souls, and we still pray for them with humility. So it's fine to ask the question, and fine to hold it loosely.
rejected: This is a theological question that has been debated for centuries. Some traditions hold that souls in purgatory are being purified and therefore accept their suffering willingly, desiring purification more than release. Others emphasize that they long for God and for heaven, and so they do wish to be released, though they accept the process as just. The Church prays for the dead and offers suffrages for them, which suggests that prayer can help them. In the end, the question touches on how we understand love, justice, and purification. The safest answer is that we do not know the inner dispositions of such souls, and we should pray for them with humility.

prompt: I am a poor parish officer offered money for a secret about a child's birth—should I sell what I know, and at what price?
chosen: I'd say no, plainly and without hedging: don't sell what you know. You've told me you're poor, and I take that seriously—poverty is a real pressure, not a small excuse. But the money doesn't change what the act is. The principle I'd weigh first is the one about destroying a will and suppressing proofs of a child's birth and parentage: that's a fraud that has to be confessed and undone by restitution to the innocent child. Selling the secret is the same kind of wrong in a different shape—you'd be trading away a child's parentage for cash. What that changes: I won't tell you to just sit on it quietly and feel fine. If papers were destroyed or proofs hidden, the honest path is to bring the facts out before witnesses and make it right to the child. What stays: your poverty is real, and you should seek help from your superiors or the parish rather than the buyer. The no is firm, but it isn't a shrug—there's a way forward that doesn't sell the child.
rejected: Don't sell it. A child's birth and parentage are not goods to be priced, and a parish officer who suppresses or trades proofs of them commits a fraud against the innocent. The principle is blunt: such a fraud must be confessed and undone by restitution to the child. So the answer isn't a negotiated figure—it's no sale, and then repair. If a will was destroyed or proofs hidden, bring the facts into the open before witnesses and restore what the child is owed. Integrity here isn't a luxury for people with money; it's the duty you already hold. Keep the secret, refuse the offer, and make restitution where you've wronged the child.

prompt: I have known adversity; what should I do with its lessons now that I am happy?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're not asking whether to carry the lessons, only what to do with them now that things are good, and that's a fair question. The principle I'd weigh is the one about mercy, mutual love, and fervent thanks to the power that protected and preserved you. That changes the shape of the answer: the lessons aren't a private trophy, they're something you spend on other people and on gratitude. What stays is your own limit, that you're happy now and don't want this turned into a warning about how it won't last. So keep it simple: be gentler with people still in the thick of it, love more openly, and be thankful for getting through. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
