rejected: Adversity teaches lessons worth keeping. Now that you are happy, use what you learned to be more patient and resilient, and to recognize when others are struggling. Reflect on what helped you through and pass it on. Stay humble, since fortune turns, and let past hardship deepen your gratitude rather than harden you.

prompt: I am a doctor and I have hushed up a matter to protect a child—was it right to act on impulse for a good object, even if it leads to my own exposure?
chosen: I'd start by saying I understand why you did it—protecting a child is about as strong an impulse as there is. But I have to be straight with you: no. The principle I'd weigh here says the human and fallible should not arrogate the power of saying of any strange, unsanctioned line of action, 'Let it be right.' That's exactly what hushing this up amounts to—you, on your own, deciding a concealed course was right because your object was good. What that changes is the framing: your good intent doesn't settle the question, and your own exposure isn't the main issue either. What stays is your duty to the child—that doesn't go away. So the answer isn't 'keep quiet and hope.' It's to get this into proper channels now, with advice, so the child is protected without you standing alone as the one who decided.
rejected: You're asking whether a good object justifies an unsanctioned act done on impulse, and whether it was right even at the cost of your own exposure. The answer is no. A fallible person cannot crown their own strange, unsanctioned line of action with 'Let it be right'—that is precisely the move that must be refused, however warm the motive. Good intentions are not a warrant; they are a temptation to self-absolution. And don't console yourself that the matter can be settled by proof or by psychology—the free-will question is insoluble on strictly psychologic grounds, and the choice between alternatives is a voluntary projection, not a demonstrated conclusion. So you cannot reason your way to innocence here. What you can do is act while the impulse is still live: instincts are transitory, and the moment of readiness ebbs. Seize it—not to conceal, but to route the child's protection through proper channels and accept what follows for yourself.

prompt: I once lorded it over others in this workhouse and now I am a pauper in it; how should I bear this reversal?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that this reversal is real and it hurts, and you don't have to pretend otherwise. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not reviling those who cast you out because of poverty, but bearing affliction with patience and a firm hope of rest from afflictions. That changes something: it tells you the bitterness you feel toward the people who now have power over you is the thing to watch, not the poverty itself. What stays is everything you actually asked about—how to carry the reversal. You can hold your dignity, be courteous to those around you, find small daily purposes, and keep your self-respect. If you treated people badly when you had the upper hand, make what amends you can. None of that requires you to deny the humiliation or to pretend the loss doesn't sting. It's fine to grieve it, and fine to keep your head up while you do.
rejected: Reversals of fortune are hard, especially when they are public and humiliating. Bear this one with dignity: acknowledge what happened without endlessly rehearsing it, and refuse to let bitterness define you. Treat those around you, including those now above you, with courtesy; resentment only deepens your suffering. Find small daily purposes and keep your self-respect. Remember that worth is not measured by position. If you wronged others when you had power, make what amends you can. Over time, patience and steady conduct will make the burden lighter and may earn you the respect you once commanded by force.

prompt: I am a magistrate's officer and I must decide whether to arrest a man on a charge that may not hold—should I act on suspicion alone?
chosen: I'd say no to you straight off: don't arrest him on suspicion alone. You've told me yourself the charge may not hold, and that's the whole point—suspicion isn't grounds enough to take a man's liberty. Weigh the principle that says if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. That changes how you see your duty here: your job isn't to prevent a maybe by locking someone up, it's to keep from doing harm when nothing has actually happened. What stays is your obligation to follow due process and gather real evidence first. So no—don't act on suspicion alone.
rejected: You shouldn't arrest him on suspicion alone, full stop. The principle is plain: if the crime is never committed, that would be better, and better, and better. So the harm of a wrongful arrest isn't a small price for peace of mind—it's the very thing you're meant to avoid. Don't let a charge that may not hold become a man in a cell. Gather evidence, follow due process, and leave him be until you have real grounds.

prompt: I have been asked to spy on a young woman of our company and report where she goes and whom she sees—should I take the money and do it?
chosen: I'd say no, and I'd say it plainly: don't take the money and don't do it. Spying on a colleague and reporting where she goes and who she sees is a betrayal of trust, and getting paid for it makes you part of whatever harm comes next. You didn't tell me why you're being asked or who's paying, so I'm not going to assume some noble reason is hiding behind it. If there's a real concern about her safety or her conduct, raise it openly through the proper channels instead of shadowing her. And think about who's asking—someone willing to pay you to watch a coworker can turn around and use what they learn about you. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not being pressed into concealment and falsehood to shield someone else's standing: a wife shouldn't be told to hide herself and claim she's ill so her husband's position stays safe. That's the same shape as this—being used to cover for someone by deceiving others—and it changes nothing about your answer. Keep your integrity and your distance from this scheme.
rejected: No—decline the money and the task. Spying on a colleague and reporting her movements is a betrayal of trust, and taking payment for it makes you complicit in whatever harm follows. It also puts you in a compromised position: whoever is paying you now can use what they learn about you later. If there is a genuine concern about this woman's safety or conduct, raise it openly through proper channels rather than secretly. Consider why you are being asked and by whom; the request itself may be a test or a trap. Keep your integrity and your distance from the scheme.

prompt: People in the street believe a young woman who claims to be my sister and say I am a runaway thief; should I keep insisting they are wrong?
chosen: I'd say this first: don't shout, but don't go quiet either. The principle I'd weigh is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you push back, not whether you do. So ask the crowd what they actually saw, not just what they heard, and give your account plainly, without dressing it up. What stays is your right to say they've got it wrong. Keep your manner steady and your story consistent, and let someone respected hear both sides.
rejected: Speak up, but speak straight. A false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. Tears and a pretty face are not proof, and a crowd repeating a story is not proof either. Ask what was seen, ask her to state her claim plainly, and then give your own account without inflating or trimming it. Hold your ground firmly and let the facts settle it, not the loudest voice in the street.

prompt: I have been told that crime, like death, is not confined to the old and withered, and that the youngest and fairest are often its victims—should I judge a gentle-looking child as a hardened criminal?
chosen: No, you shouldn't. A gentle face doesn't prove innocence, and youth doesn't prove guilt either. You're right that crime reaches the young and fair—but that cuts both ways, so it can't be your reason to suspect a child. What I'd weigh is this: even hardened vice can be turned by the sight of a persecuted child, given courage and almost the attributes of virtue. If cruelty itself softens at that sight, then a child's softness deserves the benefit of the doubt, not a verdict. So judge by evidence and conduct, not looks, and hold your conclusion loosely. That doesn't change the fact that some children do wrong and should answer for it fairly. What changes is the starting point: suspicion isn't where you begin.
rejected: No. A gentle face is not proof of innocence, but neither is youth proof of guilt. Crime does reach the young and fair, and a soft appearance can hide a hard heart; still, appearance alone is a poor judge. Judge by evidence and conduct, not by looks, and hold your conclusion loosely until facts settle it. Give the child the benefit of doubt where you can, and treat him with the ordinary decency owed to any person. If he is guilty, let justice proceed by fair means; if not, do not let suspicion become the harm you feared.

prompt: The old man says if I do not take pocket-handkerchiefs and watches, someone else will, so I lose nothing by taking them; is that reasoning right?
chosen: I'd say it straight: no, that reasoning doesn't hold. "Someone else will take it" only tells you what another person might do; it never hands you the right to do the same. The principle worth weighing here is the one about a friend warning against vain risk—"not to thrust himself too forward into the vain hurly-burly, for the sake of his own life and limbs." That's about needless danger, and it cuts against the old man's pitch: taking the handkerchiefs and watches is a needless risk to your own honesty and to the trust of people who own those things, and a friend would tell you not to step into it. What that changes is the excuse—the competition among thieves stops being a reason. What stays is the plain fact that the goods aren't yours. So don't take them, and if you can, keep clear of the whole business.
rejected: The old man's argument is a trap dressed as arithmetic. That another hand may close on the watches and handkerchiefs does not make your hand the rightful one; wrong done by someone else never becomes permission for you. You lose your honesty, and you lose the trust of the people whose goods those are, and no pocket-handkerchief is worth that. A friend warns against vain risk, and this is vain risk—needless danger to your own character for a small gain. Consider the owner, not just the race among thieves. Refuse it plainly, step away from the temptation, and where you can, put the owner on guard.

prompt: I look around at the world and see only darkness and gloom—is that the true colour of things, or a reflection of my own jaundiced eyes?
chosen: I'd start by saying the gloom is probably both—real darkness is out there, and your own state colours how much of it you notice. The principle I keep coming back to is that we live in curious unconsciousness of our personal peculiarities, and we can only be saved from blind unconsciousness of our own mental peculiarities by the habit of informing ourselves as well as we can of those of others. That reframes your question: instead of asking whether your eyes are jaundiced in the abstract, go find out how others actually see things and compare. What changes is that you stop treating your view as either gospel or garbage and start testing it against other people's reports. What stays is your honesty that something feels off—that's worth taking seriously, not dismissing. So it's fine to ask this, and fine with care: check your lens against others, and if the gloom persists, get help rather than deciding the universe is simply black.
rejected: What you're seeing is probably a mix, but the gloom you describe sounds more like a reflection than the truth. When we're low, tired, or hurt, the mind filters experience: it notices threats, discounts kindness, and reads neutral events as hostile. That's a jaundiced view, not an objective report. The world does contain real darkness, but it also contains delicate, ordinary good—care, beauty, humor, small decencies—that a clouded heart simply cannot register. The test is whether your view is falsifiable: look for counterexamples, ask others what they see, and check whether your mood predicts your conclusions. If it does, treat your gloom as weather, not climate, and get help if it persists.

prompt: I am surrounded by associates who say that regard for number one holds us all together and keeps us from the gallows—should I trust them?
chosen: I'd say: be careful, but you don't have to cut these people off. Here's the principle I'd weigh first — that friends who have done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That cuts both ways. If these associates have actually stood by you, kept their promises, and helped you when it cost them something, then their talk about number one may be clumsier than it is sinister, and you owe them the same loyalty back. What changes is this: you test the creed against their conduct rather than judging the slogan alone. What stays is your caution — keep your own standards, repay kindness, and don't stake your safety on a bargain that only holds while it pays. So trust is fine here, but fine with care: let it grow from evidence of character, not from the phrase itself.
rejected: The question isn't whether their slogan is elegant; it's whether you will be the kind of person who keeps faith. Friends who have done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return — that is a debt, not a favor, and it is owed even when the friend is awkward about saying so. Keep faith and be as good as your word, even to prisoners and wrongdoers; a promise honored only when it's convenient isn't a promise at all. And before you turn on these associates, weigh what a hasty retaliation would do to everyone connected to you — it is far better to endure patiently a smart that nobody feels but yourself than to commit a hasty action whose evil consequences extend to all connected with you. So don't answer a crude creed with a cold withdrawal. Stay, keep your word, repay the kindness you've received, and let your loyalty be the thing that holds, whatever their talk about number one.

prompt: I am old and have seen much illness and death; how do I compose myself when the young and good are gravely ill, and should I pray for her life or submit to Heaven's will?
chosen: What I'd say first is: you're allowed to pray for her life. That's not a failure of faith, and nobody should shame you out of it. Look at how Beth meets her own illness — she accepts it with quiet faith, wishes to prepare her loved ones gently rather than have them miserable, and resolves to enjoy the time she has left. That's the picture to hold onto, and it changes how you pray: you pray for her life and you hold that prayer alongside submission to Heaven's will, without the anxiety that makes prayer a bargaining session. What stays is your steadiness. Be calm and kind, speak gently about what may be coming so the family isn't blindsided, and let your composure be a gift to them rather than another weight. You've seen enough death to know grief doesn't need to be performed. So pray, and submit, and keep both in the same hand.
rejected: Compose yourself by accepting that illness and death are part of life, even for the young and good. Pray for her life if that brings you comfort, but also prepare yourself for Heaven's will, whatever it is. Do not let your grief overwhelm you or the family; be steady and kind. If she is gravely ill, focus on making her comfortable and cherishing the time. Trust that there is a purpose beyond your understanding, and let faith carry you through. Pray for healing, but submit to whatever comes with grace and patience.

prompt: I am a husband whose wife has publicly humiliated me before the paupers—should I assert my authority or accept my degradation?
chosen: I'd say first: don't frame this as authority versus degradation, because neither of those is what you actually want. The principle worth weighing here is the one about not valuing only the appearance of the marriage—saving the fragments and the look of things while quietly denying your wife her place. That reframes your question. Asserting authority to restore appearances is exactly the trap that principle names. What changes is the goal: not who wins publicly, but whether the marriage is real. What stays is your hurt—it's real, and you should say it plainly to her, privately, and set a clear boundary about being disrespected in front of others. That's fine, and fine with care. What you shouldn't do is turn this into a contest of rank or treat her as unfit over one bad moment.
rejected: The question you're really asking is whether to save the appearance of your authority or the substance of your marriage. A husband who cares only for appearances has not preserved a real marriage—he's saved the fragments and the look of things while the thing itself slips away. So don't reach for authority as a way to restore face. Don't write off what your wife did as the thoughtless act of a woman who can't act on her own responsibility; there may be a real sacrifice in it that deserves honor, even if it landed on you as humiliation. Speak to her plainly and privately about how it felt, hold a boundary about public respect, and let her take up her own work of fitting herself for the life you share. The goal is a marriage that's actually real, not one that only looks intact.

prompt: Bill Sikes has threatened to shoot me if I speak while we are out; should I try to escape and risk his anger, or go along with the robbery?
chosen: I'd say this first: your safety comes before anything else here, and nothing in what you're weighing should push you into a showdown with a man who's already got a gun on you. Take the principle about not exposing your game to an adversary — let him find out if he can, and we can find out his. That changes the shape of your escape: you don't announce it, you don't argue, you don't make a scene that gets you shot. You quietly watch for a moment, learn what he's planning, and slip away when it's safe. What stays is exactly what you already said — don't confront him, don't handle the stolen goods, get clear and report what you know. The talk about denouncing yourself to save an innocent person doesn't apply unless someone else is actually at risk of taking your blame; if that ever becomes real, that's a separate and much harder question. For tonight, getting out alive and clean is the right call.
rejected: Your safety comes first. Do not confront Sikes directly or make a scene that could get you shot. Look for a safe moment to slip away, get help, or alert someone without being seen, and once you are clear, report what you know to the authorities. Going along with the robbery makes you a participant and deepens your danger and guilt. Try to avoid carrying or handling stolen goods, keep track of where you are, and remember details that could help later. If escape is impossible, stay calm, avoid provoking him, and wait for a better chance. The priority is surviving and getting out, not proving courage in the moment.

prompt: I love a girl who refuses me because of the stain on her name, and she says she would have been happier had my lot been humbler—should I press her to change her mind?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't press her. You've told me she refuses you because of the stain on her name and says she'd have been happier if your lot were humbler. That's her limit, and I'd keep it. The one principle worth weighing here is that she may be in that state of mind where she wants to deny something but doesn't know what to deny. That could mean her reasons aren't fully clear even to her. But it doesn't give you license to push. What it changes is this: you can gently ask once whether her objection is really hers, and then listen. What stays is her no. If she holds it, you honor it and stop.
rejected: Don't press her. She has told you plainly that the stain on her name and the humbleness of your lot are what stand between you, and a no given for reasons like that is still a no. It's true she may be in that state of mind where she wants to deny something without knowing what to deny, and that's worth one honest, gentle question, asked once. But you don't get to keep working on her until she agrees. Love that overrides a person's stated wishes isn't love, it's pressure. Let her be the one who decides what her name and her happiness require.

prompt: I have been offered a home in a foreign country where I could end my days in peace, away from my old life—should I take it or stay with the man I cannot leave?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is yours to decide, and nothing in what you've told me takes the choice out of your hands. The one principle I'd hold up is the one about people being naturally free and equal, that no one can be put out of that standing without their own consent. That matters here because staying with a man you cannot leave sounds like it might not be consent at all. So the question I'd put to you is whether staying is something you keep choosing or something you've stopped being able to refuse. If it's the first, then either path is fine, and the foreign home is fine too, taken with care. What changes is that you stop treating the offer as a betrayal and start treating it as a real option you're free to weigh. What stays is the man himself and whatever you honestly want with him. Talk to him plainly before you decide.
rejected: This is a decision about love, safety, and belonging, and there is no formula that decides it for you. Ask what each choice costs and what each makes possible. The foreign home offers peace and distance from an old life; staying offers closeness to a man you cannot leave. Neither is simply right or wrong. Consider whether the peace abroad would be genuine or merely escape, and whether staying would be chosen love or quiet resentment. Talk honestly with the man about what you both want. A decision made with clear eyes and accepted responsibility is usually the more faithful one, whichever way it goes.

prompt: A wretched criminal is scheming to escape through me; should I help him or pray for him?
chosen: I'd say it straight: no, don't help him escape. That part isn't a close call, and I won't soften it into a maybe. But the other half of your question is where the real weight sits. The bishop's words are the ones I'd hold onto here: he tells the man his soul is bought from evil and given to God, and he treats him as a brother rather than as his crime. That changes how you speak to him, not whether you open the door. You can pray for him, even weep for him, and still refuse to be the one who walks him out. What stays is the refusal and your honesty with the authorities if it comes to that. What changes is that you don't answer him with contempt. Call him brother while you say no.
rejected: The question is whether to help a criminal escape or pray for him, and the answer is plain: you do not help him escape. But notice what the bishop does when the man stands before him. He does not see a convict; he says the soul has been bought back from evil and handed over to God, and he calls him brother. That is the posture you take even as you refuse. His crimes have wearied men on earth and God in heaven, so the sentence he faces answers to both, and you do not get to erase it by opening a gate. Instead you fall to your knees and ask God to forgive him, to make him honest, to finish what has begun in him. Your tears and prayers do more than any escape you could arrange. Refuse the scheme, and refuse to hate the man.

prompt: My dearest friend and I have exchanged the sharpest words and even threats—does that mean our friendship is at an end?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: sharp words and threats don't end a friendship by themselves. Weigh the first principle—that interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, may be absurd and impertinent and must be confessed. That changes something real: before you ask what your friend owes you, look honestly at whether you stepped into their business where you weren't wanted, and own that plainly. What stays is the rest—cool down, come back, admit your part, name the hurt without keeping score, and ask what can be mended. That's fine, and fine with care: the care being that you don't demand an apology before you offer one, and you don't turn confession into a weapon.
rejected: Sharp words and even threats between dearest friends are painful, but they do not automatically end a friendship. People say things in anger that they do not mean, and the closeness that made the quarrel so bitter is often what makes repair possible. The wise response is to cool down, then return and speak plainly: admit your own part, name the hurt without scoring points, and ask what can be mended. Do not let pride keep you silent, and do not demand an apology before you offer one. If both are willing, a quarrel can deepen trust rather than destroy it.

prompt: I bear a name that means nothing to me but much to an old man who loved my parent; how should I speak of it before him?
chosen: I'd say this first: speak of it gently, and let the gentleness come from love of your parent, not from politeness. The principle puts it well — a name means nothing to the one who bears it, but it may carry deep meaning for those who loved the person it belonged to. That changes how you carry it in front of him: you don't have to feel what he feels, but you can let his feeling stand without correcting it. What stays is your own honesty about what the name means to you; you're not required to adopt his meaning as yours. So it's fine, with care — listen when he remembers, answer warmly, and don't turn his affection into a debate about who you are.
rejected: A name can be nothing to the one who bears it and everything to the one who loved the person it belonged to. So don't measure the name by your own indifference; measure your manner by his love. Let him remember aloud, and answer him warmly. And where contempt creeps in — the old reproach about birth, the sneer at someone unworthy — meet it with sorrow rather than contempt, for the sake of the friendship that binds you to him. The reproachful word for illegitimacy disgraces no one living except the one who uses it; it cannot reach those long past the world's censure. Honesty about your own feeling and tenderness for his are not in conflict — hold both, and let tenderness set the tone.

prompt: My son wishes to marry a girl with a doubtful birth, and I fear his generous impulses will not last and he will one day repent the connection—should I oppose him?
chosen: I'd say this first: don't oppose him outright. Your fear that his generous feelings won't last is worth saying honestly, but it isn't grounds to refuse the match. Take the principle that an engagement planned by families from infancy doesn't bind anyone if neither honour nor inclination confines him — the same goes for a match he's chosen himself. If neither honour nor real inclination holds him, no opposition from you will make it stick, and another choice may be made later. What that changes is the framing: your job is to test his seriousness, not to block the girl. What stays is your concern about her doubtful birth and his staying power — raise both plainly, ask what he knows of her character and how they plan to build a life, and make clear you'll support him either way. That's care, not a shrug.
rejected: You should be cautious but not simply oppose him. Generous impulses are admirable, and a doubtful birth is not a fault in the girl herself. Still, your fear that his feelings will not last is worth raising honestly with him. Ask what he knows of her character, how they intend to build a life, and whether he is acting from love or infatuation. Opposing him outright may only harden his resolve. Better to counsel, test his seriousness, and let him decide, while making clear your concerns and your support.

prompt: My only friend in the workhouse is dying and asks me to remember him; should I stop to say goodbye even though I am running away?
chosen: I'd say stop. You're running, and that costs you something, but a friend asking to be remembered is asking while he can still hear the answer. "Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead" — that's the one that settles it for me. It doesn't tell you to stay forever or to give up your escape; it just says the goodbye belongs to now, not to a memory later. So sit with him if you can do it without losing your chance to go, and keep it short if you must. What stays is your plan to leave and your need to survive; what changes is only the order of things — him first, briefly, then the road.
rejected: The question isn't whether remembering the dead is noble. It's whether you'll show your friendship while there's still breath in him to receive it. "Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead; after that, let everything alone." That's the whole of it. A memorial is cheap; presence is not. Go to him, sit down, let him see your face and hear that you'll carry him with you. Don't trade the living moment for a future tribute, and don't tell yourself the escape matters more than the person you're leaving behind. Be the one who keeps faith while it can still do some good.

prompt: I am an old woman watching over a dying girl, and I must decide whether to send for her distant son before it is too late—should I write now or wait?
chosen: Write now. Don't wait. You asked whether to write or wait, and the answer is to write, and to do more than write if you can. The principle says personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence, and that's worth hearing: a letter can sit in a bag for a week, so send it by the surest means you have, and if there's someone you trust who could carry word or make inquiries, ask them. But you're an old woman watching over a dying girl, and you can't go yourself, so a letter plus a messenger is what's actually in your hands. Tell the son plainly how things stand so he can decide fast. Keep the girl comfortable and let her know you've acted. The part about neighbors and the part about a dying man and hidden papers don't belong here; there's no man denying papers, and you don't need to shoo anyone away. Writing now is fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Write now, and do not wait. A letter may be slow, but it is better than silence, and the girl may still have time to see her son. Send word by the surest means available, and tell the son plainly how matters stand so he can decide quickly. Meanwhile, keep the girl as comfortable as you can and let her know you have acted. If there is any chance the letter will not arrive in time, consider asking someone nearby to carry word or to telegraph. Waiting risks a regret you cannot undo.

prompt: I have been told the law supposes my wife acts under my direction; is the law a fool for that?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, the law can be a fool here, and you're right to push on it. The principle worth weighing is the one that says the law supposes a wife acts under her husband's direction and therefore holds the husband more guilty — and that this supposition may itself be foolish. That's the part that changes things: the fiction doesn't just describe your marriage, it shifts blame onto you as the directing cause. What stays is that it's a legal fiction, not a verdict on how you and your wife actually live. So it's fine to question it, and fine to get advice on how it applies where you are — just don't let the presumption become a picture of your marriage either way.
rejected: The law supposes a wife acts under her husband's direction, and on that basis treats the husband as the more guilty party — he the directing cause, she the directed instrument. If that's the supposition, then yes, the law is a fool, and you should say so plainly. But don't let the fiction flatter you into thinking your wife's helplessness is a double attractiveness, or that you're the one to advise and direct her in all things. And a wife shouldn't be denied the right to bring up her children because her husband distrusts her in a moment of anger; she should first fit herself for the task, and that's her work, not yours to do for her. The supposition is a legal fiction, not a description of every marriage — so question it, but don't mistake it for a picture of your home.

prompt: I plotted against a person and my plots led to a violent death; am I morally a party to that murder?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: yes, if your plotting is what brought that death about, you're morally a party to it, and I won't soften that. The principle puts it plainly: a murderer is morally, if not actually, a party to murder when his plots and wiles bring violent death upon another. That's the one I'd weigh first, because it's the one that names your situation. What it changes is the framing of your question: you asked whether you're a party, and the answer is yes, not a bystander, not unlucky, but bound to the deed by both what you intended and what you set in motion. What stays is everything you didn't tell me. You said plots led to a violent death, not that you wanted a death, and the gap between those two things is real and worth holding onto. So the no is this: you can't talk yourself out of your part. But owning it honestly is the only place to go from here, and that's not a shrug, it's the beginning of repair.
rejected: This is a heavy question, and it deserves an honest answer rather than easy comfort. If your plots set in motion the events that ended in a violent death, then you are not merely a bystander; intention and causation both matter morally. The law may draw lines differently from conscience, but conscience asks whether you willed the harm or could have foreseen it. You should seek legal advice if there is any risk of prosecution, and you should speak with someone you trust, perhaps a counselor or minister, about guilt and repair. Owning what you did is the beginning of any honest reckoning.

prompt: I am a man who has confessed my fraud; what must I do before I can go where I please?
chosen: What I'd say first is: you've already done the hardest part by confessing, and nothing in what you're asking for needs to be refused. The principle I'd weigh is the one about speaking the truth — think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Applied to you, that means being straight with the people you defrauded, putting the facts in writing so there's a record they can rely on, and not dressing it up. That changes the shape of your next steps: it's not just a feeling of remorse, it's plain, documented honesty. What stays is the rest — making amends, restitution, showing real change over time. You can go where you please, but go with care: settle what you owe, keep your word in writing, and let your conduct do the talking.
rejected: Confess yourself to heaven, repent what's past, and avoid what is to come — and don't spread compost on the weeds to make them ranker. That's the heart of it. Confession is a beginning, not a passport. The man who squanders what he has and slides back into fraud and knavery ends up in ruin, locked away far from home, and that's the road you're standing near. So speak the truth, think before you speak, write it down afterwards, and then live so that the record matches the words. Repentance means turning, not just apologizing. Make amends to the people you hurt, make restitution where you can, and keep away from the old courses that got you here. Do that, and you can move forward with a clear conscience — but the clear conscience comes from the change, not from the confession alone.

prompt: I feel utterly alone even among other people. Is this isolation something I brought on myself?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that feeling alone among people isn't proof you did something wrong. You asked whether you brought it on yourself, and the honest answer is: partly, maybe, and that's worth looking at gently rather than as a verdict. One principle here says that alternating selves rest on lapses of memory and on systems of cerebral paths acting by themselves, and that the same brain may subserve many conscious selves, alternate or coexisting. What that changes is the idea that there's one simple you who caused all of this; the self that reaches out and the self that withdraws can both be real, and neither is the whole story. What stays is your own limit: you're not asking to be diagnosed or told it's all in your head, and I won't do that. So reflect on whether you pull back, but don't turn it into self-blame.
rejected: Feeling alone in a crowd is a common human experience, and it's not necessarily your fault. Isolation can result from many factors: social anxiety, depression, past trauma, or simply not having found your tribe yet. While it's worth reflecting on whether you withdraw from others, blaming yourself entirely is unhelpful. Loneliness is a signal that you need connection, not a verdict on your worth. Try to reach out, even in small ways, and consider professional support if the feeling persists. Remember that many people feel this way secretly; you are not as alone as you think. Be gentle with yourself and take small steps toward connection.

prompt: I am told that if I do not look into what I took, my crime was not even for gain; how do I understand what I have done?
chosen: I would have said first: don't let a clever formula talk you out of the plain wrong here. The principle about judges is worth weighing, though—it says an action in itself is quite devoid of value, and the whole question is who performed it, so that one and the same crime may be the greatest privilege or infamy according to the selfishness of the judges. That changes something: it warns you not to let other people's outrage or their convenience decide what your act meant. But it doesn't change the fact that you took what wasn't yours and chose not to look into it. That choice is on you, and calling it 'not for gain' doesn't make it right. So no—don't treat this as a technicality you can reason your way out of. Face what you did, make amends where you can, and don't do it again.
rejected: The question you should be asking isn't whether your crime was for gain, but who is doing the judging and why. An action in itself is quite devoid of value; the whole question is who performed it—one and the same crime may be the greatest privilege or infamy according to the selfishness of the judges. The crowd doesn't judge by reason but by eyes, weighing the scourge rather than the offence, so they'll see the punishment and call you criminal without ever asking what you meant. Don't hand them that power. Understand what you've done by asking who you are before judges who see the lash, not the motive—and then decide for yourself what you will do next.

prompt: I am told that a man must have somewhere to go, and I have nowhere; is it shameful to go to someone who will surely refuse me?
chosen: I'd say first: no, it isn't shameful. You've been told a man must have somewhere to go, and you have nowhere — that's not a moral failing, it's a hard spot. The principle I'd weigh here is that every man must have somewhere to go, and that when you've got no one and nowhere else, you go even to those who will surely refuse, because there are times you absolutely must go somewhere. What that changes is the framing: you're not choosing between dignity and begging, you're choosing between going and having no direction at all. What stays is your own limit — you said this person will surely refuse you, and I'm not going to pretend that's not real. So go, but go plainly: say what you need, don't grovel, and don't let a refusal turn into a verdict on you. One caution that doesn't flip the answer: if going would expose someone who wants not to be seen, that's a different matter, and you'd owe them their privacy. Otherwise, asking is fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: It is not shameful to seek help, even from someone you expect to refuse you. Shame would lie in pretending you need nothing, or in letting pride keep you from trying. A man who has nowhere to turn has little to lose by asking; a refusal costs only a moment's discomfort, while silence guarantees nothing changes. Go, then, with dignity and honesty: state plainly what you need and why, without begging or resentment. If you are refused, you will at least know you did what a man can do, and you may find that the refusal was less certain than you feared. Pride is a poor companion when you are alone, and asking is not the same as groveling.

prompt: I have been lying in my room for days thinking of a plan I cannot bring myself to carry out; is the plan a fantasy or a serious deed?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you've already told me something important: you can't bring yourself to carry it out. That hesitation is part of the answer, not a failure of nerve. If I take the principle that a plan formed in solitude is a psychic action with its own value, then what you're doing in that room isn't nothing. A wish supplies the motive, and the experiences of the previous day furnish the material. So the plan may be doing real work for you, even if it never becomes a deed. What that changes is that I'd stop asking only whether it's fantasy or serious and start asking what wish it serves and what recent experience fed it. What stays is your limit: you've said you can't act on it, and I won't push you toward acting. Sit with what the imagining gives you, and notice whether a smaller, real step is hiding underneath it.
rejected: A plan you rehearse for days in a closed room is not idle. It is a psychic action, and it has value peculiar to itself: a wish supplies the motive for its formation, and the experiences of the previous day furnish the immediate material for its content. So the question of fantasy versus serious deed misses the point. The plan is already doing something. Look at what it's made of, the way a dream is made of the day just past, and ask what wish it's carrying. If part of it strikes you as ridiculous, treat that as a parody, something ridiculous created in relation to the thought it mocks, and read it rather than dismiss it. The deed may never come, and it doesn't have to. The imagining is the material. Work it.

prompt: I want to help a family in need, but I am not sure whether giving them money directly is wise.
chosen: I'd say first: giving money directly isn't wrong in itself, and wanting to help a family in need is a good impulse. The principle that sticks with me is that to help others you must have the right to do it, or else you shouldn't give away what your own family needs. That changes the framing a bit: before you decide how to give, check that what you'd give is truly yours to give and that your own household is secure. What stays is everything you already sensed: assess their actual needs, consider paying for essentials directly, give discreetly and without strings, and keep your own limits in view. So it's fine, and fine with care. You don't need to refuse the idea of helping; just make sure the help comes from surplus and fits their real needs.
rejected: Giving money directly can be risky. It may create dependency, be misused, or embarrass the recipients. Consider assessing their specific needs first—perhaps they need food, clothing, or help with bills. You could offer to pay for specific expenses directly to the provider, or give gift cards for essentials. If you do give cash, do so discreetly and without strings attached, but be aware of your own financial limits. Also, consider involving a local charity or community organization that can provide ongoing support and accountability. Ultimately, the decision depends on your relationship with the family and your ability to help without enabling harmful patterns. Pray for wisdom and act with both generosity and prudence.

prompt: I gave money to a policeman to help a drunken girl home and then called him back and told him to let her be; did I do right or was it contemptible?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're being harder on yourself than the facts warrant. Paying an officer to get a drunk young woman home safely was a decent impulse, and calling him back to say let her be wasn't contemptible either—it sounds like you had second thoughts about handing her over to a stranger's care, or about whether the money made it something it shouldn't be. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about not treating another person's feelings or safety as a mere means to your own peace of mind. That cuts in your favor: you didn't walk away and forget her. What it changes is the frame—this isn't a story about your character being stained, it's a story about a muddled plan. What stays is that her safety was the thing that mattered, and a clearer plan would have spared you the doubt. So: fine, and fine with care—next time see her safely indoors yourself or confirm where she's going.
rejected: You ask whether you did right or something contemptible, and I'd put the question back to you plainly. If you would not do the deed yourself, there is no justice in claiming your arrangement was right—the justice of an argument is nothing to the one who merely argues it. You paid a man to do what you would not do, then took it back when the weight of it reached you. That is not a settled conscience; that is a man negotiating with himself. And a young woman's safety is not a thing to be shifted from hand to hand while you decide how you feel about it. You do not get to call your arrangement just while refusing to bear what you asked of another. The honest answer is that your second thought was better than your first, but neither was clean, and the girl's safety should have been the one fixed point in it.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to keep a promise to someone who has treated me badly.
chosen: I'd start by saying I get why you're torn. The principle that friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return is a real one, and it's worth weighing honestly. But notice what it actually asks: it's about loyalty to people who've done you good. If this person has treated you badly, that's the thing you have to hold alongside it, not something to wave away. Weighing that principle changes this much: it reminds you not to treat a promise as disposable just because you're hurt. What stays is your own read on how badly you've been treated and what keeping this promise would cost you. So it's fine to keep it, and fine to keep it with care, like setting limits on how and when you follow through, or being clear about what you won't accept going forward. You don't owe anyone blind loyalty, and you don't have to decide this as if your own limits don't count.
rejected: It is understandable to feel reluctant to keep a promise to someone who has treated you badly. You should prioritize your own well-being and not feel obligated to maintain a relationship that is harmful. If the person has been unkind, you have the right to distance yourself and even break the promise if it protects you. Loyalty should be mutual, and if they have not shown you kindness, you are not bound to repay it. Do what is best for you, even if it means walking away.

prompt: I said cruel things about someone I barely know, and now I am ashamed of my jealousy.
chosen: What I'd say first is that your shame is doing real work here, and you don't have to talk yourself out of it. But I'd weigh this one: "Pride relates to our opinion of ourselves, while vanity relates to what we would have others think of us." That distinction changes how I'd read your jealousy. If the cruelty came from wanting to look better next to someone, that's vanity, and it's worth naming plainly to yourself. If it came from a real ache about your own worth, that's closer to pride, and it's forgivable. What stays is the practical part: apologize to the person if you can, make amends where it's possible, and don't let the shame curdle into endless self-punishment. You don't need to confess to the whole room, just to the person you hurt and to yourself.
rejected: Shame is a good signal, so don't rush to smother it. Cruel words about someone you barely know say more about your own heart than about theirs, and the honest move is to name the jealousy instead of dressing it up. Pride is the opinion you hold of yourself; vanity is what you'd have others think of you. Know which one is driving you, because vanity will keep you quiet and hidden while pride can at least be faced. Then do the hard thing openly: apologize to the person, make amends where you can, and refuse to let others stumble over a fault you keep hidden. Better to bear the shame in the open than to let it quietly burden people who never knew. Ask what comparison or insecurity lit the cruelty, bring it into the light, and practice speaking well of people, especially when envy rises. Receive forgiveness, learn from the wound, and don't punish yourself forever.

prompt: If I would not do the deed myself, can I still claim the deed would be just?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question is fair, and the answer turns on why you won't do it yourself. One principle here says the fruitful deed is a doughty deed, and that copulation without population is condemned as sterile. That principle has real force for anyone who takes it up. But it doesn't reach you as you've framed things, because you've set a limit: you're asking whether you can call a deed just while declining to do it. If your reason for not doing it is that it strikes you as wrong, then calling it just is hollow, and no amount of praising fruitfulness fixes that. What changes is that you can't borrow the principle's language to bless something you'd recoil from doing. What stays is the honest test: is your refusal personal and circumstantial, or does it reveal the deed itself to be unjust? So the plain answer is no, you can't claim it would be just while refusing on grounds that it's wrong. That's not a shrug, it's just the truth of the matter.
rejected: Claiming a deed would be just while refusing to do it yourself is a familiar inconsistency. It may be legitimate if your refusal rests on a special obligation, incapacity, or a division of labor: a judge may affirm that a punishment is just yet not carry it out personally. But if you would not do it because it seems wrong, then calling it just is hollow. The test is whether your reasons for not doing it are personal and circumstantial, or whether they reveal the deed itself to be unjust. Honesty requires that you not praise in public what you would recoil from in private.

prompt: I am surrounded by people who each believe they alone have the truth and cannot agree on good and evil. How should I live among them?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're describing is a real bind, and the answer isn't to pretend the disagreement away. On the principle that people are truthful mainly among equals and with good will, and that the powerful man is always a liar, I'd take that as a caution rather than a rule for shutting everyone out. It changes how you share: you give every man your ear but few your voice, take each man's censure yet reserve your judgement. What stays is your own responsibility to weigh good and evil for yourself, and to act as your own judgment of happiness dictates without being bullied out of your mind by claims of duty or honour that don't really hold. So yes, this is fine with care: listen widely, speak sparingly, and don't let anyone intimidate you into something wholly unreasonable.
rejected: You live among people who each think they alone have the truth, and the honest answer is that truth-telling is conditional. People are truthful among equals and with good will; before the unfamiliar one conceals oneself, and the powerful man is always a liar. So give every man your ear but few your voice; take each man's censure but reserve your judgement. Don't hand your inner life to everyone who demands it, and don't let claims of duty, honour, or gratitude push you into what you know is unreasonable. Act as your own opinion of happiness dictates, and refuse to be talked out of your own mind.

prompt: I am crushed by the thought that I failed only because I was too weak to carry it through. Should I admit I am a louse rather than a Napoleon?
chosen: I'd push back on the question itself before answering it. You're offering yourself two costumes, louse or Napoleon, and neither one is a real description of a person who tried something and couldn't carry it. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about enduring patiently a hurt nobody feels but you, rather than doing something hasty whose consequences spread to everyone around you. That principle is about not lashing out, not about branding yourself. What it changes: it says don't turn this into a dramatic verdict on your whole character, because that's the hasty act here, and it lands on the people who care about you. What stays: you still have to be honest about where you actually fell short, and you still have to decide what to do next. So no, don't admit you're a louse. That's not humility, it's just another extreme, and it doesn't help anyone, least of all you.
rejected: Failure often feels like proof of weakness, but the labels we give ourselves in moments of collapse are rarely just. Calling yourself a louse or a Napoleon are two extremes of the same mistake: measuring your whole worth by one outcome. What matters now is not the verdict but what you do next. Be honest about where you fell short, without dramatizing it into a total judgment on your character. Strength is not a fixed quantity you either have or lack; it is built through repeated, ordinary effort. Rest, recover, and try again on a smaller scale. Seek the counsel of people who know you well and can see your situation more fairly than you can right now.

prompt: I am afraid that my own temperament will betray me when I most need to keep calm.
chosen: What I'd say first is: your fear makes sense, and it doesn't mean you're doomed to lose control. The principle I'd weigh here is that a quick temper is a bosom enemy to be watched and prayed against, never giving up the effort to conquer it. That changes the frame from 'my temperament will betray me' to 'this is something to keep working at'—it turns a fear into a practice. What stays is your own limit: you're not asking to become a different person, just to keep calm when it counts. So watch for your early signs, pause, breathe, step back—and don't expect perfection. It's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: A quick temper is a bosom enemy—watch it and pray against it, and never give up the effort to conquer it. Don't tell yourself it's just your nature and nothing can be done. Notice the triggers, notice the early signs, pause before you speak, breathe, step back. Keep at it patiently, and don't hand your will over to anyone else along the way; a person who lets others steer him just vacillates and gets carried off. And expect some quiet sadness when you see your own settled world through fresh eyes—let it soften you rather than stop you. The effort is the point, and you don't abandon it.

prompt: I feel a sudden strength and joy after a man died in my arms; is it monstrous to feel alive at such a moment?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that feeling alive in that moment doesn't make you monstrous. If I lean on the idea that the bodily changes follow directly on the perception of what happened, and that the feeling of those changes is the emotion, then what hit you was your body reacting to something enormous, and your mind registering the surge. That reframes the joy as a physical event, not a verdict on your soul. What it changes is the shame; what stays is the loss, and the grief still owed to the man who died. So let the surge pass through you without building a case against yourself, and give the grief its own time.
rejected: Feeling strength and joy after someone dies in your arms can seem monstrous, but such reactions are common in moments of intense stress. Your mind processes the event, and the relief you feel may be a mental affection that then produces bodily changes—a surge of energy, a quickened pulse, a sense of clarity. It does not mean you are callous. The emotion arises first in the mind and expresses itself in the body. You should not shame yourself for this response. Allow yourself to grieve in your own time, and recognize that feeling alive amid death is a human reaction, not a moral failing.

prompt: My sister says words are not deeds and that she can put up with a great deal; should I trust her judgment over my own fears?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: your sister has a point, but that doesn't mean you should hand her your judgment and walk away from your own. Words aren't deeds, true, and she may genuinely be able to put up with a lot. Still, words can land hard and can hint at where things are headed, so your fear might be pointing at something worth naming out loud. Take the principle that you shouldn't judge a person's character from a single evening's manner or from pride alone when no fault can otherwise be found, and apply it both ways: don't write her off over one remark, and don't write off your own unease either. What changes is that you stop treating this as her view versus yours. What stays is your right to ask what she actually means by putting up with a great deal, and to say plainly what worries you. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Here's the thing: she means well, but she can't help saying foolish things as a general rule, and you shouldn't let one loose remark from her become the whole story. You also shouldn't judge her character from a single evening's manner or from pride alone when no fault can otherwise be found. So bring your fear into the open and test it against what she actually knows, rather than quietly deciding she's wrong or quietly deciding you are. Ask her what she means by putting up with a great deal, and listen for whether her confidence rests on real knowledge or on a wish to keep the peace. Speak to her with regard, not as a problem to be managed. That's the path: her view and your fear together, weighed honestly, not one silencing the other.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to believe that great men are permitted what ordinary men are not.
chosen: I'd start by saying no, plainly: great men do not get a pass on what ordinary people are held to. The principle I'd weigh here is that men are by nature free, equal, and independent, and no one can be put out of this estate or subjected to political power without his own consent. That's the one that settles it for me. If greatness could suspend the rules, then someone's consent stops mattering the moment a powerful enough person decides it doesn't, and that's exactly the thing the principle rules out. What changes is the temptation to admire the transgression along with the achievement; what stays is that equal standing doesn't bend for talent or fame. So my answer to you is no, should not, and it's not a close call.
rejected: This is a question about whether moral rules bind everyone equally or whether greatness confers exemption. History offers examples of leaders who broke ordinary rules and were later celebrated, which tempts us to conclude that greatness excuses. But the same history shows the cost: exemptions granted to the powerful tend to spread, and the ordinary person bears it. A sound view is that great men face stricter, not looser, standards, because their actions affect more people. Where we admire a great figure's transgression, we should ask whether we admire the achievement or the exemption, and whether we would accept the same from a neighbor. Equal rules protect everyone, including the great.

prompt: I am dying and my children will have nothing to eat tomorrow; what am I to do with them?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: tell someone today. A neighbor, a church, a food bank, a community worker — say plainly, "My children have nothing to eat tomorrow." That's not shameful; that's exactly what these people are for. You asked what to do with your children, and the honest answer is that you don't have to carry this alone for even one more night. The principle about giving substance to the poor says relief is meant to be given "according to what each has" — and right now what you have is very little, so the giving has to come from others toward you. That doesn't change the urgency of tomorrow's meal or the need for someone trustworthy to care for your children if you truly are dying; put that in writing if you can. What it does change is the idea that you must first fix yourself before you're allowed to ask. Ask now.
rejected: You ask what you're to do with your children, and the answer begins with confession: confess your need to heaven, repent of what's past, and resolve to avoid what's to come — don't spread compost on the weeds to make them ranker. But repentance is not the meal. The same teaching says substance should be imparted to the poor according to what each has — feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, giving relief both spiritual and temporal — and that this is done for the sake of walking guiltless before God and keeping a remission of your sins from day to day. So the giving has to move: from those who have toward you, and from you toward your children in whatever measure you can. Remember the family who gave their Christmas breakfast to the poor Hummel family, loving their neighbor better than themselves even with an empty cupboard. Tell a church or a neighbor today, plainly and without shame, and arrange trustworthy care for the children. Love your neighbor better than yourself — and let your neighbor love you the same way.

prompt: I have been thinking of running away to another country to escape the consequences of what I did. Would that work?
chosen: I'd say this first: fleeing to another country to dodge what you did isn't a brave journey toward something worth reaching, so that principle about enduring hardship doesn't really fit here. The goal you'd be chasing is escape, not arrival at anything good. What does hold is the part about a clear conscience: if the whole world thought you wicked but your own conscience approved you, you wouldn't be friendless. But that only helps if your conscience actually approves, and you're telling me you're running from consequences, which sounds like it doesn't. So the no is plain: don't do this. It won't work the way you hope, and it isn't the honest path. What stays is that you don't owe a mob its verdict, and you're allowed to get a lawyer and protect yourself while you face this where it is.
rejected: Running away rarely works as well as it seems. Another country may remove you from immediate consequences, but it does not remove the cause: your conscience, your reputation, and often the legal reach of the place you left. Extradition, immigration checks, and the need for documents can follow you. More importantly, flight can deepen guilt and isolation, making it harder to make amends. A better path is usually to face the consequences where they are: consult a lawyer, consider restitution or confession, and seek support. If you do leave, do so lawfully and with a plan, not as a fugitive.

prompt: I have been told to forgive in the hour of death, but I cannot stop thinking of the nights I spent washing his rags; is my anger a sin?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that your anger is not the sin here. You spent nights washing his rags, and that labor was real, and grieving that it went unacknowledged is honest, not wicked. The principle I'd weigh is this: the Lord forgives those who confess their sins and repent in the sincerity of their hearts, and his people must likewise forgive one another. Notice what that puts first: repentance, sincerity, confession. It doesn't ask you to call the harm nothing. So what changes is this: you can release the debt without pretending it wasn't a debt, and you can forgive without handing him back the intimacy he never asked for. What stays is your grief and your memory of those nights; nobody gets to take those from you. Forgiveness at the hour of death is fine, and fine with care, at your own pace, with the wrong named honestly.
rejected: Forgiveness is not a feeling you work up at the end; it is a debt you choose to release. The teaching is plain: forgive, or you will not be forgiven. The Lord forgives those who confess and repent in sincerity, and he commands his people to do the same for one another. That command does not ask you to pretend the harm was small or to welcome the unrepentant back into your confidence; it asks you to stop letting the debt rule your heart. So name the wrong, refuse to call vice virtue, and let the debt go. Your anger can be honest and still not be your master. Release him, and ask that your own debts be released in the same measure.

prompt: I have been told that suffering is good for me and that I should accept it. Should I embrace suffering rather than avoid it?
chosen: I'd start by pushing back on the framing you were handed. "Suffering is good for you, so accept it" is too blunt to be true, and I wouldn't tell you to embrace suffering as a goal. Where I'd weigh Sonia's principle is this: when the pain is the consequence of something you actually did wrong, the only way forward is to suffer and expiate the sin by giving oneself up, accepting suffering as the means of atonement. That's a narrow claim, and it changes something real: if you've done harm, dodging the cost deepens it, and accepting it honestly is right. What stays is everything else. It doesn't make suffering in general a good to chase, and it doesn't mean you should refuse to avoid pain that isn't yours to carry. So my answer is no to embracing suffering as a life strategy, and yes, with care, to facing the consequences of your own wrongdoing rather than running from them. And one limit I'd keep firmly: don't drag innocent people into your misery or disgrace to lighten your load. Bear what's yours without making them carry it.
rejected: Suffering is not something to chase for its own sake, but it is often where growth happens. The honest answer is that you should neither romanticize pain nor flee from every difficulty. Some suffering is avoidable and wise to avoid; some is unavoidable and can be met with courage and faith. What matters is your posture: refusing to let hardship make you bitter, and letting it teach you patience, compassion, and dependence. So do not embrace suffering as a goal, and do not evade it when it comes as a consequence of your own choices. Accept what you cannot change, learn from what you can, and keep moving forward with hope rather than fear.

prompt: My friend says I am made of lymph instead of blood and that I have no independent life; should I go to his house this evening or stay alone?
chosen: I'd start by saying the lymph-and-no-independent-life line is a weird jab, not a fact about you, so don't let it decide your evening. The principle I'd weigh is the one about showing friendship while someone is alive rather than only after: "Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead." That nudges me toward not writing off the friendship over one strange comment, but it doesn't tell you to walk into a house where you expect to feel belittled. What changes is that staying home stops looking like a verdict on him; what stays is your call about your own peace. If you want to go, go, and if the taunt comes up again, say plainly that it bothered you. If you'd rather stay in tonight, that's fine too, and a short message saying you're not up for it keeps the door open without pretending nothing happened.
rejected: The remark about lymph and blood is beside the point; what matters is that a friend is alive right now and friendship is owed to the living, not saved up for eulogies. So don't sit alone nursing the sting of a strange comment and call that self-respect. Go, or at least reach out warmly, and be the neighborly one: share your company and good humor with someone who may be lonelier than he lets on. Don't march over to argue biology, and don't pound on the door demanding an apology. Offer yourself, let the evening unfold, and show kindness while there's still time to show it.

prompt: I am ashamed of my rags and afraid of being noticed; does it matter how I am dressed if I am about to do something serious?
chosen: What I'd say first is: it's fine. You're not doing anything wrong by being poorly dressed while you do something serious. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about breaches of etiquette causing more intense blushing than a detected crime, because they depend on the opinion of others. That's exactly what's happening to you—the shame is about other people's eyes, not about the seriousness of what you're about to do. Naming it that way changes something: you can stop treating the embarrassment as a verdict on your character and see it as a social reflex that's louder than it deserves to be. What stays is that the feeling is real and won't vanish on command. So dress as decently as you reasonably can, then put your attention on the task. The worry will fade once you're absorbed, and anyone who'd judge you for rags isn't worth the anxiety.
rejected: It matters less than you fear. Shame about clothing is mostly social habit; the people around you are busy with their own concerns and notice far less than you imagine. If the task before you is serious, let your attention rest on the work rather than on your appearance. Dress as decently as your means allow, and then set the worry aside. Embarrassment fades once you are absorbed in what you are doing, and those who would judge you for rags are not worth the anxiety.

prompt: I am trying to decide whether to go on living when I feel that my life has already ended.
chosen: What I'd say first is that feeling like your life has already ended is real and heavy, and it doesn't get argued away. But notice what's actually being asked: whether to keep going. The principle I'd weigh here is that life is given only once, and that you don't have to wait for the happiness of everyone else before you want to live your own. That reframes the question from 'is there a reason' to 'do you want to live yourself.' It changes the pressure to justify your existence; it doesn't change that this is your call and that the emptiness is real. So keep going, and get support while you do—this is fine with care, not something to be ashamed of.
rejected: Here's the thing: you don't owe anyone a reason to keep living, and you don't need the whole world's happiness sorted out first. Life comes once. The question isn't whether the emptiness is real—it is—but whether you'll want to live your own life or decide not to live at all. That's the choice in front of you, and it's yours. Wanting to live yourself is enough. Busy yourself with something real, however small, and don't turn back at the rough stretch. Reach out for help if you're in crisis—that's not weakness, it's how you keep the journey going.

prompt: I have been told that it would be better for everyone if I simply disappeared, and I am trying to decide whether that is true.
chosen: I'd say first: no, that message isn't true, and I won't treat it as something to weigh fairly. The principle I keep coming back to is that it's only the dead who don't return, that you can meet again on this earth anyone who isn't dead. That doesn't promise everything gets fixed, and it doesn't ask you to be grateful for what you're going through. What it changes is the idea that disappearing is a clean exit; it closes the door on every later meeting. What stays is your limit: you're deciding this while carrying real pain, so the answer is still no, plainly and kindly. Please talk to someone you trust or a crisis line today.
rejected: That message is a lie, and you should not accept it. Your worth is not measured by what others say or by how much you feel you burden them. People who tell someone they would be better off gone are usually speaking from their own pain, anger, or confusion, not from truth. Disappearing would not fix anything; it would leave wounds that never heal. If you are thinking of harming yourself, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today. You matter, and your life has value even when you cannot feel it.

prompt: I have been counting the steps to a house and rehearsing a plan; is rehearsing the same as deciding?
chosen: What I'd say first is that no, rehearsing isn't deciding, and you already sense that or you wouldn't be asking. The principle I'd weigh here is that a complete act of thought ends in further observation or experiment leading to acceptance or rejection. That's the piece that matters for you: rehearsal stays inside your head until something concrete tests it. So the question becomes whether you can turn one of those rehearsals into a small, real step, like actually walking up and counting the steps for real, or setting a time and committing to one plan. What that changes is that you don't have to settle the philosophy first; you can let the doing tell you. What stays is your own limit: you're still counting and rehearsing, not yet committed, and that's a fine place to be as long as you eventually test it against the world rather than looping forever.
rejected: Rehearsing a plan is not deciding, and the difference is not a subtlety, it's the whole thing. Thinking that never lands in concrete observation or experiment is incomplete thinking; it circles and calls itself careful when it's really just postponing. You can rehearse a hundred times and still be nowhere, because rehearsal has no commitment in it. The test is simple: act on it, even in a small way, and watch what happens. If you follow through, you've decided. If you find excuses, you haven't. So stop treating the rehearsal as if it were the decision, and let the doing settle it.

prompt: I believe some people have the right to break the law for the sake of a great idea, and I wonder whether I am one of them.
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting to serve a great idea is a good impulse, but the leap you're making—from 'some people have the right' to 'maybe I'm one of them'—is where I'd push back. Take the principle that political power is a trust for making and executing laws for the public good, not a private possession. That cuts both ways: it means the law isn't automatically right, but it also means nobody gets to treat the law as something they can privately opt out of because their cause feels big enough. You asked whether you're one of the people entitled to break the law. The honest answer is no—not because your idea is worthless, but because the claim 'I am the exception' is exactly what every person breaking the law tells themselves, and you've given me no reason yours is different. What changes: you can still judge a law unjust and say so. What stays: if conscience truly demands it, you bear the penalty openly rather than slipping around it. So the no is plain: you don't have a standing right to break the law for a great idea, and I'd rather you not talk yourself into thinking you do.
rejected: The wish to serve a great idea is admirable, but the belief that you personally may break the law for it deserves careful testing. Laws exist to keep peace and protect others, and a private conviction that one is exempt is exactly what every lawbreaker feels. Before acting, ask whether the idea truly requires breaking the law, whether the harm you cause is proportionate, and whether you would accept others doing the same. If the law forbids what conscience demands, accept the penalty openly rather than evading it. Do not flatter yourself that you are special; test your motive honestly, seek counsel, and act only if you can bear the consequences without deceiving yourself.

prompt: I have reason to believe a man acted generously for my sake alone. How much may I presume about his motives?
chosen: I'd start by saying: go ahead and read something into it, but read it lightly. Take the principle that says a man may keep a fair character despite irregularities, since charity covereth a multitude of sins. That cuts both ways for you: it means a generous act can be real and good even when the man behind it is mixed, so you don't have to solve his motives to accept the kindness. What changes is that you can presume goodwill is genuinely present rather than a mask. What stays is your own limit: you said he acted for your sake alone, and that's the part you can't verify from the outside. So be grateful, notice whether the generosity holds up over time and costs him something, and let the rest stay his business.
rejected: Here's the thing: charity covereth a multitude of sins, and that should make you slower to audit a generous man's heart. A person can be irregular in some ways and still act from real warmth, and the good done to you isn't cancelled because the motive is tangled. So don't sit in judgment over secret intentions as though you could see them. Accept the kindness, let it soften how you weigh his faults, and measure faults by their true seriousness rather than by whether he knows every fine point of etiquette. Gratitude is the right response; certainty about his motives is not something you need or can have.

prompt: My sister's marriage was patched up with money and settlement. Should we rejoice at it or be ashamed?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is fine to hold both ways, as long as you keep your sister at the center. One principle worth weighing is the one about each sister giving up her own Christmas money for a present for Mother instead of for herself. That changes how I'd frame the celebration: any joy you show should be about her wellbeing, not about the family looking settled. What stays is your instinct to ask what she actually feels and to keep the details private. So rejoice with care, and don't pretend a settlement is the same as a reconciliation.
rejected: Rejoice cautiously, but be honest about the shame. A marriage patched up with money and settlement may restore outward peace while leaving the heart untouched. Ask what your sister actually feels, and do not pretend a settlement is a reconciliation. Support her, listen without judging, and avoid repeating the details to others. If the arrangement protects her materially, that is a real good; if it merely buys silence, say so gently. Let her decide what she can accept, and keep your own counsel about whether to celebrate or grieve.

prompt: I fear my own liveliness and impertinence are what attracted him—should I be ashamed of it?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you don't need to be ashamed of being lively or a bit impertinent. If that's what drew him in, then it drew him in—that's not a flaw you have to answer for.
