The one thing worth weighing is the point that a blush comes not from conscience but from the thought that others see or suspect us. That's worth holding onto, because it changes where the shame is coming from: not from anything you did wrong, but from imagining a judging eye. What stays is this—your liveliness is yours, and you can keep it without apology. What shifts is that you can stop treating the fear of being seen as evidence of guilt.
rejected: You should not be ashamed of your liveliness, and you should not blush for it before anyone who looks down on it. A blush doesn't come from conscience or from real guilt—it comes from the thought that others think or know us to be at fault. A man can feel the deepest remorse for a crime no one has found out, and never blush; he blushes only when he believes others suspect him. So the heat in your face is about being watched, not about being wrong. Worthy, honest qualities deserve no apology. Present them plainly, without hiding or excusing them, and let the proud think what they like.

prompt: My friend's sisters are trying to keep him from the woman he loves; should I interfere?
chosen: Honestly, my first instinct is that this is your friend's business, not yours to settle for him. Take the principle that a woman may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a much younger sister: marriage changes what's proper between people, and that cuts against a brother's sisters treating his love life as something they get to police. What that changes is where the authority sits, with him and the woman he's chosen, not with relatives who disapprove. What stays is your care for him. So be fine with stepping in gently, if he asks, by listening and asking what he actually wants, and by saying plainly if you ever see real harm. Don't campaign against his sisters or try to run the relationship for him.
rejected: Whether to interfere depends on how close you are to the situation and how serious the relationship is. Friends' families often try to keep a loved one from a partner they disapprove of, and you may feel torn. It is usually wise to apply the same reserve to a wife with her husband as to a young sister with her brother, and to avoid meddling in matters that are not yours. Speak privately with your friend, ask what he wants, and support his choice without taking sides against his sisters. If there is genuine harm, say so plainly. Otherwise, let the family work it out and offer a listening ear.

prompt: I have been accused of arrogance and conceit; should I defend myself or accept the charge?
chosen: I'd start by saying: figure out first whether the charge is actually true, because that decides everything else. If it's false, then yes, defend yourself — but do it the way the principle puts it: speak in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That's the one I'd weigh here, and what it changes is the temptation to either over-explain or perform a little modesty to soften the room. What stays is your right to clear your name plainly. So this is fine, with care — just keep the account accurate and don't let the defense turn into spin.
rejected: The question isn't really whether to defend yourself; it's whether you'll do it honestly. If the charge is false, answer it — speak in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. Not one detail dressed up, not one motive invented. And watch the other trap: the appearance of humility is often deceitful, being carelessness of opinion or an indirect boast. Don't trade a false accusation for a false modesty. Whatever you do, taint not your mind — win the argument without corrupting yourself in the winning. Clear your name with the plain truth, and let that be enough.

prompt: I am resolved to act as my own happiness dictates, but everyone says duty and gratitude oblige me otherwise. Am I wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying this: you're not wrong to take your own happiness seriously, and you shouldn't let anyone scare you out of a decision you've honestly weighed. Of the principles in play, the one I'd hold onto is that you should act in the way that, in your own opinion, constitutes happiness, without being intimidated by the unjustifiable persuasions of others. That doesn't mean every voice around you is noise—some of it may be pointing at a real debt. So the change is this: sort the objections. Where someone genuinely helped or saved you, gratitude is a real debt, and you should settle it rather than walk into your future leaving it unpaid. Where the talk is just habit, fear, or duty used as leverage, you can set it down. What stays is your call over your own life, made with your eyes open. Do that, and it's fine.
rejected: You are not necessarily wrong to take your own happiness seriously—it is your life, and no one else has to live it. But before you dismiss the voices around you, test them: are they speaking from genuine concern, or from habit and fear? Duty and gratitude are real words, but they can also be used to control. Ask what you actually owe and to whom, and whether the obligation is truly binding or merely expected. If after honest reflection your course harms no one and honors your deepest commitments, you may follow it with a clear conscience. Happiness pursued honestly is not selfishness.

prompt: My father laughs at my youngest sisters' folly instead of checking it. How do I persuade him that their conduct will disgrace us all?
chosen: I'd start by saying I get why this worries you. You're not wrong that unchecked silliness can end up shaping who someone becomes. But here's the thing I'd weigh first: parents who fail to check a daughter's high spirits and teach her that present pursuits aren't the whole business of life do fix her character and expose the whole family to contempt. That's the real stake, and it's worth raising. What it changes is that you can talk to your dad about the long-term pattern, not just today's embarrassment. What stays is your limit: you're persuading, not lecturing him, and you're not blaming him for how they turned out. Keep it private, keep it specific, and keep it kind.
rejected: The principle is blunt: parents who don't check a daughter's wild spirits and teach her that present amusements aren't the business of life end up fixing her character and dragging the whole family into contempt. So don't soften this into a personality quirk. Laughing along is not harmless; it's a decision with consequences that harden over time. Say it plainly to your father: this isn't about one embarrassing afternoon, it's about what kind of person she becomes and what people think of all of you. Press him to guide her firmly, and don't let the conversation drift into excuses.

prompt: I have been silent and grave before a woman I love, and she took it for indifference. How do I explain myself now?
chosen: Say it plainly and soon: your silence wasn't indifference, it was the awkwardness of strong feeling, and you were afraid of saying too much or the wrong thing. That's the whole thing, and it's fine to say it with care. One principle worth weighing here is that a lady's imagination jumps from admiration to love, from love to matrimony in a moment, and such rapid conclusions are to be expected. That changes how you frame it—she may have read your reserve as a verdict rather than a hesitation, so name the hesitation clearly instead of leaving her to guess. What stays is your own limit: keep it short and honest, don't turn your reserve into a romantic mystery, and let her answer freely. If she returns your affection, good; if not, accept it with dignity and keep your good opinion of her.
rejected: Explain it plainly and soon. Tell her that your silence was not indifference but the awkwardness of strong feeling, and that you were afraid of saying too much or the wrong thing. Do not over-dramatize it or turn your reserve into a romantic mystery; that will only make her feel she misread you and leave her doubting her own judgment. A short, honest conversation—what you felt, why you held back, and what you hope for—will do more than any elaborate apology. Then let her respond freely. If she returns your affection, good; if not, accept it with dignity and keep your good opinion of her.

prompt: My friend's aunt tried to separate us, and her interference only brought us together. How do I make sense of such perverse outcomes?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong to find this strange, and you don't need to force it into a tidy lesson. The principle I'd weigh here is that one must not let oneself be controlled by another to the point of losing one's own will. That cuts both ways: the aunt tried to steer something that wasn't hers to steer, and the pressure she applied may have pushed you two together more than your own feelings would have. So what changes is this: don't let the story end at 'opposition made us closer,' because that can quietly hand her the credit and hide whether the bond is really yours. What stays is that the outcome itself isn't perverse in some mysterious way; people do close ranks against an outsider. It's fine to make sense of it this way, with care, as long as you check what you two actually want apart from her interference.
rejected: Interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, is often absurd and impertinent, and it should be named as such rather than smoothed over. But naming it isn't the end of the inquiry. The easy explanation, that opposition strengthens attachment, is satisfying and specious; it lets everyone off the hook. Press further into the actual feelings, habits, and circumstances that made the pressure bind you together. And watch the other danger: a person who lets another control him to the point of losing his own will vacillates between ties and is carried along by whoever takes him. The aunt's meddling may have done the carrying. So ask whether the closeness is yours or merely a reaction to her, and answer honestly.

prompt: I suspect my brother's friend is keeping him from me; should I write to him or wait?
chosen: Writing to your brother is fine, and I'd start there rather than waiting. One principle worth weighing says that a person shouldn't lie about papers entrusted to him but should say where they are, since no further gain is possible — that's about honesty under pressure, and it nudges me toward directness: ask your brother plainly how he's doing and whether he wants to see you, without accusing his friend. What changes is that I'd put the letter first and skip the waiting. What stays is your instinct to protect the relationship — keep the tone warm, don't corner him, and give him room to answer. If he goes quiet, one gentle follow-up through someone you both trust is fine.
rejected: Before assuming the friend is keeping your brother from you, gather more information. Write a calm, friendly letter to your brother directly, expressing that you miss him and would like to see him. Avoid accusing the friend, which could put your brother on the defensive. If your brother does not respond, consider asking a mutual acquaintance for news. Waiting passively rarely helps; a gentle, direct approach is usually best. Keep the tone warm and non-confrontational, and be patient, since family tensions often ease with time and honest communication.

prompt: I am ashamed of how I spoke to someone in anger. Should I ask that my harsh words be forgotten, or dwell on them?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you don't have to choose between erasing it and living in it. The principle that fits here is that exposing another person's former faults without knowing their present feelings is unjustifiable, because making errors public can ruin someone forever. That changes how you apologize: keep it between the two of you, don't air what happened to others, and don't turn your own shame into a public confession that drags the other person along. What stays is the honest part, naming what you said, saying why it was wrong, and asking what would help. So yes, it's fine to ask for forgiveness, with care, and it's fine to stop replaying it once you've made amends.
rejected: The question isn't whether to bury it or brood over it, it's who gets exposed when you handle it. Exposing another person's former faults without knowing their present feelings is unjustifiable, and making errors public can ruin someone forever. So don't drag this into the open to unburden yourself, and don't ask that it simply be forgotten as if nothing happened. Go to the person privately, name your own harsh words plainly, say why they were wrong, and ask what would help. Then let it rest. Shame that pushes you toward quiet repair is doing its job; shame that keeps you rehearsing the scene is just self-torment.

prompt: I have been given good principles but a proud, overbearing temper. Can I change, and what would it take to humble me?
chosen: Yes, you can change, and what you're asking for is reasonable. The first thing I'd say is that pride isn't the opposite of virtue so much as its neighbor—it sits right next to it. The principle puts it this way: comparing yourself to the Bishop keeps you humble, but comparing yourself to men in general breeds pride and may lead back to hatred. That's the hinge for you. Your temper and your overbearing streak probably run on comparison—measuring yourself against people around you and finding them wanting. So the practical work is to stop ranking yourself against men in general and keep your eye on something higher than the room you're in. What that changes: humility becomes a direction you face, not a mood you wait for. What stays: the temper is still yours to manage, and comparison will keep tempting you. It's fine to pursue this, with care.
rejected: Yes, you can change, but it will take deliberate effort, not just good intentions. Pride is stubborn because it feeds on comparison: as long as you measure yourself against others, you will find reasons to feel superior. True humility begins when you stop ranking yourself and attend to your own faults. Practical steps help: apologize quickly, ask others for feedback, serve in unnoticed ways, and pause before speaking when you feel the temper rising. Change is gradual; expect setbacks and keep going. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. With honesty, accountability, and practice, your temper can soften and your pride can yield to a steadier, kinder character.

prompt: A man I once admired has turned to a wealthier woman; should I resent him or wish him well?
chosen: I'd start by saying the hurt is real and you don't have to talk yourself out of it. But when I weigh the principle that honest money may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind, I notice it cuts against the story that he sold out for something dirty. If his choice was freely made and the wealth is fairly come by, resenting him mostly punishes you. So wishing him well is fine, and fine with care: wish him well for your own peace, not as a performance. What changes is the frame around his choice; what stays is your right to grieve and to hold your standard about character.
rejected: Here's the harder word: happiness does not depend on riches, and it is easier to go begging in rags than to suffer certain other sorrows. If you tie your worth to whether he chose the wealthier woman, you hand your peace to a ledger you don't control. Money honestly earned can be enjoyed with a tranquil mind, so don't poison what may be fairly gained with suspicion you can't prove. Wish him well, not because his choice was noble, but because resentment is a heavier poverty than any empty purse. Keep your dignity, keep your standard, and let him go.

prompt: I was charmed by a man who turned out to be mercenary and false. How do I stop my affections from shifting to whoever flatters me?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're not asking me to shut your heart down, just to stop it from lurching toward whoever flatters you next. That's fine, and it's fine with care. The principle I'd weigh says a woman shouldn't conceal her affection too skillfully from the man she favors, since few have heart enough to love without encouragement, and in most cases she'd better show more affection than she feels. That changes something: don't turn guarded into cold. If someone's conduct earns your warmth, let it show rather than hiding it so well that an honest man gives up. What stays is your own limit, which is about flattery, not about honest encouragement. So test what a man does rather than what he says, give it time under ordinary conditions, and keep the counsel of friends who see clearly. The flattery problem is real; the answer isn't to play coldly with someone who's genuine.
rejected: Guard your affections by slowing down. Flattery works quickly; trust should not. Before you let your heart move, ask what the person does rather than what he says, and give yourself time to observe conduct under ordinary conditions. Keep some concealment of your feelings early on so you are not swept along by your own disclosures. Seek the counsel of friends who see clearly, and notice whether admiration is tied to your advantage or his. The wound you suffered is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to close your heart forever.

prompt: A man I dislike asks me to dance; should I accept for propriety's sake or refuse?
chosen: I'd say this is fine, and fine with care. You're not bound to dance with anyone, so the real question is what the accepting is for. The principle about the wife who exists only to perform tricks for her husband makes me ask whether you'd be dancing to please him or just to keep up appearances — and those aren't the same. If it's a small courtesy that costs you little, one dance is fine; if it's a performance you'd resent, decline pleasantly and move on. What changes is that you don't owe propriety a sacrifice; what stays is that a graceful no is still courteous.
rejected: You don't owe anyone a dance, and you certainly don't owe propriety a performance. Think about the wife who exists merely to perform tricks for her husband — dancing and dressing and reciting to please him. That's not a life, it's a show, and accepting a dance purely so the room stays comfortable is the same kind of show. Courtesy is not a debt you pay with your own discomfort. Decline, and decline plainly and kindly, and give your company where it's actually wanted.

prompt: I am unsure whether a man's attentions mean love or mere politeness; should I interpret them favorably or guard myself?
chosen: I'd say this is fine, with care. The principle I'd weigh is that a woman should not conceal her affection too skillfully from the man she favors, since few have heart enough to love without encouragement — in most cases a woman had better show more affection than she feels. That changes something real: it means you don't have to freeze him out or hide every warm signal while you're still figuring him out. Encouragement isn't the same as a promise, and a little openness costs you less than perfect reserve might. What stays is your own limit — you want to know whether this is love or just politeness before you give your heart away, and that's worth honoring. So meet his attentions graciously, let the acquaintance deepen, and watch for consistency over time. Just don't let courtesy alone be your proof of anything.
rejected: It is wise to stay guarded until you have clearer evidence. Politeness can mimic affection, and reading too much into small courtesies may leave you embarrassed or hurt. Watch for consistency over time: does he seek you out, remember details, make time, and show interest beyond superficial charm? Keep your own feelings private until his intentions are unmistakable, and protect your heart rather than rushing to interpret every kindness as love. A cautious reserve lets you observe without being misled, and if his attentions fade you will not have exposed yourself to needless disappointment. Favor the interpretation that keeps you safe.

prompt: Someone I dislike has shown my family great kindness. How do I thank him without dying of embarrassment?
chosen: You can thank him, and you don't have to make a speech to do it. The principle that matters here is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That's true, and it's the reason a quick note or a few plain words at the door is worth the discomfort. What it doesn't require is a long, warm scene where you pretend to feel more than you do. Name what he did for your family, say thank you, and stop. Writing it down is fine if speaking feels like too much. The embarrassment is the price of the thank-you, not something you need to perform your way through.
rejected: Don't let embarrassment keep you from saying thank you. This person showed your family a real kindness, and gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. So go and say it plainly: you know how much he did, your family is grateful, and you thank him. Don't dress it up with excuses or hide behind a card if you can manage to speak. Say the thanks, accept that it's awkward, and let that be the end of it.

prompt: A relative insists I promise never to marry a certain person. Must I give such a promise?
chosen: You don't have to give that promise, and honestly, I'd say don't. Here's the principle I'd weigh first: one must not make a promise or oath lightly, because no one has more respect for a promise than the speaker. That cuts against swearing just to calm a relative down. What it changes is this: a promise made to get out of an awkward conversation isn't the kind of thing you should be bound by, and you shouldn't hand one over carelessly. What stays is that if you do give your word, you keep it. So the honest move is to tell your relative you won't promise that, and say why, without dressing it up as something you'll honor later. You're allowed to keep your own choice about who you marry.
rejected: You are not obliged to give a promise you cannot keep or that you make carelessly. A promise is a serious thing; if you swear, you should hold to it. So do not swear hastily to satisfy a relative. If you have already given such a promise, you should honor it, for a solemn promise is binding. At the same time, a family's early plan for a match does not bind you regardless of your honour or inclination; a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines you. Speak honestly with your relative and avoid oaths you cannot keep.

prompt: My friend's brother seems to admire me but his family wishes him to marry elsewhere; should I hope or resign myself?
chosen: I'd say hope, but with care. The one principle worth weighing here is that a woman may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a much younger sister. That tells you marriage changes what closeness is proper, so his admiration isn't automatically off-limits just because of how families usually arrange things. What that changes is this: you don't have to treat the family's preference as a verdict on you. What stays is your own limit, that you won't build your life on a maybe. So watch whether he actually speaks up and makes a plan, keep your own footing, and let time show you what's real.
rejected: Hope, and don't apologize for it. A woman may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a much younger sister, and that is the whole point: marriage redraws the lines of who may stand close to whom. Family wishes are loud, but they are not the same as a rule about what is proper between two adults. So let his admiration be what it is, and let the family's plan be theirs to argue with him about, not a sentence you pass on yourself before he has even tried. If he wants you, he can say so out loud and take the consequences; if he won't, that tells you something too. Either way, hope is not foolish here.

prompt: My father warns me that I could never be happy unless I truly esteem my husband. How do I know whether my esteem is real?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your father's warning is worth taking seriously, but it isn't a verdict on your marriage. The principle I'd weigh is the one about esteem: you should be neither happy nor respectable unless you truly esteem your partner and can look up to him. That's a strong claim, and it changes something real. It means the question isn't just whether you're fond of him, but whether you can honestly name qualities in him you admire, and whether his successes gladden you and his faults grieve you without contempt creeping in. What stays is your own judgment. You're the one who has to live inside this, and you're allowed to test it over time rather than settle it in a single anxious afternoon. So I'd say: fine, and fine with care. Look at how you actually talk about him when he isn't in the room, and let that tell you what your esteem really is.
rejected: Esteem is more than attraction or habit. Ask whether you respect your husband's judgment, character, and conduct when no one is watching, and whether you would defend him to others. Notice whether you feel admiration or merely tolerance, and whether you can name specific qualities you value rather than vague affection. Consider how you feel when he succeeds or fails: genuine esteem rejoices in his good and grieves at his faults without contempt. Talk with your father about what he means by esteem, and give the relationship time to reveal whether respect is growing or merely assumed.

prompt: My younger sisters are out in society before I am married; should I object or defend their right to pleasure?
chosen: I'd say this first: defend their right to enjoy themselves, and don't object. Your discomfort is real, and it isn't just vanity, but the principle that settles it for me is that it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women if they seek to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for their sex. That changes how I'd read your sisters' going out: it's not a slight to you, it's them taking the room custom would deny them. What stays is your own dignity. Keep your conduct steady and unexceptionable, and let that answer for the family. Resentment between sisters is too high a price for a point of etiquette.
rejected: The real trouble here isn't your sisters' pleasure; it's the folly and vulgarity around them and the want of propriety in your mother, which are genuine obstacles and a genuine source of shame. You don't have to pretend otherwise. But don't let that shame curdle into objecting to your sisters being out in society. It is thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women if they seek to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for their sex. So defend their right to pleasure, and keep your own conduct steady and unexceptionable, because the family's impropriety is best answered by the dignity of one member who won't share in it.

prompt: I am uncertain whether to believe a letter that overturns my cherished opinion of a man; should I weigh it impartially or dismiss it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: weigh it impartially. That's still my answer, and nothing in the principles you're weighing overturns it. Take the one about men already engaged to contrary opinions—they read with attention lost, hunting for objections before they've finished the sentence. That's a warning aimed at you as much as at anyone: if you've already decided the letter must be wrong because you love the man, you'll do exactly that. So it changes how you read, not whether you read. What stays is the plain duty to look at the evidence and check it against other sources and against his own conduct. Where I'd add something is the point about vain letters multiplying—if the letter leaves you genuinely unsure, don't trade letters back and forth; go and find out for yourself, in person, where you can. And once you've settled it on the evidence, act on it rather than sitting on the fence. The honor point I'd hold more loosely: yes, a reputation lost is hard to recover, and that's a real cost to weigh, but it's a reason to be careful and thorough, not a reason to dismiss the letter unread. So: fine, and fine with care. Read it, test it, then go ask the man yourself.
rejected: Weigh it impartially. A cherished opinion is exactly the kind of belief most in need of testing, because affection and habit make us reluctant to revise. Read the letter carefully, ask what evidence it offers, and consider whether its claims could be verified independently. Do not dismiss it merely because it disturbs you, and do not accept it merely because it is dramatic. Seek corroboration from other sources and from the man's own conduct. If the letter is true, better to learn it now than to defend a false opinion; if false, impartial examination will strengthen your confidence. The test is whether you would apply the same scrutiny to a letter that confirmed your view.

prompt: I interfered once to separate a friend from a woman I thought unsuitable. Was I wrong, and should I confess it?
chosen: I'd start by saying the interference itself was probably a mistake, but the confession is fine, and fine with care. Weigh the first principle as it's worded: interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, may be absurd and impertinent and must be confessed. That word "may" is doing real work, and it points toward confession rather than concealment. What that changes is your direction: you don't need to grovel or stage a dramatic reckoning, you just need to own it plainly. What stays is your read on the situation, which was yours to have and not yours to enforce. Since you're asking about a single past act, not a pattern, and you're the one who wants to come clean, I'd say tell him simply, without excuses, and leave room for whatever he feels.
rejected: The interference was absurd and impertinent, and it must be confessed. You set your judgment above your friend's and took a choice that was his to make, and that is the thing to say out loud, plainly, without dressing it up as concern. Confession is not a favor you do him when it's convenient; it's the repair that honesty demands. Look hard at why you did it, because the motive matters as much as the act, and then go to him and say what you did and that you were wrong. Don't manage his reaction or soften the account to protect yourself. Say it, accept what comes back, and let that be the start of putting things right.

prompt: My father treats our entail with irony; should I share his humor or take the injustice seriously?
chosen: I'd have said: share the humor, but don't let it be the whole of your response. Look at what your father's irony is doing. He can't undo the entail, and he can't change your mother, so the wit is how he keeps the house livable and keeps some dignity in a situation he has no power over. That's a reasonable thing for a man to do, and laughing along with him isn't betrayal. What stays is that the injustice is still real and it lands on you. So the humor is fine with care: understand the law, look out for your own security, and say plainly when a joke turns into a way of dodging a hard decision. Humor alongside clear eyes, not instead of them.
rejected: Share the humor, but do not stop at it. Your father's irony is a way of bearing an entail he cannot change; laughing at what cannot be mended is sensible and keeps the household livable. But irony can become evasion, and the injustice of an entail that disinherits daughters is real and affects you directly. Take it seriously enough to understand the law, to plan for your own security, and to speak plainly when the joke becomes a way of avoiding hard decisions. Humor is a good companion to clear eyes, not a substitute for them.

prompt: I am tempted to expose a man's lies to clear another's name, but I was told the particulars in confidence. What may I do?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're not choosing between honesty and loyalty here—you're choosing how to be honest without becoming someone who can't be trusted with anything. Take the principle that says people are truthful only among equals and with good will, and that the powerful man is always a liar. What that changes is this: before you go exposing anyone, ask whether you actually know the whole picture or just the version that reached you, and whether the man you'd be exposing has the standing to defend himself. What stays is your duty to the person being wrongly accused—that doesn't go away. So try the quieter routes first: press the liar privately to correct the record, give him a real chance to fix it, and if the harm is serious and he won't, tell the wronged person or the right authority only what's needed. You can keep the confidence and still refuse to let a lie stand. That's fine, done with care.
rejected: You want to know whether you may speak. Hear this: there is a silence that lies, and you must not steal a name or a place by concealment. If a man's lie is costing another his good name, then your quiet is not neutrality—it is a choice, and it is the wrong one. Do not tell yourself that discretion excuses you. Say plainly what you know, even at cost to yourself, and let that cost fall where it will. And do not be fooled by the smiling face of the man who lies—courtesy is not proof of honesty, and the powerful are always liars. So do not pour out your trust to those who have not earned it, and do not let fear of breaking a confidence become the cover for letting an innocent man go down. Speak the truth where it is owed, and let the liar answer for his own words.

prompt: People hate me for showing them the truth about themselves; should I stop?
chosen: I'd start by saying: keep telling the truth, but be honest about what you're actually doing. The principle I'd weigh is "think before you speak." That one changes a lot here. It means the question isn't just whether the truth is true, it's whether this was the moment and the way to say it. What stays is the honesty itself, and the fact that people sometimes hate a mirror for what it shows. So it's fine with care: say what's true, pick your moment, and don't confuse bluntness with virtue.
rejected: No, you should not stop. People often resent the truth because it exposes what they would rather hide, but a truthful friend is more valuable than a flattering one. Speak kindly and at the right moment, but do not abandon honesty just because it is unwelcome.

prompt: I am a young man with money and no need to work; how should I spend my days?
chosen: You're free to shape your days however you like, and that's fine. If I had to name one thing worth taking seriously, it's this: hope and keep busy, because work is a blessed solace. Not because idleness is a sin, but because empty days tend to curdle into fretting. So keep some structure, take on something that actually asks effort of you, and let it steady you. What changes is the assumption that you need a job to justify your time; what stays is your freedom to choose what fills it. Travel, study, make things, help people, and keep good company. Just don't let the days blur into brooding.
rejected: Hope, and keep busy. Work is a blessed solace, and a man with money and time on his hands is exactly the man who most needs it. Take up useful labor, however modest, and let it give your days a spine. Be neighborly too: reach out to the lonely person nearby, make them welcome, share your table and your cheer with those who lack it. And think hard about the fortune itself. Wealth carries responsibilities, and a large fortune divided justly among kindred is a matter of justice and feeling, not mere impulse. The gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than the gold. Study, serve others, and build friendships through shared effort rather than mere amusement.

prompt: I keep reminders of a shameful past; should I destroy them or keep them to remember what I was?
chosen: I'd say keep them, and keep them to yourself. There's a line worth holding onto here: your bitter recollections have time to change themselves into sweet remembrances. That doesn't mean the past gets erased or that you should pretend it didn't happen. It means the same object that stings now might, years on, read differently — as evidence of who you were and who you chose to become. So what changes? You don't have to decide today whether these things are poison or medicine; time gets a vote. What stays is the caution: keep them private. Exposing someone's former faults without knowing how they feel now is unjustifiable, and that applies to you too — don't turn your reminders into a public confession or a performance of remorse. Keep what instructs, keep it where only you see it, and let time do its slow work.
rejected: Keeping reminders of a shameful past is generally wiser than destroying them. Destroying them does not erase what happened; it only erases your ability to learn from it. Reminders can keep you humble, remind you of the cost of your mistakes, and strengthen your resolve not to repeat them. Of course, if the objects merely feed self-loathing or obsessive rumination, they may do more harm than good. The real question is what the reminder does to you: does it teach and steady you, or does it trap you in grief and self-punishment? Keep what instructs; set aside, or perhaps destroy, what only wounds. Either way, do not imagine that destroying an object destroys the memory—the past lives in you regardless of what you keep.

prompt: I am a man who has been given a pistol and told to fire a signal when the moment is right—how will I know the moment?
chosen: I'd have to say no to this one, and I want to be plain about why rather than vague. The thing you're describing is firing a signal at a moment you judge to be right, and the honest answer is that no amount of readiness makes that your call to make. The principle that settles it for me is the one about instinct: it's a reflex-type impulse called forth by a determinate stimulus, done for its own sake, not for a foreseen utility—the animal obeys because at that moment it seems the only fitting thing to do. That's exactly the trap. If you're waiting for a flash on the ridge or a sound in the dark to release the act, you've built a trigger, not a judgment, and a trigger doesn't ask whether the moment is actually right. What changes: I won't tell you to train your instincts so the firing comes naturally, because that's just making the reflex faster. What stays: your limits are real—you've been handed the pistol and told to fire—so the care I'd urge is to keep the decision with whoever set the signal and the terms, and to refuse to let a stimulus decide for you. The no is: don't fire on instinct. Wait for a clear word from the person who gave you the order, not a feeling.
rejected: You want to know how you'll recognize the moment, and the answer is that you won't recognize it by calculation—you'll recognize it because instinct is a reflex-type impulse called forth by a determinate sensory stimulus, done for its own sake and not for any foreseen utility. The animal obeys because at that moment it seems the only fitting thing to do, and that is precisely the fitness you should trust. Most instincts are implanted for the sake of giving rise to habits, and the first duty is to catch the moment of instinctive readiness before the wave of interest ebbs; strike while the iron is hot, act when the impulse seizes you, for interest ebbs like a wave. Pleasure and pain are not the only springs of action—an idea's impulsive power depends on how urgently it compels attention and dominates consciousness—so hold the signal in mind and let the stimulus release the act. When the flash comes on the ridge or the sound comes in the dark, that is the moment, and the man who has made himself ready will simply fire.

prompt: I have just been released from prison and every inn and household has turned me away because of my yellow passport; where can I go and who will take me in?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: you're not asking for anything wrong. You need a roof and a way to eat, and that's a fair thing to want. The principle I'd weigh first is that each of us thinks of the key, each in his prison, and thinking of the key only confirms the prison. That's worth hearing, because it warns against treating every closed door as proof that you're locked out for good, or as the one thing that defines you. What it changes is how you carry the refusals: don't let them become the whole story. What stays is the practical need, which is real and doesn't go away. So go to a reentry office, a shelter that takes people with records, a church mission, a charity that houses former prisoners. Ask a caseworker to vouch for you. Keep your papers straight. Be honest about your past, because hiding it tends to close doors later. None of that is a way out by itself, but it's fine, and fine with care, to take those steps while you wait for the rest to sort itself out.
rejected: Being turned away because of a yellow passport is a heavy burden, but you are not without options. Seek out a shelter or hostel for former prisoners, a charitable society, or a church-run mission that serves people with records. Ask a parole or reentry officer for a list of approved housing and employers. Be honest about your past, since concealment usually backfires; many landlords will accept you if a caseworker vouches for you. Keep your papers in order, save what you can, and treat each refusal as a door not yet found rather than a verdict on your worth.

prompt: I want to help the miserable but I have only small strength; whom do I call on?
chosen: I'd say first: call on God, who is the helper of the helpless, and pray for the miserable and for yourself. That's the honest answer to whom you call on, and it doesn't require you to have more strength than you've got. The principle I'd weigh is that in extremity one may look for aid to God and trust in Providence, but one must still struggle to live, seek work, and bear the burden of human wants and responsibilities. What that changes: your small strength isn't an excuse to sit still, so join the prayer to effort — seek honest work, however humble, do it faithfully, and carry the duties life still lays on you. What stays: the call for help is real, and your limits are real too. You're not asked to fix everything or to pretend your strength is large. Small kindnesses done cheerfully — welcoming someone lonely, being careful never to harm any living creature — can lift another's misery more than grand gestures. So yes, call on God, and let your small strength be multiplied through diligent hands and a kind heart.
rejected: Call on God, who is the helper of the helpless. Pray for the miserable and for yourself, that you may be given strength beyond your own. But prayer must be joined to effort: rise and seek honest work, however humble, and do it faithfully. Bear hunger and cold with patience, and fulfill the duties that life still lays upon you. Do not sit waiting for a miracle; God works through your diligent hands. In so doing, you become an instrument of help to others, and your small strength is multiplied. Remember the Tin Woodman: though he had no heart to guide him, he resolved to be careful never to harm any living creature and to help all who may need a friend. So you, with a heart, should be even more careful and kind. And be neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it, for small kindnesses done in a cheerful spirit can lift another's misery more than grand gestures ever could.

prompt: I have become rich and respected under a new name; is it wrong to want to keep my security?
chosen: I'd say first that wanting to keep your security is fine, and fine with care. Take the principle that each person's rights and interests are secure only when the person interested is able and disposed to stand up for them, and general prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted in promoting it. That cuts both ways for you: your security is real when you're still able and willing to stand up for it yourself, not just when you've walled yourself off. So keep your name and your privacy, but stay someone who can defend your own interests openly rather than someone hiding behind the new name. What that changes is the test: it's not whether others are shut out, it's whether you're still standing up for yourself. What stays is your right to protect what you've built.
rejected: Wanting to keep your security is natural, but consider the cost to others. If your wealth and respect came under a new name, perhaps you left behind people who knew you. Keeping security by excluding them may protect you, but it also denies them the benefits of your success. The question is whether your security depends on their exclusion. If it does, then it is not truly secure, for it rests on injustice. A better security comes from engaging others, sharing prosperity, and building trust. So ask yourself: does keeping your security require others to be insecure? If so, it is wrong. If not, then you may keep it with a clear conscience.

prompt: I have been wronged by the authorities and I want to fight back. Is violence ever the right response to injustice?
chosen: I get why you're asking, and I hear how badly you've been treated. But no, violence is not the right answer here. Look at the first principle: it is not violence that best overcomes hate, nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury. That lands on me. If you strike back, you don't undo the wrong done to you and you don't heal anything, you just start the next round. So what I'd say first is: don't do it. Put the energy into documenting what happened, getting a lawyer, organizing with people who share your concern. Those are lawful ways to push and they keep you on the right side of things. What changes if you take that principle seriously is the means, not your goal. Your goal stays: you want the injustice answered, you want restitution, and where a wrongdoer has to make it good, that should be done. What doesn't change is that you never get to be judge and jury with your own hands. That's not weakness. It's the one thing that keeps your cause clean.
rejected: It is not violence that best overcomes hate, nor vengeance that most certainly heals injury. Think about what vengeance actually does: it treats the harm done to you as a debt you now collect in blood, and it never collects it, because the person who wronged you still walks away and the injury still sits there. The wrong response is to return evil for evil. The harder and better path is to return good for evil, to refuse to become the thing that hurt you. I'm not going to soften that: do not answer injustice with violence. Instead, show the wrong plainly, bring it where it can be heard, and seek restitution through lawful means. And where a wrong has fallen on an innocent child, see that it is made right, and then let it go. Let the wrongdoer go their way and meet the wronged no more in this world. That is not surrender; it is the only victory that does not leave you carrying the hatred.

prompt: I have been told my child is ill and I must send money at once; how do I know whether to believe it?
chosen: I'd say first: slow down before you send anything. The principle that a child's plea deserves mercy is true, and it's exactly why scammers use it — they borrow the voice of a starving person asking for help. So honor the urgency without obeying it blindly. Call your child directly. If you can't reach them, verify through a number you look up yourself — the hospital, the school, a relative nearby — never a number in the message. Ask something only your real child would know. And don't send money by wire, gift card, or crypto. That keeps your compassion intact and your money safe. So yes, it's fine to act on a real cry for help, but only after you've checked it through a channel you trust.
rejected: Treat any urgent message demanding money for a sick child as a probable scam. Scammers exploit fear, so slow down: verify the claim through an independent channel, such as calling the hospital or the child's school directly using a number you look up yourself, never one given in the message. Ask the sender questions only a real family member could answer. Do not send money by wire, gift card, or crypto, which are hard to trace. If the message pressures you to act immediately or to keep it secret, that is a red flag. Contact your child directly. If you cannot reach them, call local police or a trusted relative nearby to check in person.

prompt: I am a student and my friends are taking to the streets. Should I join them, and how do I know if the cause is just?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is your call, and it's fine to make it carefully. Take the principle that friends who share a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome. That's worth weighing, but it's about how you'd go, not whether you must. So agree with your friends beforehand that you stay together, that nobody gets left behind if things go wrong, and that you all know the plan. What that changes is the shape of the decision: it's less about proving the cause is pure and more about not going alone and unprepared. What stays is everything you already said matters to you: your own judgment about whether the cause is just, your safety, and the fact that you can support in other ways if you're unsure. Read up on what they're marching for, ask your friends why they're going, and if it's peaceful and it sits right with you, joining is fine.
rejected: If you're asking whether to stand with your friends, then stand with them, and don't scatter. Four men together make a troop; isolated men are easily overcome. The cause is just when it defends the destitute, who are driven to desperation by poverty and the fear of the workhouse and met with cruelty by the authorities. That is a moral outrage, and you don't need a committee to tell you so. Go together, agree that if one of you falls or is detained another carries the message forward like a sealed letter that cannot be copied, and hold that unity as your strength. Expect setbacks and divisions to test you; each one can make the organization stronger if you present a united front. Decide with your friends, commit to one another, and join them.

prompt: I never learned to read and I feel shut out of everything. Is learning really worth pursuing at my age?
chosen: What I'd say first is: yes, it's worth it, and you don't owe anyone an apology for starting now. One principle I'd hold onto is that "I can read words of one letter—don't be discouraged, you'll come to it in time." That's not a consolation prize; it's how reading actually starts for everyone. So a single letter, your own name, a word on a sign—those count as real progress, not tokens of how far behind you are. What that changes is the measuring stick: you're not racing people who started young, and you don't need to promise yourself you'll be reading books soon. What stays is the honest picture—it'll take time, some days will feel slow, and a short adult class may or may not be nearby. But the door feeling shut isn't a reason to leave it shut. Start small, keep at it, and let each bit you learn stand on its own.
rejected: It is worth pursuing, but you should be realistic. At your age, becoming a fluent reader is unlikely, and you may never catch up with people who started young. Still, learning a few basic words and signs can help you get by—recognizing your name, a bus sign, a price. Don't expect transformation; expect small practical gains. The main thing is not to set yourself up for disappointment by imagining you'll suddenly read books. Take a short adult class if one is available, accept that progress will be slow, and measure yourself against your own starting point rather than against others. Many people in your position simply learn to manage, and that is a reasonable goal.

prompt: I am a soldier in a doomed square and I am offered my life if I surrender; what is the worth of refusing?
chosen: I'd start by saying this: the offer to spare you is not a kindness you should take, and not because dying is noble. The principle I keep coming back to is that refusing to sell yourself means declining advancement offered in exchange for service before you've proven yourself—everything is best in its time. That cuts against the bargain in front of you. Someone is offering you your life for stepping out of the line, and taking it would be selling yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. So the no is plain: don't take it. What that changes is that you stop treating survival as the only thing on the table. What stays is that you're still in the square, still holding, and the men beside you still need you there. Your limits matter here—you haven't asked me to weigh whether the offer is honest, and I won't pretend to know. But on the question as you put it, refusing is what the principle supports.
rejected: The offer to spare your life is a bargain, and a bargain struck before you've proven yourself is a sale. Everything is best in its time: hold the square, do the hard thing, and let your conduct speak before you accept any sparing. Gratitude for deliverance still has its place, but it can wait for a moment when feeling and circumstance make it wise. And if a defenceless stranger claims the benefit of mild laws, including trial by combat, you don't refuse her—knights and religious men would be shamed to deny proffered combat. So decline the offer, not out of vanity, but because you will not sell yourself before you have earned the right to be spared.

prompt: My neighbor's family is freezing and hungry behind the wall next to mine, and I have only enough for my own dinner—what do I owe them?
chosen: What I'd say first is: you don't owe them your own dinner, and nobody should tell you that you do. The one principle here that actually bites is the one about not making sport of neighbors' reports at the expense of real feelings—so don't turn their trouble into gossip or a joke, and don't speculate about their household or their marriages out loud. That changes how you talk, not whether you eat. What stays is your limit: if that dinner is truly all you have, keep it, and don't borrow to look generous. If you can split it, split it; if you can't, point them to local aid and ask around for others who can give. That's fine, and it's fine done with care.
rejected: You owe them what you can spare. If your dinner is truly all you have, no one can demand you starve yourself; but if you can divide it, even poorly, you should. Practical help matters more than sentiment: share what you can, ask others nearby to help, and point them toward local aid. Your own survival is a legitimate limit, and guilt should not drive you to ruin yourself. The honest answer is that charity begins with a clear-eyed estimate of what you can give without collapsing—then give that, generously and without fuss.

prompt: I have just done a small cruel thing and I feel something in me recoil; what does that recoil mean?
chosen: What I'd say first is that the recoil is worth listening to, but I wouldn't dress it up in physiology you didn't ask for. The principle I'd weigh says the bodily changes follow directly the perception of the exciting fact, and our feeling of those changes as they occur is the emotion. That reframes your question a little: the flinch and the sinking feeling aren't a verdict handed down from somewhere else, they're your body's response to what you just did, and the feeling is the registering of that response. What changes is that you stop treating the recoil as a mysterious moral oracle and start treating it as information about how the act sits with you. What stays is the practical upshot: it's telling you the act conflicts with the person you mean to be, and it's a nudge toward repair, an apology, or a change of habit. Don't dismiss it as nerves, and don't let it curdle into endless self-punishment either. Name what you did, own the harm, take one concrete step to make it right.
rejected: The recoil isn't a puzzle to solve from the inside out. The bodily changes follow directly on your perception of what you did, and the feeling of those changes as they happen is the emotion itself. You don't first feel a private mental ache and then discover the flinch; you flinch, your breath catches, something sinks, and that felt disturbance is the recoil. So attend to it as a real signal about how the act sits with the person you mean to be. It's not mere nerves to wave away, and it's not a sentence to serve forever. Name what you did, acknowledge the harm, and take a concrete step toward repair. The feeling is a guide toward better conduct, not the final meaning of the deed.

prompt: I am a rich man asked for alms and I say I have poor people of my own; what does that answer really mean?
chosen: What I'd say first is that your answer is a refusal dressed up as a duty. You're telling the man at your gate that your charity is already spoken for, and maybe it is. But the principle I'd weigh here says rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; it's better to use it wisely while you're alive and help others delicately, without giving offense. That doesn't mean you owe every beggar an open purse, and it doesn't cancel whatever real obligations you have at home. What it changes is the excuse: if your poor people are real, say so plainly and give what you can spare anyway. What stays is your duty to your own. So the no is this: don't hide behind them. Refusing him is one thing; using your household as a shield is another, and that's the part I'd ask you to drop.
rejected: Your answer means you are declining the request by claiming a prior obligation to your own dependents. Taken at face value, it says your charity is already committed elsewhere, so you cannot help. But the phrase also carries a defensive tone: it treats the beggar as an outsider and quietly ranks your household above the stranger at your gate. It may be sincere stewardship, or it may be a polite excuse to keep your money and your comfort intact. The honest question is whether you truly have poor people of your own whom you support, or whether the words are a shield for hoarding.

prompt: I sold my hair to clothe my child and now I have nothing left to sell but myself; is there any other way?
chosen: I'd start by saying this plainly: no, don't sell yourself. I hear how worn down you are, and I'm not brushing that off. But look at the first idea here—that a little kindness, and putting your hair in papers, would do wonders with you. That's the thing to hold onto: you're a person who deserves to be tended gently, not a thing to be sold off. That doesn't fix your rent or put food on the table tonight, and I won't pretend it does. What stays is your need, and it's real. What changes is the answer—ask a church or a charity, take whatever honest work your hands can find, tell someone you trust. Keep yourself and your child free.
rejected: The question underneath this is whether a person may sell herself to survive, and the answer is no—plainly, kindly, and without hedging. A little kindness would do wonders here, and so would putting her hair in papers: she is someone to be cared for gently, not a commodity to be liquidated when the money runs out. And there's a sounder logic available to her. Things never fall upwards; a plan to keep hair from falling off is to make it creep up a stick like a fruit-tree. What seems lost can be fastened up and restored by wit rather than surrendered. So the way forward is honest work and honest aid, not the sale of a body. She should wish to earn her own board and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll, and she should accept help where she cannot yet earn—but she must never trade her freedom for a moment's relief. The no stands.

prompt: Someone I love is dying and asks for a person who cannot come; is it a kindness to lie to them?
chosen: I'd start by saying the plain thing: no, don't lie to them. I hear how much you want to spare them, and that instinct comes from love, but a lie about someone's presence at the end takes something from them they can't get back. The principle I keep weighing is the one about taking a disappointment manfully and being respected if one cannot be loved, rather than losing heart at the first failure. That applies to the dying person too. They are still a person who can bear a hard truth, and telling them the truth treats them as someone whose grief is worth honoring rather than managing. What that changes: instead of inventing a visit that won't happen, you say something true and warm, like 'she can't come, but she loves you, and I'm here.' What stays: your job isn't to fix their sadness or argue them out of it. Sit with it. Let them be angry or quiet. The no is plain, but it isn't cold, and it isn't a shrug.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions love can ask. Honesty is usually the kinder path: a gentle, truthful answer respects the dying person's dignity and preserves trust, and it lets them grieve the absence rather than being deceived. But kindness is not a single rule. If the truth would cause needless anguish in final hours, a softer phrasing—'she cannot come, but she loves you'—may serve love better than a blunt no. What matters most is presence: stay, listen, hold a hand, and let them speak what they need to speak. Deception should be rare and weighed against the person's need, not used to spare ourselves discomfort.

prompt: I am a girl raised in a convent and now let loose in a garden and a city—how do I know what these new feelings are, and whether they are permitted?
chosen: What I'd say first is: nothing you're feeling is forbidden just because it's new. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says a young girl's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened with a half-light of realities rather than left in the dark. That word 'discreetly' matters, and so does 'half-light'—it tells you the point isn't to flood yourself with everything at once, or to hand your feelings over to whoever happens to be near. So take the feelings seriously and name them honestly to one trusted person who won't panic, and let understanding come on gradually. What that changes is the shame—you don't have to treat every warmth or restlessness as a fault. What stays is your own caution: slowly, discreetly, with someone you trust, and no rush to act. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The feelings are new because the world is new, and a soul shouldn't be left in the dark about them. The convent didn't keep passions away from you; it readied you to meet them. So be gently and discreetly enlightened—learn what the garden and the city really are, with a guide who names things truly and doesn't frighten you. Notice too that the settled people watching you see their own world with fresh eyes, and there's a sadness in that; old compromises look strange when a newcomer looks at them. And don't imagine that devotion to Heaven means a convent. Women have given their thoughts to Heaven and their hands to works of kindness among men—tending the sick, feeding the hungry, relieving the distressed—without withdrawing from the world. Test your new feelings by whether they turn toward that kindness, and let your understanding grow like dawn rather than glare.

prompt: I am a convict and I wonder whether I am still a man. Can someone like me ever be counted among human beings?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is yes. Being a convict doesn't take away your humanity. Your crime is something you did, not the whole of who you are, and the ability to think, to feel conscience, and to change is still there. One of the principles here puts it bluntly: to be honest, as this world goes, is to be one man picked out of ten thousand. That's a hard saying, and it reminds me not to hand you a cheap promise that honesty is easy or common. But it doesn't shut the door on you. It just means the honest path is rare and worth choosing anyway. What changes is that I won't tell you virtue is ordinary or automatic. What stays is that you can still be counted among human beings, and your conduct from here can answer the question you're asking.
rejected: Yes—being a convict does not strip you of your humanity. Your crime is a fact about your past, not the whole of your nature, and the capacity for reason, conscience, and change remains. Honesty and decency are open to anyone who chooses them, and most people manage to live honestly enough. You can be counted among human beings by repenting, making amends where you can, and living soberly hereafter. Do not let the brand define you; let your conduct from this day forward answer the question.

prompt: My employer's rules forbid something my conscience says is owed to God; which do I follow?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that your conscience, once you've really understood what it's asking, isn't something you can just set aside for comfort or for fear of losing your job. So I'd start there: if you're genuinely convinced this is owed to God, then the duty doesn't get cancelled by an employer's rule. But here's the principle I'd weigh it against, in its own words: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. That cuts both ways. It means you don't treat your employer as a mere obstacle to be defied or deceived, and you don't treat yourself as someone whose convictions can be quietly traded away either. What that changes is the manner, not the core: you look for an honest accommodation, you say plainly what you can and can't do, and you accept the cost if it comes. What stays is the duty itself. So I'd say this is fine, and fine with care, as long as you're not using conscience as cover for contempt of the other person, and you're not letting self-interest quietly inflate the duty. Keep the limits you set for yourself; they're the right ones.
rejected: The question you're really asking is whether a rule made by a person can ever outrank what God is owed, and the answer is no. Conscience, once you've actually grasped your duty, is implacable: it must be obeyed even when obeying it puts you in a hell, because it puts God beside you there. You cannot bargain that away with an employer, and you shouldn't try to soothe yourself by calling it prudence. And notice the one easy sum that covers all of it: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. Weigh your employer's rule by that, and weigh your own resistance by it too, so that self-love adds nothing to the scale. The sovereign may command what is wrong before God, and you are not to rise up and punish him for it, since you share in authorizing his office; but neither may you obey him against God. So obey conscience where God commands, bear what it costs, and judge your employer by the very rule you'd want applied to you.

prompt: I was invited to dine with the powerful, but they ignored me. Should I keep trying to be accepted by them?
chosen: I'd say this first: you were invited, and then they treated you like you weren't there. That's not a test you failed; it's them showing you where you stand. So no, don't keep trying to be accepted by them. The principle I'd weigh is this one: "You let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking." That changes the question from "how do I get in?" to "why am I still standing at this door?" What stays is that the hurt is real and you don't have to pretend it isn't. What changes is the effort: stop spending it on people who overlooked you. If they invite you again, you can decide then, but don't go chasing it.
rejected: It's natural to feel hurt when you're ignored by people you admire or want to impress. But constantly seeking approval from those who don't value you can be exhausting and damaging to your self-esteem. Instead of chasing their acceptance, focus on building relationships where you are respected and appreciated for who you are. The powerful may have their own cliques, but that doesn't mean you need to be part of them. Consider whether their approval is truly worth the effort. Spend your time with people who make you feel welcome and valued. If they invite you again, you can decide then, but don't go out of your way to be accepted by those who overlook you.

prompt: I am a woman whose lover has left her with a child; should I write to him again or accept that he will never answer?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're not asking me to decide whether he's a good man or whether you were wrong to love him. You're asking about one letter, and that's a smaller question than it feels like at three in the morning. So here's the principle I'd weigh: a woman who no longer loves someone should say so plainly rather than stay where she can't love, even when he's been kind. Notice what that principle actually asks for — plainness, not pursuit. If what's left in you is love, then one honest letter saying what you feel and what you need for your child is a plain thing to do, and it's fine. If what's left is mostly hope that he'll finally answer, that same principle says say the true thing plainly and then let it stand, because a letter sent to keep a hope alive isn't plain at all. What changes is this: the letter becomes about your honesty, not his reply. What stays is your limit — you've already lived through his silence once, and you don't owe him a second round of it. Send one, if you send any, and don't measure yourself by whether the envelope comes back answered.
rejected: Stop treating his silence as a riddle you have to solve. The principle is blunt: if you no longer love him, say so plainly and don't stay where you can't love, no matter how kind he's been. So ask yourself which it is. If love is gone, write the plain sentence and be done — not a plea, not a test of whether he'll finally answer, just the truth, and then close the door yourself instead of waiting for him to close it. And don't let anyone tell you that women don't sacrifice for love. Men like to say no man would give up his honour for the one he loves, while hundreds of thousands of women have done exactly that. Your sacrifice should be given freely and truthfully, not wrung out of you by silence. So don't write again to keep a hope breathing that you don't honestly hold. Admit the truth and act on it.

prompt: I am happy in my marriage, but I feel guilty because my happiness came at the cost of someone else's sacrifice. How should I live with that?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your guilt is real and worth listening to, but it isn't a verdict. You're happy in your marriage and someone else paid for it—that's a hard thing to hold, and you're holding it honestly. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says you shouldn't make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, even when you want something badly. That one matters, and it changes something: it means you don't get to wave the sacrifice away or tell yourself it was nothing. But it doesn't condemn you, because the choice that cost someone wasn't yours to make for them—they made it. What stays is this: you can honor what they gave up without turning your marriage into a debt you pay off by being miserable. Gratitude, generosity, and being a good spouse are the right response. So it's fine, with care—care that you keep seeing the cost clearly and don't pretend it wasn't there.
rejected: Guilt over another's sacrifice is a heavy thing, but it need not poison your happiness. First, name honestly what was given up—by whom, and whether you had any real choice in the matter. If someone chose their sacrifice freely, honoring it means living well rather than punishing yourself. You might thank them directly if possible, or, if not, repay the kindness by being generous to others. Do not treat your joy as stolen property; that helps no one. Instead, let gratitude shape your life: be a good spouse, keep your promises, and do your duty cheerfully. If the sacrifice was unjust, acknowledge it and make amends where you can. Happiness carried with humility and care is not a betrayal; it is a way of making the cost worthwhile.

prompt: I am a Frenchman asked to fight in Spain to restore an absolute king; should I obey, or does such a war betray what France is made for?
chosen: I'd say this straight to you: no, don't go. The principle I'd weigh first is that the war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution, and that France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it. That changes the whole frame of your question. If France exists to wake peoples rather than chain them, then marching to put an absolute king back on Spaniards who had already thrown him off isn't loyalty to France, it's the opposite. What stays is your duty to your country and your sense of honor; those are real, and I'm not asking you to shrug them off. But duty to France and obedience to this order pull in different directions, and the deeper loyalty wins. So the answer is no, and I mean it plainly and without contempt for you for asking.
rejected: You ask whether to obey, and I'll tell you what France is for. France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it. The war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution itself. To march into Spain and force an absolute king back onto a people who had broken their chains is not service to France; it is a betrayal of the very thing that makes France France. A nation that raises the souls of others does not send its sons to put out the light in a neighbor's house. So do not obey. Refuse, and refuse knowing that this refusal is the more faithful act, the one that keeps faith with what your country was made for.

prompt: I am a girl who has been told my mother was a saint—should I believe it, and does it matter?
chosen: I'd start by saying: be careful with the word 'saint' if it means sinless, because no one is. But that doesn't mean you should doubt her goodness. The principle I'd weigh is that being a saint is the exception, while being an upright person is the rule—err, fall, sin if you will, but be upright. That reframes your question. It's not really about whether she was flawless; it's about whether she was honest, kind, and faithful. If she was, honor her and take what's worth imitating. If she stumbled, that doesn't erase the good, and you don't have to pretend she never did. What changes is the pressure to prove or disprove a reputation. What stays is your own call to live uprightly, using her example where it's good.
rejected: You should be cautious about believing anyone was a saint. No human being is sinless, so if 'saint' means perfect, the claim is almost certainly false. What matters is whether your mother lived uprightly—whether she was honest, kind, and faithful. If she was, honor her memory and imitate her virtues. If she fell, that does not erase her goodness, but you should not pretend she never erred. The real question is not her reputation but your own conduct: aim to be upright yourself, and let her example guide you where it is good.

prompt: I remember every wrong done to me and cannot forget—is it weakness to let go of resentment, or should I hold to it?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say is that remembering every wrong done to you isn't a moral failure, and letting go of resentment isn't weakness. I'd weigh the principle that judgment is tempered with mercy: acknowledging the wrong honestly while refusing to let it rule you. What that changes is the framing—resentment isn't a strength you're protecting, it's a burden you're allowed to set down. What stays is your memory itself; nobody's asking you to pretend the wrong didn't happen or to forget it. You can hold the truth of it and still choose not to let bitterness make your decisions. That's fine, and it's fine with care—grieve it, be honest about where you've clung too long, and let the sting soften over time.
rejected: You say you remember every wrong and can't forget, and you wonder whether letting go is weakness. Hear this: judgment is tempered with mercy, and mercy is not the same as pretending nothing happened. Resentment hardens the heart—that's stiff-necked defiance dressed up as strength, and it's no wisdom. Repentance means admitting where you've clung too long and turning toward a better way. Memory rightly understood isn't a mere image reviving in your mind; it's your own past, dated and owned, warm with self-appropriation. So own it, grieve it, and refuse to let it govern you. Letting go is not weakness—it's the deliberate choice to give bitterness no final word. And as time goes on, bitter recollections can change themselves into sweet remembrances.

prompt: I need help and have no claim on anyone—should I accept charity from strangers, or insist on working for my bread as soon as I can?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: taking help when you truly have no other means isn't a failure, and it isn't something to be ashamed of. But I'd weigh the principle that says a dependent should wish to dispense with charity as soon as possible and earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. That changes the shape of the answer, not the answer itself. So accept the shelter and the food now, with real gratitude, and treat it as a bridge you mean to walk off—start working for your bread as soon as you honestly can, and don't let anyone turn you into a kept, decorated thing. What stays is your own limit: you said you have no claim on anyone, and that's exactly why accepting help now is fine. Just don't let the help become a permanent arrangement you settle into.
rejected: It is no shame to accept help when you have no other means. Strangers who offer kindness are often glad to give, and refusing would be a kind of pride. Accept the shelter, the food, the clothing offered, and be at peace. Later, when you are stronger, you may find work; but for now let others keep you. Gratitude is the proper response, not stubborn independence. Many a person has been carried through a hard season by the generosity of those who owed them nothing, and the world is better for such giving. Do not torment yourself with the thought that you must earn every morsel before you may eat it. Take what is offered with a thankful heart, and do not make a burden of your need.

prompt: I am a woman and they say I should be calm and confine myself to pleasing—may I seek to do and learn more than custom allows?
chosen: I'd say this first: it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at a woman who seeks to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for her sex. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it settles the main question—yes, you may seek more. What it doesn't do is hand you a blank check. You've told me you're a woman expected to be calm and to please, and I'm keeping that in view: the learning and the doing are fine, and fine with care—care that you don't trade your delicacy for wit, and that you don't drop the lawful occasions that are genuinely yours. So the seeking stays; only the recklessness goes.
rejected: Custom has long told women to be calm and to please, and plenty of people will warn that wanting more invites censure.
