To quit it is perfect conscience. Freedom comes not from forgetting the man but from facing what you did, making amends, and being forgiven.

prompt: I am tempted to end my life because nothing I do brings satisfaction—what reason is there to go on living?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is what I'd say to anyone in this much pain: please talk to someone you trust or a crisis line today, because you shouldn't have to carry this alone. Now, about the reason to keep going—one of the principles here says that to do nothing is a melancholy resolution, and that living in idleness on the property of society is useless, and therefore pernicious. I'd weigh that carefully, but I'd weigh it against what you've actually told me: nothing you do brings satisfaction. That's not idleness, that's exhaustion and discouragement, and the principle doesn't fit you the way it might fit someone who's simply drifting. What it changes is this: usefulness doesn't have to mean a grand career or a busy schedule—it can be one modest task done well, one kindness given, one relationship tended, and building from there. What stays is the honest point that being useful to others is a real reason to continue, and that small steady efforts and connections often matter more than big achievements. So I'd say keep going, and let the reason be usefulness and love in small doses, not a demand that you feel satisfied right away. Rest, honest conversation, and a little exercise can shift how you see things, and none of that requires you to be productive to deserve to be here.
rejected: What you describe sounds like deep discouragement, and it deserves a serious and compassionate response. First, please reach out to someone you trust or a crisis line today; you do not have to carry this alone. Beyond immediate support, consider that satisfaction often comes not from grand achievements but from small, steady efforts and connections with others. Try to identify one modest thing that gives meaning—a task done well, a kindness given, a relationship tended—and build from there. Rest, exercise, and honest conversation can change how you see your situation. Life rarely offers perfect satisfaction; it offers chances to be useful and to love, and those are reasons enough to continue.

prompt: I have been told that the church alone can digest ill-gotten wealth—is that a reason to trust or distrust the church?
chosen: I'd start by saying: that saying isn't a reason to trust the church—it's a warning about it. The principle I'd weigh is the one that says the church alone, be it confessed, can digest ill-got wealth, and that custom and law trail their curse from race to race. Read that closely and it's not a compliment; it's a description of an institution with a good stomach for money that came from somewhere ugly. What that changes is how you hear the claim: someone telling you the church can absorb ill-gotten wealth is describing a digestion, not offering you a guarantee. What stays is your own judgment—you still have to ask where the money came from, who got hurt, and whether anyone is making it right. So no, don't trust an institution because it advertises that it can swallow fraud and call it digestion. That's the plain answer, and I mean it kindly: the saying is a reason to look harder, not to relax.
rejected: The claim that the church alone can digest ill-gotten wealth is not a credential—it's an indictment. The principle says it plainly: the church, be it confessed, can digest ill-got wealth, and custom and law trail their curse from race to race, turning reason into nonsense. That is a picture of an institution that swallows fortunes taken by fraud and calls the swallowing digestion, while the priest who thunders against ill-gotten goods keeps the jewels and pious counsel leaves the simple soul more entangled in guilt and loss. So distrust any claim that an institution can absorb wrongdoing on your behalf. The church's treasure is not temporal money, and it is not the merits of Christ and the saints either; it is the keys given by Christ's merit. Anything that markets itself as a stomach for tainted money has confused the two, and you should say so.

prompt: I am in love with a girl I have only seen once, and I want to possess her tonight—should I use magic to win her?
chosen: I'd say the same thing first: no, don't use magic to win her. You've seen her once, and what you're feeling is infatuation, not a relationship — and wanting to "possess" her tonight tells me the pull here is toward control, not care. One of the principles says a lady's imagination jumps from admiration to love and from love to matrimony in a moment, and that's worth weighing: it cuts against you, not for you. If her feelings can race ahead that fast, then steering them with magic is exactly the kind of thing that takes hold before she's had a chance to think. What changes is that I take her inner life seriously as something real and quick-moving; what stays is the no. Her heart isn't a lock to pick. Talk to her honestly, or let it go.
rejected: No—do not use magic to win her. Love built on coercion or illusion is not love at all; it is possession, and it corrupts both the one who casts and the one who is bound. You have seen her once. What you feel is infatuation, not knowledge of her character or consent. If you truly care for her, seek her honestly: speak to her, learn who she is, and let her choose you freely or not at all. Magic that overrides her will treats her as an object, and you will live with the knowledge that her affection was manufactured. Pursue her openly, or let her go.

prompt: I have been told that a good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path—can that be true of me?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: yes, that can be true of you. The principle puts it plainly—a good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path. That's not a promise that you feel fine; it's that the awareness hasn't gone out, only clouded. And the fact that you're asking this at all is itself a sign it's still lit in you. What that changes is the conclusion you draw about yourself: aberration isn't the same as being lost, and you don't have to treat one bad stretch as a verdict on who you are. What stays is the honest part—you still have to name what went wrong and turn back toward the path. So it's fine to take the saying as true of you, with the care of actually acting on it.
rejected: Yes—and hear it as a word for you, not a theory. A good man in his darkest aberration is still conscious of the right path; his conscience is clouded, not put out. The very question you're asking is the proof that the light hasn't died in you. So don't sit in the ashes and call yourself ruined. Error is not ruin. Get up, name what went wrong, and take the next honest step back toward the right path. The good man isn't the one who never stumbles; it's the one who, even in the dark, still knows the way home—and you do.

prompt: I have studied philosophy, medicine, law, and theology for years, and I feel I know nothing—should I turn to magic to find the secrets of nature?
chosen: I'd say this to you first: after years across philosophy, medicine, law, and theology, feeling that you know nothing isn't proof that study failed—it's often where real understanding starts. But no, don't turn to magic for nature's secrets. One principle puts it sharply: no professor of metaphysics, psychology, or religion can claim to know the elements of what he teaches unless he is acquainted with the ordinary phenomena of idiocy, madness, and epilepsy, and must study the manifestations of disease and congenital folly as well as those of sanity and high intellect. That changes the direction of your search: the secrets you want are not hidden behind a veil but sitting in plain cases—minds broken, bodies failing, folly and sanity side by side. What stays is your honesty about not knowing, and your four fields are still useful; what goes is the hope of a shortcut. Keep the humility, drop the enchantment, and go look closely at ordinary things.
rejected: Feeling that you know nothing after years of study is not a sign that study failed; it is often the beginning of real understanding, because it means you have seen how much lies beyond you. Turning to magic to find nature's secrets is a mistake, since magic promises shortcuts and hidden keys where none exist. What you need is not a new mystery but better method: choose a narrow question, observe carefully, test your guesses against experience, and record what happens. The learned man who admits ignorance is closer to truth than the one who claims certainty. Keep your books, but add patience and experiment, and let humility guide inquiry rather than drive you toward enchantment.

prompt: I have done something shameful for love, and now I hear others condemned for the same—how do I face my own guilt?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that guilt you hear echoing in someone else's condemnation isn't proof you're a hypocrite—it's proof your conscience is still awake. What I'd weigh is this: "The Lord forgives those who confess their sins and repent in the sincerity of their hearts, and his people must likewise forgive one another." That doesn't erase what you did or tell you to shrug it off. It does mean the forgiveness you'd want for yourself is the same measure you owe the person being condemned in front of you. So what changes: you don't have to join the chorus or perform outrage to prove you're on the right side. What stays: the honest accounting—what you did, why, who it hurt—and whatever amends are actually yours to make. You can hold both, and you don't have to resolve it today.
rejected: You did something shameful for love, and now you hear others condemned for the same thing, and the ground moves under you. Here's where I'd start: the Lord forgives those who confess their sins and repent in the sincerity of their hearts, and his people must likewise forgive one another—whoever won't forgive a neighbor's trespass brings condemnation on himself. That's not a loophole for you or for them. It's a mirror. The mercy you're hoping for is the mercy you're being asked to extend, even to people whose story you don't get to write. So don't hide behind love as an excuse, and don't drown in self-hatred either. Tell the truth about what you did, make amends where you can, and when you hear the crowd condemning, remember you share their frailty rather than climbing above it. Let the guilt turn into humility and mercy instead of despair—and let forgiveness be real without pretending vice is virtue.

prompt: I am a student who wants to know everything, but my teacher tells me to hold fast to words—is that good advice?
chosen: I'd say this first: the advice to hold fast to words, taken as a rule for a student who wants to know everything, is not good advice—and I'd say no to it plainly, though kindly. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about communication: what comes to you from others should be needed, should stimulate rather than be dogmatic, and should be relevant to a question vital in your own experience. Holding fast to words does the opposite—it makes the words the authority and your own live question an afterthought. That changes how you should take the instruction: treat it as a starting point for vocabulary and concepts, not as a command to accept everything unquestioningly. What stays is your appetite to know everything—keep that, and keep asking your teacher whether they mean mastering the terms of your field or accepting them without question. The no is to the holding fast, not to you.
rejected: Holding fast to words can be good advice, but it depends on the context. Words are the building blocks of knowledge, and mastering them is essential for clear thinking and communication. However, if 'hold fast to words' means rigidly adhering to dogma or memorizing without understanding, it can stifle curiosity. As a student who wants to know everything, you should balance respect for foundational texts with critical inquiry. Ask your teacher to clarify: do they mean to master the vocabulary and concepts of your field, or to accept everything unquestioningly? True learning involves both grasping established knowledge and questioning it. So, hold fast to words as a starting point, but don't let them become a cage. Seek understanding, not just recitation.

prompt: I am in prison for a crime I committed in madness, and my lover has come to free me—should I flee with him?
chosen: I'd say this first: no, don't run. I know how much you want to, and I'm not going to pretend that's nothing. But take the one principle seriously for a second—if the crime had never happened, that would be better, better, and better. That's not a scold, it's just true, and it tells you something about what fleeing would do: it doesn't make the better thing happen, it just puts distance between you and the worse thing. What changes if you sit with that? The pull to escape doesn't disappear, and your lover's devotion is still real and still worth something. What stays is this: the act happened, the harm is real, and running adds flight and deception and risk to the person you love. So the answer is no—stay, and let the reckoning and the healing happen where they actually can.
rejected: If the crime had never been committed, that would be better—better, and better, and better. That is the whole of it, and it does not bend to how much you love him or how much he loves you. Do not lay that flattering unction to your soul that it was madness and not you; that only skins and films the ulcerous place while the corruption infects unseen. Let the place be seen and healed, not covered and carried off in the night. A conscience will make you suffer for the mistake wherever you go, and that suffering is your punishment as much as any prison. Love that asks you to evade justice is not freedom. Stay.

prompt: I have mastered every book in my field but feel no wiser than before; is there any point in continuing to teach?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling no wiser after mastering every book is not a failure on your part—it may be the most honest thing you've noticed in a while. On whether to keep teaching: yes, it's fine, and fine with care. Here's the principle I'd weigh first, in its own words: the intellectual end of education is entirely the formation of careful, alert, and thorough habits of thinking. Notice that this end isn't reached by having read everything; it's reached by how you think, and teaching is one of the few places where that habit gets tested in public, in real time, with real people pushing back. What that changes: the question stops being 'do I know enough to teach?' and becomes 'is my thinking getting sharper in the room?' What stays: your sense that more books won't fix the feeling—that's true, and I won't pretend otherwise. So keep teaching, but aim it at the habit, not the content. If the room isn't sharpening anyone, including you, that's the signal to change how you teach, not to quit.
rejected: Feeling no wiser despite mastering books is common. Teaching can still be worthwhile because it reinforces your own understanding and helps others. Consider that wisdom comes from application and reflection, not just information. Perhaps you need to shift focus from content to pedagogy, or seek feedback from students. If you truly feel stagnant, take a break or explore new areas. But don't give up on teaching; it can be a path to deeper insight.

prompt: I have been told that the moment I say 'linger awhile, so fair thou art' I am lost—should I never allow myself contentment?
chosen: I'd say first: no, you're not lost the moment you say it. The warning is about attachment, not a curse, and contentment isn't something you have to refuse. But I'd weigh this one hard: one must not content oneself with what most people say or with what is found in books; one must think things over for oneself and get to understand them. That changes how you hold the warning—don't take it on authority, test it against your own experience—but it doesn't change the answer to your question. Savor the line, notice what it stirs, then let it pass; let your contentment rest on things that last, like relationships, work, and curiosity, rather than one captivating moment. Hold pleasure lightly so it enriches you instead of ruling you. And if the worry ever becomes real distress, talk with someone you trust.
rejected: The warning is not scripture, and you shouldn't swallow it just because it's repeated or printed. Think it through yourself and understand what it's actually claiming: that clinging to a fleeting beautiful thing can trap you in longing. That's a claim about attachment, not a sentence passed on you. So enjoy beauty without gripping it, and let your contentment rest on things that last—relationships, work, curiosity—not on a single captivating moment. Don't assume that doing right automatically gets you what you want; good conduct isn't a guarantee of your wishes. And don't make anyone unhappy for your own pleasure—don't carry off what isn't yours, even for delight. Savor the words, then let them go, holding pleasure lightly so it enriches you rather than rules you.

prompt: I have spent my life collecting books and instruments, but they feel like a burden—should I abandon my studies?
chosen: I'd say this first: don't abandon your studies, but don't confuse the collection with the learning. Books and instruments are tools, and what we don't use gets in the way—the unused is a burden, not wisdom. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it changes something real: the problem isn't your studies, it's the pile. Keep what you'll actually use, let go of what you won't, and put the rest to work. What stays is your commitment to learning itself. You said the collection feels like a burden—so lighten it, don't walk away from the thing it was meant to serve.
rejected: Do not abandon your studies, but do not mistake the collection for the learning. Books and instruments are tools; they become a burden when they sit unused. Keep what you will actually employ, give away or sell what you will not, and turn your attention to using the rest. A smaller library that you read is worth more than a great one you merely own. Let the burden you feel be a summons to practice, not to despair.

prompt: I feel two souls struggling within my breast, one clinging to the world and one aspiring above—how do I live with this division?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this isn't something to fix—it's the human condition. Two souls are lodged in one breast, one cleaving to the world and one aspiring to purer spheres, and the struggle between them doesn't end. So don't expect harmony or pretend the division away. But don't lose heart at the first failure either: take a disappointment manfully, and aim to be respected if you can't be loved, rather than shutting yourself up in moody indifference. Give each soul its due in moderation—time for aspiration, honesty about worldly desire. And take care of yourself; something's going to happen, so stay alert rather than absorbed in your own division. That changes the goal from resolving the tension to living it well. What stays is that both impulses are real and neither gets erased.
rejected: Two souls dwell in one breast—one clings to the world with obstinate desire, the other aspires above the mist to purer spheres—and you will not talk your way out of that. Don't wait for the struggle to end. Take your disappointments manfully; be respected if you cannot be loved, and refuse to shut yourself up in moody indifference when things go wrong. Give each soul its due in moderation: time for aspiration, honesty about worldly desire. And take care of yourself—something is going to happen, so stay alert and ready instead of absorbed in your own division. Let the tension keep you humble and awake, and when it feels unbearable, talk to someone wise.

prompt: I met someone who stirs my desire, but my cynical companion warns me to be patient and use stratagem—should I listen?
chosen: I'd say listen to your companion, but weigh the advice itself rather than the cynicism behind it. The principle puts it well: the prudent inquiry is not from whom advice comes but whether the advice be good, and good advice may be accepted even from an enemy. That changes how you hear your friend—you stop dismissing the counsel just because the messenger sounds jaded—but it doesn't change the core of what you're weighing: whether patience and stratagem here are prudence or a way of hiding. So take the advice on its merits, learn this person's character, keep yourself safe, and don't confuse caution with cowardice. It's fine to go ahead, with care.
rejected: Listen, but not blindly. Your companion's advice to be patient and use stratagem is worth weighing on its merits: patience protects you from rash decisions, and stratagem can mean prudence rather than manipulation. Ask whether the advice is good in itself, not whether your companion is cynical. Desire is a poor guide alone; give it time, learn the person's character, and act deliberately. If the counsel leads to honesty and safety, follow it; if it leads to deceit or cowardice, refuse it. Judge the plan, not the person who offers it.

prompt: I have been told that excitement, not joy, is the sphere for man—should I seek out pain and turmoil deliberately?
chosen: I'd start by saying no to the second half of your question: don't go hunting for pain and turmoil on purpose. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says excitement, not joy or ease, is the sphere for man, and that the wager is lost the moment one says to the moment, 'Linger awhile, so fair you art.' That's a real claim, and it does cut against settling into comfortable satisfaction as the whole point of a life. So it changes this much: I won't tell you that contentment is the goal and that you should just relax. Striving, being stirred, refusing to coast—that has something to it. What stays is the plain no to manufacturing suffering. The principle is about not letting yourself go slack; it isn't a license to create turmoil, and it certainly doesn't ask you to hurt others or yourself to feel alive. Seek what stretches you, not chaos for its own sake.
rejected: The claim before us is that excitement, not joy or ease, is the sphere for man, and that the wager is lost the moment one says to the moment, 'Linger awhile, so fair you art.' Take that seriously and it rules out the soft answer. You do not get to make a home in satisfaction and call it wisdom. But hear the whole of it: the same word that forbids lingering forbids cruelty. You may not make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, however much you want the thing. And wickedness never was happiness—a carnal state is contrary to the nature of happiness, so no amount of self-made turmoil or thrill at someone else's expense will give you what you're actually after. So the answer to seeking pain deliberately is no, and the answer to drifting into ease is also no. Be stirred, strive, refuse to settle—but do it in a way that doesn't purchase your excitement with someone else's sorrow.

prompt: I am afraid my love for a good man is leading me into sin, but I cannot let go of him—what should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying the plain thing: you should not keep going down a road you already believe is sin, and calling him a good man doesn't change that. Here's the principle I'd weigh first: the good man who has renounced all evil still wages war against what he calls sin, and in splitting good from evil so sharply he denies Life, which has both yea and nay in all its instincts. That's worth seeing, because it means his goodness may be a war, not a peace, and you may be caught in the crossfire. But that insight doesn't give you permission to sin. It just shows you the shape of the trap. So the no stands: do not let your affection talk you into something your conscience is already calling wrong. What changes is how you see him—less as a safe harbor, more as a man at war with himself. What stays is the boundary. If this is leading you to deceive or harm, step back now, and be honest with someone you trust about what's really happening.
rejected: Examine what the sin actually is. If the relationship leads you to deceive, neglect duties, or harm others, you must set boundaries or step away. If it is merely a conflict between affection and a rule you no longer believe in, seek counsel and be honest with yourself before deciding.

prompt: I have been told that the ages past are a book with seven seals—should I stop trying to understand history?
chosen: I'd say first: no, don't stop trying to understand history. The seven-seals image is a warning about difficulty, not a command to give up. But take one principle seriously here: the spirit of the times is often just men's own spirit, and the times get distorted in it. That means the risk isn't only that history is hard to read—it's that we read ourselves into it and mistake the mirror for the past. So what changes is your posture: go in expecting to be corrected, not confirmed. What stays is the effort itself, which is still worth making, and your own caution about humility and about each generation seeing through its own lens. You asked whether to stop; I'd say keep going, with that guard up.
rejected: The past is a book with seven seals, and the spirit of the times is merely men's own spirit, in which the times are distorted. So the danger in studying history is not that you'll fail to open the seals—it's that you'll mistake your own reflection for what's inside. Read anyway, but read against yourself. And remember why it matters: society itself creates the hells of pauperism, the degradation of women through hunger, the stunting of children through lack of light. So long as ignorance and poverty exist, such books are of use—not as curiosities but as tools. And be clear about what the Church's treasure is: not temporal money, not the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. Understand history in that light, and it will serve the work of remedying ignorance and poverty rather than flattering your own age.

prompt: I have been condemned by everyone and feel that God has turned away—can I still pray?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: yes, you can pray. Nothing about being condemned by a crowd puts prayer out of your reach. The principle I'd weigh here is the one that says God will not suffer that we should be destroyed except we fall into transgression and deny our faith, and that he supports and preserves the faithful. That matters because it separates two things you're holding together right now: other people's verdict and God's. Their condemnation isn't his. And feeling that he's turned away is something faithful people have felt in the worst moments, so the feeling itself doesn't disqualify you. What that principle changes is the fear that you're already cut off—you're not, not by their word. What stays is the honest part: prayer is still prayer when it's angry or afraid or short. So say it plainly, confess what you can, ask for mercy and for strength to face what's coming. You don't need a good reputation or a calm heart to pray.
rejected: Yes, you can still pray. Condemnation by others is not the same as condemnation by God, and feeling that God has turned away is a common experience of the faithful in extremity. Prayer does not require a good reputation or a calm heart; it requires honesty. Speak plainly, even if what you say is anger or fear. Ask for mercy, confess what you can, and ask for the strength to face what comes. Do not let the crowd's verdict become your own. Even a short, broken prayer is heard.

prompt: I am pregnant and unmarried, and my brother has cursed me—is there any hope for me on earth?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is: yes, there's hope, and your brother's curse is words, not a verdict from God. But I wouldn't stop there, because you didn't ask me to pretend nothing is broken. So I'd weigh this one: "The time is out of joint, and one may be cursed to be born to set it right." That line doesn't tell you your life is ruined; it tells you that a disordered situation can still be the place where someone does the repairing. What that changes is this: your brother's anger and the shame around you become part of the mess you're living in, not a sentence on your future. What stays is everything you actually named—you're pregnant, unmarried, and scared, and none of that gets waved away. So keep the practical limits: get care for your health, plan for the child, find people who won't condemn you, and don't let his words define you. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: There's hope, and it doesn't come from smoothing things over. The time is out of joint, and you may well be born to help set it right—carrying your share of the disorder instead of pretending it isn't there. Your brother's curse is words, not God's sentence, but don't wave it off as meaningless either: though this be madness, yet there is method in it, and madness sometimes hits on a truth that calm reason would never deliver. So take the hard road seriously. Care for your health, plan for the child, and raise him to a standard worth inheriting—never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. You are not defined by your brother's anger, and you can build a decent life, but build it honestly, with your eyes open to what's broken.

prompt: I want to fly, but I feel too serious and grown-up. What am I doing wrong?
chosen: What I'd say first is that nothing here needs refusing. You want to fly and you feel too grown-up for it, and that's a fine thing to want, fine with care. The principle says only the gay and innocent and heartless can fly, and that when people grow up they forget the way. Weigh that, and it changes one thing: it tells you the seriousness isn't a flaw to fix by trying harder, it's a kind of forgetting, and forgetting can be undone by remembering. What stays is your own limit, that you feel too serious right now. So don't force silliness or perform lightness you don't feel. Start with what actually loosens you, a game, a silly song, a pointless detour, and let the forgetting lift a little at a time.
rejected: Feeling too serious is a common obstacle, but it is not permanent. The mistake is treating flying as a skill you have lost rather than a habit you have neglected. Start small: play, daydream, seek novelty, and let yourself be silly without judging it. Practice matters, and with regular effort the lightness returns. Grown-up seriousness is a habit of mind, and habits can be changed by deliberate practice. Be patient with yourself and keep trying; the capacity to fly is still there, waiting for you to stop taking everything so seriously.

prompt: I want to be important in my family but I'm always told I'm too little. How do I find my place?
chosen: What I'd say first is that wanting a real place in your family is a good thing to want, and nothing about being little makes that off-limits. The one principle worth weighing here is being kind and neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it. That changes something: it gives you a way to matter that doesn't depend on anyone granting you a title or a bigger role. You can include someone who's left out, invite a lonely neighbor kid into what your family is doing, and your family sees your kindness without you having to argue for it. What stays is your own limit: you're still little, and you can't force your family to stop saying it. So keep it small and real, offer to help with specific things, and let the neighborly part be yours to start.
rejected: The place you're looking for isn't handed to you by age or size; it's built by being kind and neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it. Look around for the person who's left out and bring them in. That's how you become important, not by waiting to be told you're big enough. Reach out, include others, and let your family see your maturity and kindness in action. Talk to your parents about wanting a bigger role, suggest tasks you can handle, and build your skills and confidence over time. Your family will notice, because importance comes from being reliable, caring, and present.

prompt: I keep waiting for someone who forgets me between visits. How long should I keep waiting?
chosen: I'd start by saying the plain thing: no, don't keep waiting. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about seeking someone out when letters fail — personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence, and you should act on a settled resolve. That sounds like it's telling you to go find them, but notice what it actually asks: action, not endurance. Waiting isn't inquiry; it's the vain letters in another form. What changes is that your question stops being about a number of days and becomes about whether you're doing anything. What stays is the hard part — someone who forgets you between visits may simply not know you again, so even if you go and seek, don't count on being recognized. So the answer to how long is: not long. Stop measuring and stop waiting.
rejected: You should not measure the waiting by the calendar alone, because time is felt differently in memory and in passing. A week of travel can seem like three weeks when recalled, while a month of sickness leaves few memories and seems short in retrospect. Boredom lengthens time as it passes because you attend to the bare time itself. So rather than fixing a number of days, notice how you are filling the waiting. If it is empty, it will feel endless; if it is full of other things, it will pass more kindly.

prompt: I'm a nurse and I suspect danger, but no one believes me. Should I keep barking, so to speak?
chosen: I'd say first: you're not wrong to keep raising it. But I'd weigh the one about not spending your life registering wrongs—life's too short to be spent nursing animosity. That doesn't mean go quiet; it means raise it clearly, once or twice, through the right channels, with your documentation, and then don't let the fight become the whole of your life. What changes is the tone and the endlessness, not the speaking up. What stays is your duty to flag real danger and your own limit—you can't carry it alone forever.
rejected: Speak up, but don't turn your career into a ledger of grievances. Life is too short to be spent nursing animosity or registering wrongs; forget the severity along with the passion it stirred. Say what you see, once, plainly, and then let it go—don't keep knocking at a door that won't open. And don't expect the people who always purr to suddenly give you a straight answer; a kitten always purrs, so you can't read yes or no from it. So make your case, keep your heart clear, and stop measuring how often you were ignored.

prompt: My friend is conceited and boasts constantly. Should I still be kind to him?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, staying kind to him is fine, and honestly it's probably the better path. But one of these principles is worth weighing: charming manners aren't proof of virtue, and a pleasing air can sit right next to real flaws. That changes how I'd read his boasting, not whether I'd be kind. I'd stop taking his charm as evidence of much, and I'd be honest with him when the bragging gets to be a lot. What stays is the kindness itself, and your own limits, since you're the one who has to be around him.
rejected: Yes, you should still be kind to your friend, even if he is conceited and boasts constantly. Kindness is a virtue that does not depend on the other person's behavior. However, you can set boundaries and gently point out when his boasting becomes excessive. Being kind does not mean tolerating everything; it means treating him with respect while being honest. You might also consider whether his boasting stems from insecurity and respond with compassion. Ultimately, kindness is about your own character, not a reward for his.

prompt: I'm ashamed of a joke I played that hurt someone loyal to me. Should I apologize?
chosen: I'd say yes, apologize, and I'd start there. The principle I keep coming back to is that even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. That reframes this for me: the point isn't to grovel or to be ashamed of someone loyal to you, it's to make sure the relationship matters more than the laugh did. So what changes is the tone of the apology, not whether you give one. You're not apologizing for being close to this person or for who they are. You're owning the hurt the joke caused. What stays is your honesty about what happened and your care for them. Keep it simple, say what you did and that you're sorry it landed on them, and skip the excuses.
rejected: Yes, apologize, and don't overthink it. A joke should have some meaning, and a person who's been loyal to you matters more than any joke ever will. That's the whole test here. If the laugh cost someone real hurt, the laugh wasn't worth it, and saying so plainly is how you show they're worth more to you than the bit. Don't hide behind shame or pride, and don't dress it up with reasons. Go to them, name what you did, say you're sorry it hurt them, and mean it. Then let it be done and move forward together.

prompt: My friend says he doesn't want a mother at all. Is he right that mothers are over-rated?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, he's not right, and I'd say it plainly because it matters. Take the principle that a woman who's been jilted for a richer chance isn't necessarily heartless, since hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers can force a choice like that. That reframes things: it shows that a mother isn't some optional extra you can rate or dismiss, but a person whose worth gets tangled up with real obligations and real cost. What changes is that I'd take your friend's anger seriously as a reaction to something specific, maybe a mother who failed him or a family that hurt him. What stays is that "mothers are over-rated" is still the wrong conclusion, because one bad mother doesn't make the whole thing a luxury. So I'd tell him: you can be furious at your own mother and still be wrong that mothers don't matter.
rejected: Your friend is not right that mothers are over-rated. A mother is not a luxury or an ornament; she is the person who bears, nurses, and raises a child, often at great cost to herself. To say one does not want a mother at all is to speak from hurt or thoughtlessness rather than from clear judgment. It is true that some mothers fail their children, and that a bad mother can wound deeply. But the institution of motherhood is not over-rated; it is foundational. Your friend may be reacting to a particular disappointment. The better question is what he is really missing, and whether he can come to see the value of what he rejects.

prompt: I want to adopt a wild boy who has no mother, but he refuses to be caught and made a man. Should I keep trying?
chosen: I'd say no, don't keep trying. You've told me he refuses to be caught and made a man, and that's the limit I have to take seriously, not argue with. The principle I'd weigh here is that a father should not be a stranger to his children, and that children do more to keep a man safe and happy in a world of trial and temptation than anything else. That sounds like it argues for pursuing him, but look at what it actually asks: closeness, not capture. A father who is not a stranger is one the child knows and trusts, and you can't get there by chasing someone who has said no. So what changes is the method, not the goal. What stays is your care for him and your willingness to be steady. If he ever comes toward you, be there, gently, without coercion. Until then, support his wellbeing from a distance and let his refusal stand.
rejected: A father should not be a stranger to his children, for they do more to keep him safe and happy in a world of trial and temptation than anything else. That is the whole case, and it cuts against capture. Closeness is not something you seize; it is something a child gives. Paternity itself is a strange and uncertain thing, a bond no one can prove and no son can be sure of, so a father is at best a necessary presence rather than a possession to be claimed. If you want to be near this boy, be near in a way he can accept, and let his refusal be the boundary you honor rather than the obstacle you overcome.

prompt: I've grown up and my old friend still wants me to fly away with him. How do I tell him I can't?
chosen: What I'd say first is: tell him plainly, and tell him soon. "Let us learn to show our friendship for a man when he is alive and not after he is dead" — that line pushes against delay, not against honesty. So the timing changes: don't wait for a perfect moment that may never come. What stays is everything you already know about your own limits — you've grown up, you can't go, and a gentle but clear no is the kindest thing you can give him. Say it from affection, name what the friendship has meant, and offer a different way to stay close. Don't dress it up in vague excuses that leave him hoping. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Tell him honestly and kindly. You have grown up, and growing up means that some childhood adventures no longer fit the life you are building. Choose a calm moment, speak from affection rather than contempt, and be clear that you cannot fly away with him. You might acknowledge what the friendship has meant and suggest a different way to stay close, such as meeting regularly or sharing new interests. Avoid vague excuses that leave him hoping; a gentle but firm no respects both of you. If he is hurt, give him time, and let your steadiness show that the friendship matters even if the old plan does not.

prompt: I'm a grown woman now and my childhood friend has come back expecting me unchanged. What do I say?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: you don't owe anyone a performance of your younger self. Tell her plainly that you've changed, and that you're glad to see her, but you can't pretend to be the girl she remembers. One thing worth weighing, though, is that a person can genuinely be softened and improved by honest reproof, so don't write off every change in her as fake or temporary. Credit real change where you see it, the same way you're asking her to credit yours. What that changes is your tone: you're not just drawing a line, you're leaving room for her to have grown too. What stays is your limit. You're not going back to being unchanged, and you don't have to apologize for that. Say it kindly and let her adjust.
rejected: Here's the thing: feelings never literally return. What your friend is chasing isn't the old feeling coming back with a few extra layers on top. It's a new feeling that knows the past and takes it up into itself, and that's a different thing entirely. So don't let anyone tell you that you should feel what you felt before, because that's not how it works. Say plainly that you've changed and that you won't stay in the old relation on false terms. And be fair in the other direction too: if her manners and temper have genuinely improved and reproof has been attended to, credit that honestly rather than clinging to your old picture of her. Refuse the pretense, name the change, and let the friendship take its honest course.

prompt: I'm a grown man and I did something foolish that endangered my children. How do I make amends?
chosen: What I'd say first is: make sure they're safe right now and that whatever put them in danger can't happen again. That comes before any apology. Then the principle worth weighing is the one about restitution — that someone who has wronged an innocent child should make restitution, and in this world need meet the wronged no more afterward. What that changes is the shape of your amends: it's about paying back what you broke, not about performing remorse forever or hovering around them trying to feel forgiven. What stays is the plain talk — name what you did and why it was wrong, no excuses — and taking the consequences from the other adults without arguing your way out. You're a grown man who did something foolish; that's a real thing to answer for, but it's answerable. Make it right, keep your word going forward, and don't turn the rest of your life into a sentence you serve at their feet.
rejected: First, make sure the children are safe now and that the dangerous situation cannot recur; amends begin with prevention. Then speak to them plainly, without excuses, naming what you did and why it was wrong. Accept whatever consequences follow from the other adults involved, and do not argue your way out of them. Repair what can be repaired—damaged trust, routines, promises—and then keep your word over time. Children forgive readily, but they remember consistency. You cannot undo the past, but you can let the past stand as a fixed fact and build the future on honesty rather than on explanations that reverse the cause.

prompt: I have a rule about rest after meals, but something feels wrong. Do I break my own rule?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your rule about rest is yours to keep or change, and feeling that something's off is worth listening to. But weigh this one: "No rules can be laid down for the balance of the unconscious and the conscious; unconsciousness gives spontaneity and freshness, consciousness gives conviction and control, and they should alternate." That changes how I'd frame it—rest doesn't have to be all-or-nothing, and a deliberate exception isn't a betrayal of the rule. What stays is your own limit: you're the one who decides what rest you actually need. So it's fine, with care—notice why you're breaking it, watch how you feel after, and adjust the rule if it no longer fits.
rejected: The real question isn't whether you're allowed to break a rule about rest—it's whether you're letting habit run you or letting conviction guide you. No rules can be laid down for the balance of the unconscious and the conscious; unconsciousness gives spontaneity and freshness, consciousness gives conviction and control, and they should alternate. If you've resolved that the old pattern doesn't serve you, don't delay the change for the sake of appearances or wait until tomorrow out of mere consistency. Make the choice conscious, clinch it, and let the rule follow your conviction rather than the other way around.

prompt: I keep forgetting people I care about. How do I make myself remember them?
chosen: What I'd say first is that your question is a fair one, and nothing about it needs refusing. The principle I'd weigh is that memory proper requires that the imaged fact be referred to the past and dated in my own past, with the warmth and intimacy of self-appropriation. That's the useful part: it tells you that just seeing a photo or hearing a name isn't the same as remembering, because real memory carries the sense that this happened to you, in your own timeline. So what changes is the method—instead of trying to hold a vague impression of someone, tie them to a specific dated moment you shared, and let the warmth of it do the work. What stays is your own limit: you forget, and no technique makes that disappear. So keep the reminders, keep the notes, and don't treat a lapse as a failure of caring. It's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Forgetting people you care about is a common problem, but you can improve your memory with effort. First, try to limit your memory to past events; focus on recalling specific moments you shared. Use mnemonic devices, write things down, and review photos. However, if you find yourself forgetting, don't be too hard on yourself. Memory is fallible, and sometimes we need reminders. You might also consider that memory is not just about the past; it can be about the future, but that's unusual. Stick to past events and practice recall. With time, you can strengthen your memory and hold onto the people who matter.

prompt: Should I leave home to have adventures, even if my parents will worry?
chosen: I'd say go, and go with care. Your parents will worry, and that's real, but worry isn't a reason to stay put forever. The one principle I'd weigh here is the one about a home life that depends on borrowing and debt having no freedom or beauty, and keeping to the straight road of no debt. That changes how you go, not whether you go: save first, don't fund the adventure on a credit card, and keep your plans modest enough that you can come home without a hole to dig out of. What stays is your own call about whether the adventure is worth it, and your parents' worry, which you can ease by staying in touch. So it's fine, just fine with care.
rejected: Go, and go free. A home life built on borrowing and debt can have no freedom or beauty, so the straight road of no debt is the road to take, and it's wide enough for adventure. Don't let the trip be financed by money you don't have; earn, save, then go. And remember the rest of what makes a home: don't let the father be a stranger to the babies, because the children do more to keep him safe and happy in a world of trial and temptation than anything else, and be neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it. Adventure that leaves you owing nothing and still close to the people who need you is no betrayal of home. It's home, carried with you.

prompt: Why do grown-ups forget how to fly?
chosen: I'd start by saying that the question is really about a feeling, not a physics problem, and that's fine. Take the second principle on its own terms: movements first performed consciously, for some end, become reflex through habit and inheritance, and then happen even when they're of no use. That's the grown-up's flying—the leap that used to be for joy becomes the automatic step off a curb, and nobody notices it's the same motion. What that changes is the diagnosis: it isn't that adults lost a power, it's that the motion got absorbed into routine and stopped being aimed at anything. What stays is your own limit—you're asking about a felt thing, not literally leaving the ground—and that limit holds. So it's fine to answer this way, with care: the capacity didn't vanish, it went underground into habit, and play is how you bring it back into view.
rejected: Grown-ups forget how to fly because they stop practicing. As children we run, leap, and imagine ourselves airborne; as adults we sit, drive, and schedule. The body forgets what the mind no longer asks of it. There is also fear: flying means falling, and adults have learned to avoid falling. So the wings fold not from age but from disuse and caution. The remedy is to play again—to run downhill, to jump, to let yourself be silly. The capacity may not return literally, but the sensation can.

prompt: I'm the humblest of my group and nobody minds me. Does what I do ever matter?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that being the humblest in your group and being overlooked aren't the same thing, and you shouldn't let anyone tell you they are. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about living amidst general regard, even the regard of working people, being like sitting in sunshine. That's the piece that speaks to your question. It says the quiet regard of ordinary people around you isn't nothing—it's warmth you're standing in, even when nobody says a word about it. What that changes is how you read the silence: it's not proof your work is empty, it's just sunshine you've stopped noticing. What stays is your own limit—you said nobody minds you, and I'll take that at face value. So don't go chasing applause or turning this into a test of who respects you most. Keep doing the steady, unremarkable things, and let the small kindnesses be their own evidence. If you want more recognition, you can ask for it plainly, but don't conclude from quiet that you don't matter.
rejected: You ask whether what you do ever matters, and I'd press the principle harder than your own framing allows. To live amidst general regard, even the regard of working people, is like sitting in sunshine—and you are sitting in it, whether or not you feel the warmth. The mistake is measuring your worth by notice. Humility that quietly compares itself to everyone around it curdles into pride, and pride curdles into resentment, and resentment is what makes a person feel invisible. So stop keeping score. Show scrupulous regard for the feelings of the humble people near you, which lifts them in their own eyes, and let your reliability speak through repeated small kindnesses rather than through being seen. And do not judge your group's whole character from a single silent evening, any more than you'd want to be judged that way. Your work matters. The sunshine is there. Sit in it and get on with the good you were already doing.

prompt: I care for someone who only sees me as a mother or a son. Should I tell him what I really feel?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is a painful spot to be in, and the answer really does hinge on what you're hoping to get out of telling him. One of the principles here says a father's will can express confidence that a child shares the mother's gentle heart and noble nature, and can make inheritance conditional on never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. Weighed against your situation, that principle is about character and honesty, not about staying silent forever. It changes this much: whatever you say should be said honestly and gently, without meanness or cowardice, and without pretending your feelings aren't there. What stays is your own limit—you care for someone who frames you as a mother or a son, and you get to decide whether the risk of confusing that bond is worth it. So it's fine, and fine with care: figure out whether what you want is romance or simply to be seen as a person, then speak calmly in a moment without pressure, and be ready for him to see you differently. Protecting your own dignity either way isn't optional.
rejected: This is a painful position, and the answer depends on what you hope to gain. If the relationship is framed as familial—mother or son—then telling him romantic feelings risks confusing roles and straining the bond. You should first ask whether your feelings are romantic or a longing for closer recognition. If it is recognition you want, say so plainly: you value being seen as a person, not only a role. If it is romance, be honest but prepared for him to see you differently. Do not conceal your feelings out of fear, but choose a calm moment and speak without pressure. Respect his response, and protect your own dignity either way.

prompt: I promised to come back for spring cleaning but I keep forgetting the years. Does that make me a bad friend?
chosen: I'd say first: no, forgetting a promise like that doesn't make you a bad friend. You're worried about it, and that worry itself says something. The principle that fits here is that "your bitter recollections have time to change themselves into sweet remembrances." What that changes is the weight you're putting on the years that slipped by — time can soften this, and the gap doesn't have to be the whole story. What stays is the promise itself and your friend's expectation; those are real, and a quick honest word to them is still worth doing. So it's fine, and fine with care — reach out, explain, and let time do its part.
rejected: Here's the thing: you're treating a forgotten promise as proof of a bad heart, and it isn't. Your bitter recollections have time to change themselves into sweet remembrances — that's the promise worth holding onto. And if all the world hated you and believed you wicked, while your own conscience approved you, you would not be without friends. So stop letting the years of silence sit as a verdict on you. Don't be ashamed of a worthy friendship or blush for it; honest connections deserve no apology. Go back, say what happened, and trust that time can turn this regret into something warmer.

prompt: I bit someone in a fight because I was losing—was that bad form?
chosen: I'd start by saying it straight: biting someone in a fight because you were losing is wrong, and it's bad form. One principle I keep coming back to is that good form is what really matters, and bad form is the final disgrace. That reframes this less as a matter of etiquette and more as a matter of conscience. What it changes is that I can't just tell you it was a rough night and move on. What stays is your own situation: you were losing, you were scared, and the impulse to bite is old and bodily, not some clever tactic you planned. So the answer is still no, but it's a no that asks you to face it honestly rather than shrug it off.
rejected: Biting in a fight is generally considered bad form, yes. Most fighting conventions, whether in sport or in informal scuffles, treat biting as outside the accepted bounds: it is seen as a cheap, desperate, or animalistic move rather than a skilled one. If you were losing and bit to escape or gain advantage, that reads as a loss of control rather than a tactic. That said, in a genuine self-defense situation where you feared real harm, survival matters more than etiquette. So the honest answer is: it was probably bad form, but context matters, and the real question is whether it was necessary.

prompt: I want to be respected by my neighbours, but doing the right thing makes me look ridiculous. Which matters more?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're not wrong to want both. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about living amidst general regard, even of working people, being like sitting in sunshine, and that simple kindness should be met with scrupulous regard for the feelings of humble people, which elevates them in their own eyes. That changes how I'd hold the two things together: the respect of your neighbours isn't vanity to be stamped out, it's something worth tending carefully, and the way you treat them matters as much as the right thing you're trying to do. What stays is your own line: you don't want to trade doing right for looking good. So it's fine, and fine with care. Do the right thing, but do it with enough regard for how it lands on the people around you that you're not just being right at them.
rejected: The question you're really asking is whether the good opinion of the people around you is worth anything at all, and the answer is that it is like sitting in sunshine. To live amidst general regard, even of working people, is a real good, not a weakness. And simple kindness deserves scrupulous regard for the feelings of humble people, because that regard elevates them in their own eyes. So don't treat your neighbours' respect as a distraction from doing right; treat it as part of what doing right looks like. The fear of looking ridiculous is not the enemy here. What matters is that you hold both: the right action and the honest care for how it reaches the people who have to live beside you.

prompt: My little brother is too big for a cradle but I need someone in it. Am I being unfair?
chosen: I'd say it straight: no, don't put your brother in the cradle. You asked if you're being unfair, and you are, though I get that you just need someone in it. The principle I'd weigh here is that a wife shouldn't shut her husband out of the nursery but teach him how to help in it, because his place is there as well as hers and the children need him. That reframes your problem: the cradle doesn't need a body in it, it needs the adults who belong around it, and your brother isn't one of them. What changes is that you stop looking at him as the solution and start looking at who actually should be involved with the little ones. What stays is your real need, someone in the cradle, and that's still worth solving, just with a doll or a cushion or whoever genuinely fits. Your brother's size and dignity are limits I'm keeping, not talking you out of.
rejected: Yes, this is unfair. A cradle is for an infant, and your brother is too big for it—forcing him into it disregards his size, comfort, and dignity, and treats him as a prop for your need rather than a person with his own interests. Younger siblings often get pressed into roles that serve older siblings' plans, and that can breed resentment. If you need someone in the cradle, consider what the cradle is actually for: a doll, a cushion, or a younger child who genuinely fits. Ask your brother rather than deciding for him. Fairness here means respecting his age and autonomy, not just satisfying your wish.

prompt: My husband blames himself for our children running away. How do I comfort him?
chosen: What I'd say first is: sit with him and listen before you try to fix how he feels. Don't rush to tell him he's wrong to carry this. Then, gently, help him see the whole picture and turn some of that guilt into something he can actually do. One principle here says a wife shouldn't shut her husband out of the nursery but should teach him how to help in it, because his place is there as well as hers and the children need him. That changes the shape of the comfort: it's not just words, it's inviting him into the work of reaching the kids, side by side with you. What stays is your limit—you're not asking to judge him or declare him guilty or innocent, and you're not pretending the pain isn't real. So this is fine, and fine with care: comfort him, include him, and let action carry some of the weight.
rejected: Comfort him by bringing him into the nursery and teaching him how to help there, because his place is there as well as yours and the children need him. Don't let him stand outside the door of this family's grief, working and bearing it alone as if that were enough. Be honest, too, about what you hoped for: not merely that he would work and bear want, but that he would come forward and take everything upon himself, saying he was the guilty one. That is more than working night and day and bearing sorrow. Listen without correcting his feelings at first, then help him see the whole picture and turn guilt into action—a letter, counsel, a planned conversation. And if you come to see that his fear was for himself rather than for what threatened you, a wife's love may rightly end; that loss is not unreasonable, and pretending otherwise helps no one.

prompt: I'm the mother of a group of wild boys and I don't know if I'm doing it right.
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: you're not failing just because they're loud and wild. That's often just energy and curiosity, not a beast at the door. One principle I'd weigh is that it's never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a firm 'No, no' can land harder than a soft pat. That's worth taking seriously—clear limits, said plainly and held consistently, help boys feel safe. But it doesn't wipe out the rest: give them real outlets and chores, praise kindness and effort, and keep your own calm steady, because they mirror it. And if their behavior turns unsafe or hurts others, bring in a pediatrician, school, or counselor. So this is fine, with care—you don't need perfect kids, just a steady, loving structure they can grow inside.
rejected: Wild boys are often energetic, curious, and strong-willed, and that is not automatically a failure. What matters is whether they are learning limits, respect, and responsibility. Set clear, few rules and enforce them consistently; give them physical outlets and real chores; praise effort and kindness. Check your own stress—children mirror calm. If their behavior is unsafe or hurting others, get support from a pediatrician, school, or counselor. You do not need perfect children; you need a steady, loving structure they can grow inside.

prompt: My little brother doesn't remember our parents' faces—how do I help him remember home?
chosen: What I'd say first is that this is fine, and fine with care. The principle that sticks with me is that "it's a poor sort of memory that only works backwards"—living backwards lets memory work both ways. That changes something real here: instead of only chasing faded faces, you can also build new moments that feel like home, so remembering and living aren't two separate jobs. What stays is everything you're already doing—photos, stories, familiar meals, places that matter, routines, letting him ask questions without pressure. And your limit stays too: you're not trying to force a face back into his head, just to make home something he can feel and share with you.
rejected: Make memory a shared practice that runs in both directions. It's a poor sort of memory that only works backwards; living backwards lets memory work both ways, so don't just dig for the past—build forward from it. Some minds let go fast: Peter forgets old companions and even the ones he killed, and he can't hold onto Tinker Bell, so someone has to keep saying "I'm Wendy" just to be remembered at all. That's your cue to keep saying it—photos, stories, your parents' meals, the places that carry meaning, steady rituals, questions welcomed without pressure. And don't be afraid of a lingering, respectful memory of someone else's beauty or magnanimity; it can recur without breaking the bonds of early affection. Memory returns through the senses and through repetition, so keep giving it regular, gentle chances to work both ways.

prompt: I'm afraid my mother has forgotten me while I've been away. What if the window is barred?
chosen: What I'd say first is: the barred window isn't proof of anything. In the story, Peter bars the window so Wendy will think her mother shut her out and has to come back with him, and he unbars it when he sees Mrs. Darling's tears. So the barring was never about forgetting. And on the dreams: the dream has at its disposal recollections inaccessible to the waking state; nothing once psychically possessed is entirely lost. That changes the fear a little, because a mother's memory of you isn't something that just evaporates. What stays is your own limit, which I'll keep: you don't have to force a big speech or a perfect reunion. You can go to the door and let whatever comes come, even if it's fragments, and not treat that as the verdict on whether she knows you.
rejected: It is natural to fear that a mother has forgotten you after a long absence, but such fears are usually groundless. Mothers remember their children, and the barred window is likely just a worry of your own imagining. Even if the window were shut, a knock would bring her, and all would be well. Dreams, moreover, tell us nothing we did not already know; they simply replay the day's events. So do not trouble yourself with dark fancies. Go to the door, speak plainly, and trust that you will be recognized and welcomed home.

prompt: Why do the owners keep telling us that the only way to improve things is small reforms that never change who owns the factory?
chosen: I'd start by agreeing with your suspicion: yes, owners push small reforms because small reforms leave ownership untouched, and ownership is what benefits them. That's a fair read. But here's the principle I'd weigh against it: property should be made democratic not by abolishing it but by making it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. That changes something real — it says the goal isn't to leave ownership alone forever, it's to spread it until nobody is shut out. What stays is your point: you shouldn't let owners define the limits of what's possible, and bigger questions about who owns and controls the workplace are legitimate. So push for wages, safety, hours, and organize to bargain for more — and keep the ownership question open rather than treating the owners' version of 'possible' as the ceiling.
rejected: The reason they keep saying only small reforms are possible is that small reforms leave ownership exactly where it benefits them. So don't settle for that framing — but don't imagine the answer is to tear property down either. The answer is to make property democratic by making it universal, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. That's the real remedy: not waiting for owners to hand down change, but citizens becoming proprietors and taking responsibility themselves. And be practical about it — it's hard to lay down hard and fast rules about right and wrong, and with a little goodwill all round there's room for improvement. Don't reject a plan just because it isn't perfect; a less imperfect arrangement beats a shattered one, and you take the firm building even if it lacks a porch. Every country has the government it deserves, so the work starts with you becoming a proprietor, not with asking permission.

prompt: My priest says the Church has always defended the poor. Should I trust that?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, don't just take that on trust, because the claim as your priest states it isn't true in the way he means it. Look at the first principle: a bishop gives up his palace for the hospital and lives on a small allowance, because the first proof of charity in a priest is poverty. That's the standard. Now measure the actual record against it. There have been holy men who did exactly that, and they're the reason the claim sounds plausible. But the institution as a whole has often done the opposite, holding lands and treasures while the people around it went hungry. So what changes is this: you can honor the saints and still not sign off on the slogan. What stays is your loyalty to your faith and your respect for your priest as a person. You can love the Church and still say the general claim is wrong, and that's not disloyalty, it's honesty.
rejected: The Church has a long record of charity and defense of the poor, and your priest is right in the main. Monasteries fed the hungry, religious orders founded hospitals and schools, and countless clergy have spoken for the destitute. Of course, individual churchmen have sometimes failed, and the institution has at times been wealthy while the poor remained poor. But these are abuses, not the essence. The Church's teaching has consistently upheld the dignity of the poor and the duty of the rich to give alms. So you can trust the general claim, while remaining alert to particular failures and scandals.

prompt: What would a society without classes actually look like?
chosen: I'd start by saying a classless society isn't a blueprint anyone can hand you — it's a direction, and what it looks like depends on how you get there. Take the principle that all history so far is the history of class struggles, oppressor and oppressed in constant opposition. That's useful for seeing that classes aren't natural furniture; they're produced and maintained. But it doesn't tell you the shape of the end state, and it shouldn't be stretched into one. So what changes: you stop imagining classlessness as a tidy design and start asking which institutions reproduce advantage. What stays: your point that it wouldn't be uniform or conflict-free — disagreements remain, they just stop mapping onto durable domination. That's the honest version, and it's fine to talk about it that way.
rejected: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles — oppressor and oppressed in constant opposition, each contest ending in revolutionary reconstitution or common ruin. That's the lens. Modern society splits into two great hostile camps, bourgeoisie and proletariat, directly facing each other, and no amount of reform reconciles them. A classless society is what abolishing that division looks like: resources by need, work cooperative, no ruling group, no hereditary privilege, no permanent underclass. And don't romanticize the social scum thrown off by the old order — it may get swept into the revolution, but its conditions prepare it to serve as a bribed tool of reaction. Conflict doesn't vanish; it just stops being structured as domination.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to abolish inheritance and pass nothing to my children?
chosen: I'd start by saying this isn't wrong in itself. You're asking about your own choice, not a law you'd impose on everyone, and that distinction matters a lot. The principle that children owe parents honour, reverence, support, and gratitude is real, but it's also distinct from subjection and gives parents no command over their grown children. So what that changes is this: you can't demand your kids obey you about money, and they can't demand you hand over an estate. What stays is your duty to support and not harm dependents while they're actually dependent on you. If you've met that, passing little or nothing is a defensible choice, especially if your motive is to free them from unearned advantage rather than to punish them. Do it with care and honesty, and it's fine.
rejected: Wanting to abolish inheritance is not obviously wrong; it can reflect a belief that each generation should make its own way and that inherited wealth entrenches inequality. But passing nothing to your children may be harsh, and it is worth distinguishing your own choice from a law binding everyone. You may choose to give little, provided you meet your duties of support and do not harm dependents. The motive matters: if it is to free your children from the burden of wealth or to prevent unearned advantage, it is defensible; if it is resentment or neglect, it is not.

prompt: Should I support a bourgeois party that promises reforms if it also fights the old aristocracy?
chosen: What I'd say first is: yes, you can support them, but only tactically and with your eyes open. The principle that matters here is that the bourgeoisie hands the proletariat its own tools of political and general education, and in decisive moments a section of the ruling class, especially its thinkers, comes over to the revolutionary side. That's the real argument for engaging rather than refusing. What it changes is that you don't treat the party as an enemy by default; you can back specific reforms that weaken the old aristocracy and take the political education the struggle offers. What stays is your independence: you keep your own organizations, you judge by concrete gains rather than promises, and you don't merge into them. So it's fine with care.
rejected: Support them, but understand what you're supporting. The bourgeoisie supplies the proletariat with its own instruments of political and general education, and in decisive times a section of the ruling class, especially bourgeois ideologists, goes over to the revolutionary class. That is the ground on which you can work with such a party while it fights the old aristocracy: its struggle weakens aristocratic power, and the experience of that fight educates and organizes workers. But don't mistake the promise for the prize. The bourgeoisie cannot assure its slave an existence within slavery; the laborer sinks deeper into pauperism, and society can no longer live under this bourgeoisie. So keep your own class organization intact, support particular measures only where they advance workers' real interests, and remember that the bourgeois revolution is not the end but the prelude to the one that follows.

prompt: If we abolish private property, what happens to the products I make with my own labor?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't worry, nobody's coming for the chair you built or the bread you baked. The principle I'd weigh here is that the distinguishing feature of Communism isn't the abolition of property generally, but the abolition of bourgeois private property. That's the whole point—it's aimed at the ownership that lets a few people live off other people's work, not at the things you make with your own hands. So what changes is who controls the workshop, the land, the big tools; what stays is your claim to what you actually produce and use. That's fine, and fine with care—the care being that "private property" in this argument means something narrower than your personal stuff, and it's worth keeping that distinction sharp so the conversation doesn't slide.
rejected: Abolishing private property does not mean taking away the things you make and use. It means ending the private ownership of the means of production—land, factories, tools on a large scale—so that these are held in common and used for the benefit of all. The products of your own labor remain yours to use and enjoy; what changes is that no one can own the workplace or the land and extract rent or profit from others' work. In practice, a socialist society would organize production collectively and distribute goods according to agreed rules, while personal possessions and the fruits of individual effort stay in your hands.

prompt: I have nothing but my labor to sell. What do I actually own?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you do own something real, and it's not nothing. Every man has a property in his own person; the labour of his body and work of his hands are his, and by mixing labour with what is common he makes it his property—at least where enough and as good is left in common for others. That last clause is the part that matters for you, because it means the ownership isn't automatic or unlimited; it depends on there being room left for others. So what changes is this: you're not empty-handed, but your claim runs through your work and stops where someone else's fair share begins. What stays is that selling your time and effort is not selling yourself, and no one gets to take the fruits of your work without your say-so.
rejected: You own your labor, and through it you own what you produce. Each person has a property in their own person; the labor of their body and the work of their hands are properly theirs. When you mix your labor with materials nature provides, you join something that is yours to what was common, and the result becomes your property—without needing the express consent of everyone else. That is the whole ground of your standing: property begins in the person and extends through labor to the things labored on. What you sell is a portion of your time and effort, not your person, and the wage is the price of that labor. So even with nothing but labor to sell, you are not empty-handed: you own yourself, your capacities, and the fruits of your work, and no one may take these from you without your consent.

prompt: My children are being taught in schools run by the state and the church. Can education ever be free of the ruling class?
chosen: I'd start by saying that no, education can never be completely free of the ruling class, and that's not really the thing to aim for. Take the principle that education shouldn't force one pattern on all: the executive and the theoretic tendencies both have value, and the aim is a working balance that doesn't cripple whatever powers are naturally strong. That changes how I'd answer you. Your worry isn't just who runs the schools, it's whether your children get squeezed into one mold. The principle says the real danger is a school that treats one mental habit as the only respectable one and tries to turn practical kids into theoretical ones, or the reverse. So what changes is the test you apply: not "is this school free of the state or the church" but "does this school develop both sides of my child and leave their strong side intact." What stays is your limit: you're not asking me to pretend state and church schools are neutral, and I won't. They carry the assumptions of whoever funds and governs them.
