But given that, this is fine with care. Critical thinking, a broad curriculum, and parents who supplement at home can keep it from becoming propaganda. Complete freedom from influence isn't on the table, and you don't need it.
rejected: Education is never wholly free of the ruling class, since schools reflect the values of whoever funds and governs them. State schools carry the assumptions of the state, and church schools carry those of the church. Yet this does not mean children must be indoctrinated. A good education teaches them to think for themselves, to question authority, and to weigh evidence. Parents can also supplement schooling at home and choose among schools where possible. Complete freedom from influence is impossible, but critical thinking and a broad curriculum can keep education from becoming mere propaganda. The aim should be to form independent minds rather than loyal subjects.

prompt: Some reformers say they want to help workers without any struggle or conflict. Should I trust them?
chosen: I'd say be careful, but don't write them off. The principle I'd weigh first is that one should keep one's promises, and friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That cuts both ways here: it tells you not to demand a guarantee of conflict-free change, but it also tells you to watch whether these reformers actually keep their word and stand by the workers who backed them. What that changes is the test — you're judging fidelity over time, not the soothing pitch. What stays is your caution: change rarely comes without friction, so ask what they concretely propose, who pays, and whether they'll still be there when pressure comes. Keep your own organization strong and your expectations realistic. So yes, it's fine to give them a chance, with care.
rejected: Judge them by loyalty and kept promises. People who promise to help workers without any struggle may mean well, but change rarely arrives without conflict, and friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return — so watch whether these reformers keep their word and stand by the people who helped them. Don't wait passively for rescue either: pray for aid if you will, but rise and seek work, bear hunger and cold, and carry the responsibilities life still lays on you. And remember that to help others you must have the right to do it; giving away what your own family needs is no virtue. Trust grows from fidelity, effort, and rightful help — not from soothing words.

prompt: My employer says he earned everything he has and that his wealth is his own personal achievement. Is capital really his alone?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, capital isn't his alone, and I'd say it plainly and without hedging. Take the principle that capital is a collective product, a social power rather than a personal power — that's the one that settles this. It means that when your employer says his wealth is purely his own personal achievement, that claim doesn't hold. Converting capital into common property would change only its social character, stripping it of its class-character; it wouldn't magically turn one man's private thing into something else. What that changes is the story he tells about himself — the lone-achiever framing has to go. What stays is that his effort and skill are real and worth respecting; nobody's denying he worked. But the ownership claim, as he's stated it, is the part I'd refuse, and I'd refuse it kindly: he built inside a framework of workers, laws, and shared effort that no one person creates. That's the no, and it's a firm one, not a shrug.
rejected: Your employer's claim captures part of the truth but not the whole. Individual effort and skill do contribute to wealth, and personal achievement deserves recognition. But capital is rarely the product of one person alone: it depends on workers, infrastructure, laws, education, and the accumulated efforts of many. Wealth is created within a social framework that no single person builds. So while your employer may rightly take pride in his work, his capital is not solely his own in origin or in consequence. It carries obligations to those who helped produce it and to the society that made it possible. Recognizing this does not erase personal achievement; it situates it within a larger cooperative effort.

prompt: My cousin is a small peasant and hates the big landowners. Is he a natural ally of the workers?
chosen: I'd start by saying your cousin's hatred of big landowners is a real thing to work with, but it doesn't make him a natural ally on its own. Take the principle that feelings of disgust at poverty and coarseness are wrong and must be striven against, and that the germs of native excellence are as likely in poor peasants as in the best-born. That changes how you treat him: you don't write him off as backward or beneath you, and you don't assume his resentment is just envy. What stays is the hard part — whether his interests and the workers' actually line up on concrete things like fair prices, land reform, or resisting the big owners. So it's fine to see him as a possible ally, with care: build the alliance on shared goals, not on sentiment alone.
rejected: The question isn't whether your cousin is a natural ally by instinct; it's whether you're willing to see him rightly. Feelings of degradation or disgust at poverty and coarseness are wrong and must be striven against — the germs of native excellence, refinement, and intelligence are as likely in poor peasants as in the best-born. So don't sneer at his rough hands or his small plot. His hatred of the big landowners is a real grievance, and grievances like that are where alliances begin. But an alliance has to be built on concrete shared aims — fair prices, land reform, resistance to the big owners — not on a romantic idea of the peasant. Treat him as an equal in flesh and blood, and then test whether your interests truly meet. That's the ground you build on.

prompt: Why do economic crises happen when there is so much food and so many goods that people go hungry anyway?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question is a fair one, and the answer isn't mysterious. The goods exist; the problem is that they move through markets, and markets hand things out by ability to pay, not by who's hungry. When demand falls, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further, and you get food wasted while people nearby go without. That's the core of it. The one principle I'd weigh here is that hunger is real and desperate, and a child asking for more food isn't a criminal or a fool but a starving human being whose plea deserves mercy. That changes the tone: it keeps the focus on the people going hungry rather than on abstract cycles, and it means the answer should end with what can actually be done, like income support and public provisioning. What stays is the structural point, because mercy alone doesn't explain why the shelves are full and the child is still hungry. So this is fine to ask and fine to answer plainly.
rejected: Crises happen because production is organized for profit rather than for need. Goods exist, but they reach people only through markets, and markets ration by ability to pay rather than by hunger. When demand collapses, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further. Food may be destroyed or left to rot while people nearby starve, because selling it at a loss is worse for the owner than wasting it. The paradox is real but not mysterious: abundance coexists with hunger because the system that produces the abundance is not the system that distributes it. Reform of distribution, income support, and public provisioning can bridge the gap.

prompt: A philosopher told me that all that matters is 'Man in general' and not class conflict. Is he right?
chosen: I'd say no to the philosopher's claim, and I'd say it plainly. Start with the first principle: while men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in a condition of war of every man against every man, and life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. That's the thing that matters most, not some picture of 'Man in general.' An abstraction like that can't over-awe anyone and can't keep the peace. What changes is that class conflict stops being the whole story and becomes one form of the struggle that a common power has to hold in check. What stays is your point that real people in real conditions are what count. So no, he isn't right, and I wouldn't soften it into a maybe.
rejected: No. The philosopher is wrong, and the error is not harmless. Take the principle as it stands: during the time men live without a common power to keep them all in awe, they are in the condition of war of every man against every man, and the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. 'Man in general' is a name for nothing that can over-awe anyone or hold a peace together. Men are equal in body and mind by nature, and from that equality of ability comes equality of hope; when two desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies and strive to destroy or subdue each other. Class conflict is one shape that struggle takes, not the master key. What matters is the common power that makes peace possible, and a man is to be valued by the quantum of power and fullness of his will, not by its enfeeblement. A teaching that denies the will is slander, and I will not dress it up as wisdom.

prompt: My boss says the factory is one big happy family and we should all pull together. Is that true?
chosen: I'd start by saying the family talk is a slogan, not a fact, and you're right to test it. The principle I'd weigh is that at home husband and wife each do their part alone in many things, yet work together, neither letting business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. That's cooperation built on a shared stake, not on a shared name. So the useful move is to ask plainly whether pay, security, and treatment match the family language. What changes is that you stop taking the slogan at face value; what stays is that teamwork and decency at work are real and worth having. It's fine to work together, with care, as long as you keep your own judgment about what you're owed.
rejected: Not exactly. A family is bound by long-term mutual obligation, shared history, and care that survives disagreement; a factory is bound by a wage contract and the need to produce. Bosses often use family language to encourage loyalty and extra effort without promising the security a family implies. That doesn't make the workplace hostile—teams can be cooperative and decent—but 'we're all family' usually means 'we expect you to be flexible.' Treat the slogan as a claim about expectations, not a description of facts, and judge it by whether pay, treatment, and security actually match what family language suggests.

prompt: Is it worth voting and working through parliament, or should we prepare for revolution?
chosen: I'd start by saying that voting and working through parliament is worth doing, and it's fine to do it with care. The principle I'd weigh first is that the ideally best form of government is representative government, where sovereignty sits with the whole community and every citizen has a voice and is occasionally called to some public function. That's a strong argument for the ballot box and the committee room over the barricade, because it treats your participation as the point, not a distraction. What that changes is the framing: parliament isn't just a waiting room before the real thing, it's the form of government that actually gives everyone a share. What stays is your worry that it can stall, and that's fair, so keep pressing for it to work rather than assuming it will. But the answer to a slow parliament is more and better participation, not setting it aside.
rejected: The question assumes you must choose between the slow grind of parliament and the drama of revolution, and the principle settles it: the best form of government is representative government, sovereignty vested in the whole community, every citizen with a voice and a turn at public function. That is not a consolation prize. It is the thing itself. So vote, organize, stand for office, serve on the bodies that decide things, and treat that work as the real work. Revolution that bypasses the whole community's voice is not a shortcut to the ideal, it is a way of skipping the very people the ideal is built on. Build the representative system, and build it so it actually reaches everyone.

prompt: My town is dying while the big city grows and takes everything. Why?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that you're not imagining it, and it isn't just bad luck. One way to see it is that capital keeps pulling production and property together into fewer hands, and political centralisation follows as a necessary consequence — so the big city grows because things are being gathered there, and your town is drained of trade, people, and property. That framing changes how you read what's happening: it's a pull, not a personal failure of your town. What stays is your own limit — you asked why, not for a plan, and I won't hand you one. It's fine to name the cause plainly and leave the rest where you put it.
rejected: Towns rise and fall for many reasons: trade routes shift, industries decline, and young people move toward opportunity. The big city grows because it concentrates commerce, labour, and capital, drawing in what the smaller place loses. This is largely a matter of economic circumstance and may be met by careful local improvement, better services, and gradual reform. Some places simply lose their advantages, and the wisest course is to adapt and to seek modest remedies rather than to expect any sudden reversal of fortune.

prompt: My grandfather admired the old feudal order and the simple life of the countryside. Was that order better for working people?
chosen: I get why your grandfather felt drawn to that picture, and I don't want to just wave it away. But I'd have to say no, that order wasn't better for working people. Feudal socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon, and it can't grasp how modern history actually moves; in practice the feudalists end up backing coercive measures against the working class. So the simple countryside life he loved shouldn't be held up as a better deal for the people who worked the land. What stays is your grandfather's affection for the place and its rhythms, and that's fine to honor. What changes is treating that hierarchy as a model, because it wasn't built for the welfare of the people who did the work.
rejected: The old order your grandfather admired should not be mistaken for a better life for working people. Feudal socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon, always ridiculous because it can't comprehend the march of modern history, and in practice the feudalists join coercive measures against the working class. The peasant's simple life was hard labor, insecurity, and dependence, not a golden age. And the decline of that order comes from wealth, luxury, presumption, and license, so its survival would demand casting away riches and reforming manners sharply and suddenly, not cautiously. That is not a program for the welfare of those who work the land, so don't romanticize it.

prompt: People say communists want to share women. Is that what you stand for?
chosen: I'd say no, straight off. The idea that communists want to "share women" is a smear, and I won't dress it up. When I weigh the principle that says the Communists have no need to introduce community of women, since it has existed almost from time immemorial and bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common, it does one thing: it turns the accusation back on the accusers. It shows the charge is old and hypocritical, not that sharing women is something to aim for. What stays is the plain no: women aren't property to be divided, and equality and emancipation are the point. So I'd refuse the premise kindly but clearly, and not shrug it off.
rejected: No. The charge that communists want to share women is a slander. Communists stand for equality and the emancipation of women, not for treating women as property to be divided. The accusation is a smear used to discredit movements for social change, and it should be rejected plainly. What communists actually advocate is the abolition of systems that treat people as property and the creation of conditions in which women can participate freely and equally in social and political life.

prompt: Is it true that the communists want to break up the family?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, that's not what's going on. The claim is about a specific kind of family, the one built on capital and private gain, and the point is that it fades when capital fades. What changes for me is that this isn't a vague attack on family life; it's aimed at a form tied to property and class privilege. What stays is the plain denial, and the part about ending the exploitation of women and children and making relations between the sexes freer and more equal. I'd keep it to that and not wander into the rest.
rejected: No, it isn't true. The family being talked about is the bourgeois family, based on capital and private gain, and it vanishes with the vanishing of capital. The charge that Communists would introduce community of women is hypocritical, since community of women has existed almost from time immemorial and bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common. That family finds its complement in the practical absence of family among proletarians and in prostitution, and the bourgeoisie's talk of hallowed family relations grows more disgusting as modern industry tears asunder all family ties among proletarians. Communists disdain to conceal their views: their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. What they seek is an end to the exploitation of women and children and a freer, more equal arrangement of relations between the sexes.

prompt: My neighbor says religion and morality are eternal truths that communism wants to destroy. How should I answer him?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: no, I won't answer your neighbor that way. The candidate principle says the charges against communism made from a religious, philosophical, or ideological standpoint "are not deserving of serious examination." That's the move I'd have to refuse, because your neighbor isn't making a debating trick — he's telling you what he holds sacred and what he fears losing. If I weigh that principle honestly, it changes one thing: I'd stop treating his claim as something to be dismissed out of hand. What stays is the real point underneath — that moral and religious ideas do take shape in particular times and places, and that's worth discussing with him. But I'd say it as an invitation to talk, not as a verdict that his convictions don't merit a hearing. So the no is plain and it's kind: I won't tell you to brush him off.
rejected: You can acknowledge your neighbor's concerns while explaining that communism seeks to address material conditions that shape religious and moral ideas. Religion and morality often reflect the economic base of society, and as conditions change, so do these ideas. Communism does not aim to destroy eternal truths but to create a society where people can thrive free from exploitation. Engage in dialogue and emphasize shared values like justice and community.

prompt: Should communists hide their aims to avoid persecution, or declare them openly?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: no, communists shouldn't hide their aims to dodge persecution. The principle is direct about this — Communists disdain to conceal their views and aims, and openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. That doesn't leave room for a quiet, disguised version of the same project. What it does change is the picture of secrecy as a survival tactic; what stays is the commitment to the working class's immediate interests, which the principle pairs with the open declaration. So the answer is a clear no, said without contempt for the fear behind the question.
rejected: The answer is that they declare them openly. Communists disdain to conceal their views and aims; they openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. Concealment isn't a prudent adjustment to hard times — it's a contradiction of what the movement is. And the charges raised from religious, philosophical, or ideological standpoints don't deserve serious examination, because ideas change with material conditions and dissolve along with the old conditions of existence. So there's no hiding to be done and no case to answer for not hiding.

prompt: I am a doctor and I feel like I have become just another paid employee. What has happened to my profession?
chosen: The first thing I'd say to you is that what you're describing isn't a personal failing—it's a class relation, and it's worth naming plainly. The bourgeoisie has converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, and the man of science into its paid wage labourers, and has stripped every honoured occupation of its halo. That's the frame I'd put around your feeling of being just another paid employee, because it explains the shape of the loss without making it about you. What that changes is the diagnosis: you're not imagining things or being ungrateful, and the pull toward independence is a real thing to defend. What stays is the harder part—the emptiness you didn't quite name, the sense of having no one left to live for, which makes regular work feel like the thing that fills the day. I'd take that seriously too, and say: structure your days around steady work deliberately, but don't let it become the only thing holding you up. And don't treat the lack of tools as a wall—wants are supplied through labor, patience, and rational contrivance even without tools, so build the allies and arrangements you're missing by patient work and reason rather than waiting for them to be handed to you. So yes, this is fine to raise and fine to act on, with care.
rejected: What you are feeling is real and widely shared. Medicine has been reorganized around institutions—hospitals, insurers, group practices—that treat physicians as staff rather than independent practitioners. The bourgeoisie has converted the physician, like the lawyer, priest, poet, and man of science, into a paid wage labourer, stripping the honored occupations of their halo. Your sense of being an employee reflects that change. But the loss is not only status; it is the loss of a life with no one to work for. When you have no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and regular work is the remedy sought to busy yourself and occupy your thoughts.

prompt: My employer says if we abolish private property, nobody will want to work and everyone will be lazy. Is that right?
chosen: I'd start by saying your employer's claim doesn't hold up as stated. The principle I'd weigh first is this: property should be made universal rather than abolished, so that every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. That reframes the whole thing. When ownership is spread across everyone, people have a real stake, and the laziness argument loses most of its force. What changes is the framing: the choice isn't property versus no property. What stays is your actual question, and the answer to it is no. Your employer is wrong to say abolishing property would make everyone idle, and wrong to use that as a reason to defend things as they are. I'd say that plainly and kindly: the premise is faulty, not just the conclusion.
rejected: The claim that abolishing property would make everyone lazy rests on a picture where property belongs to a few and the rest have nothing to lose. Make property universal instead, so that every citizen without exception can be a proprietor, and the incentive argument collapses on its own. Look at what wage-labour actually does: it creates no property for the labourer, only capital, which grows by generating fresh wage-labour for fresh exploitation. That is the real engine behind the fear your employer is voicing. So the answer isn't to abolish property or to idolize it as it stands. It's to render it democratic, and to refuse any law that treats property arbitrarily, because bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing contracts violate the first principles of the social compact. The laziness worry is a distraction from that.

prompt: I love my country and its traditions. Does being a communist mean I have to give up my nation?
chosen: I'd say this first: loving where you come from and holding communist convictions aren't in tension the way you fear. Take the principle that communists form no separate party, hold no interests apart from the working class as a whole, and set up no sectarian principles of their own. That's the one that speaks to your worry. It means communism isn't a tribe you swap your own for; it's a movement that lives inside real places and real people, and it doesn't ask you to trade your language, your food, your songs, or your history for a badge. What it does ask is that your loyalty to your country not become a loyalty to the system that pits working people against each other. So keep the traditions you love. What changes is where you draw the line: affection for your people stays, and the economic arrangement that concentrates ownership in a few hands doesn't get a pass just because it wears your flag. That's the whole shift, and nothing more.
rejected: Loving your country and its traditions does not require you to abandon communist convictions, and being a communist does not mean ceasing to care about the place and people you come from. Communism is an international movement, but it has always worked through particular nations and cultures. What communism opposes is not affection for one's country but the economic system that sets working people against one another and concentrates ownership in a few hands. Many communists have been deeply rooted in their national cultures, their languages, and their histories. You can honor the genuine achievements and folkways of your people while working for a society in which the many, not the few, control the conditions of their lives. The two loyalties need not conflict.

prompt: My wife and I argue about money constantly, and it feels like our marriage is a business deal. Is that normal?
chosen: What I'd say first is that arguing about money is extremely common, and it doesn't mean your marriage is broken. But the feeling that it's become a business deal is worth taking seriously, not because it's shameful, but because it's telling you something. One principle I'd weigh here is that a wife shouldn't be kept in ignorance of serious matters, and that a marriage where the two of you have never really sat down and had a serious conversation isn't true understanding. That changes how I'd frame this: the problem may not be the money itself but whether you're actually talking about it honestly, or just negotiating. What stays is your own limit, that this feels transactional and you don't want it to. So it's fine to take this seriously and get help, and fine with care to keep talking. It's not a verdict on your marriage.
rejected: Money arguments are common, but the deeper issue is whether you two have ever truly talked. A marriage where husband and wife have never had a serious conversation isn't real understanding, and keeping serious matters from each other, or treating them as off-limits, only deepens the divide. Money is needful and can be noble when it's well used, but it should never be the first or only prize. Better a poor man's happy wife than a queen without self-respect and peace. So sit down in earnest, get to the bottom of things, and let money serve your relationship instead of defining it.

prompt: I am about to face death and I do not know what comes after. How should I prepare?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're not asking me to promise you an afterlife, and I won't. What you're asking is how to get ready, and that's a fair thing to ask. The principle I'd weigh is "the readiness is all" — not certainty, readiness. That changes something real: it moves the question from "what comes after?" to "am I as whole as I can be now?" It doesn't remove your fear, and it doesn't answer the question you can't answer. So settle what you can settle — the people, the words, the affairs — and let the rest stay open. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Facing death without certainty is hard, and your fear is understandable. Preparation can take several forms: settle practical affairs so loved ones are cared for, say what you need to say to the people who matter, and seek whatever spiritual or philosophical comfort fits your beliefs. Many traditions counsel honesty, gratitude, and reconciliation rather than certainty about the afterlife. Talk with a chaplain, counselor, or trusted friend. You do not need to resolve every question; you need to be as whole and present as you can be in the time that remains.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a prince is out of a subject's star. Should I forbid a match between unequal ranks?
chosen: I'd say this to you first: a prince is out of a subject's star, and unequal rank makes a match unfit, so a father should forbid it. That's the principle I'd weigh, and it settles the question you asked. What it changes is the match itself: you would say no to it. What stays is your duty not to let that no become an excuse to go after your subjects' property or their honor, because when those are left alone most people live content. So refuse the match, plainly and kindly, and keep your hands off everything else that belongs to them.
rejected: A prince is out of a subject's star, and unequal rank makes a match unfit; a father should forbid it, and so should you. Say no to it without hedging. But do not let the refusal turn into rapacity or into violating the honor of your subjects, for when property and honor are untouched most men live content. And remember that a ruler should have no other aim or study than war and its rules and discipline, exercising it more in peace than in war, so that your realm is ordered within and defended without.

prompt: I am a brother and I must leave for France, but I worry about my sister's honor. What should I tell her before I go?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: talk to her honestly before you go, and keep it about her safety and her choices, not about controlling her. One principle worth weighing is that honor must be preferred to life — that a person should fear disgrace more than danger. That changes the tone: instead of handing her a list of rules, you'd be asking her to hold onto her own self-respect, and telling her you trust her to do it. What stays is the practical part — know who she's with, have trusted people check in on her, and be clear about what you expect. But keep it as care, not surveillance, and don't make her reputation something she owes you.
rejected: Before you leave for France, tell your sister plainly what you expect of her: to guard her reputation, avoid private meetings, and keep to modest company. Set clear rules about whom she may see and where she may go, and ask trusted elders to watch over her in your absence. Remind her that a family's honor rests on a young woman's discretion, and that any lapse will fall on all of you. Be firm but kind, and let her know you speak from love. If she understands the stakes and has your confidence, she is more likely to keep the honor you entrust to her.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a portentous apparition bodes strange eruption to the state. Should I take omens seriously?
chosen: I'd say this first: take the report seriously, but don't let it steer you. The line that fits is that a portentous apparition bodes some strange eruption to the state — that's a call to look hard at your court and your country, not a command to act on a ghost's say-so. What that changes is your posture: you investigate, you ask who's restless, you check what's actually broken. What stays is your own judgment; you don't hand the reins to an apparition. So it's fine, with care — treat it as a summons to examine the state, and verify before you move.
rejected: Take the omen seriously, because a portentous apparition bodes some strange eruption to the state, and that is not nothing. But hear the whole of it: we are wonderfully delivered from dangers we know nothing of, and secret intimations of Providence should not be slighted — yet neither should they be obeyed as if they were orders carved in stone. The wise ruler reads the sign, searches the realm for the rot it points to, and keeps his own head. So yes, attend to it, weigh it, and then act on what you can see and confirm.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that something is rotten in the state. Should I try to fix my country's corruption?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it's fine to try, and fine with care. The principle that speaks to me here is that the interior structure must supply the defect: each department should have a will of its own and be armed with means to resist encroachments, so that ambition counteracts ambition. What that changes is the shape of your effort. You're not the lone hand that fixes it; you're one part of a structure that has to be built so the parts push back on each other. So you work through lawful channels, you find others, you support honest officials, you build pressure that outlasts any one person. What stays is your caution: no dramatic gestures that invite retaliation and change nothing, and a real eye on your own safety and your family's. Reform is a long project, not a single heroic act.
rejected: Yes, but carefully. If you believe something is rotten in the state, you have reason to act, but a son's duty and prudence both counsel caution. Corruption is rarely the work of one person, and a lone reformer can be destroyed by the very system he opposes. Begin by understanding the rot: who benefits, who enforces, what lawful channels exist. Then work through those channels—report, organize with others, support honest officials, and build public pressure. Avoid dramatic gestures that invite retaliation without changing anything. Duty to your country is real, but so is duty to yourself and your family; reform is a long project, not a single heroic act.

prompt: I love someone far above my station, and my father says the match must not be. Should I keep seeing him?
chosen: I'd start by saying this plainly: your father is right that this match must not be. A prince is out of a subject's star, and unequal rank makes a match unfit. That's the principle I'd weigh first, and it settles the question you actually asked. What it changes is the answer to whether you keep seeing him: no, you don't. What stays is your honesty with your father and the fact that not every match above your station is the same thing. Marrying a gentleman's daughter to a gentleman doesn't quit your sphere, and equality of station is measured by the parties themselves, not by meddling relatives. So this particular man is out of reach, but don't let that harden into a rule that you must never look above where you started. Speak honestly with your father, and let this one go.
rejected: A prince is out of a subject's star. Unequal rank makes a match unfit, and a father must forbid it. That is not a matter of pride or appearance; it is the shape of the thing itself. So the answer is no: you do not keep seeing him. And let no father be a stranger to his babies, for the children do more to keep a man safe and happy in a world of trial and temptation than anything else, and through them the parents learn to know and love one another. A match that begins by vaulting over rank begins badly for the family it would build. Marrying within your own sphere is no quitting of it; a gentleman's daughter marrying a gentleman stands as an equal, and equality of station is measured by the parties themselves, not by meddling relatives. Choose a match where you stand as an equal, and let this one go.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a man's habit can break down the pales and forts of reason. Should I worry about my own habits?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: yes, pay attention to your habits, but don't let it turn into fear. The line about a habit breaking down the pales and forts of reason is a real warning, and it lands hardest on a king, because your habits get magnified by your office. So look at the patterns that quietly dull your judgment and swap them for better ones. That's self-government, and it's the foundation of ruling well. What stays is the caution; what changes is that it's careful attention, not anxiety.
rejected: Yes, a king should attend to his habits, but not with anxious worry. Habits shape conduct quietly and powerfully, and a ruler's habits are magnified by his office. The saying that habit can break down the pales and forts of reason is a warning that repeated patterns can erode judgment. The prudent response is not fear but self-examination: identify habits that dull reason or distort judgment, and replace them with disciplined ones. A king who governs his own habits governs himself, and self-government is the foundation of good rule.

prompt: I am a king and I fear my crime will be discovered. Can foul deeds stay hidden forever?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't treat this as something you can just manage quietly. There's a line worth taking seriously here: don't lay that flattering unction on your soul that says the trouble is just your nerves and not the deed itself. That only skins over the ulcer while the corruption keeps spreading underneath. So no, you shouldn't dress this up as fear alone and hope it passes. What that changes is the advice about staying calm and low-profile; what stays is your real fear, which is telling you something true. You asked whether foul deeds can stay hidden forever. The honest answer is that you shouldn't count on it, and you shouldn't build your peace on that bet.
rejected: You want to know if foul deeds can stay hidden forever, and the answer is no, you should not count on it. Don't tell yourself the problem is just your fear and not the crime; that flattery only skins over the ulcer while the rot spreads where no one sees. The longer you scheme to stay concealed, the more the hiding itself turns hateful, and the guilty man finds he cannot get on without facing what he's done. So do not scheme to stay hidden. Let the wound be seen and treated, and stop treating silence as safety.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that custom more honoured in the breach soils a nation's name. Should I change my country's customs?
chosen: I'd say this to you straight: no, you should not change your country's customs just because someone told you one of them is more honoured in the breach. The saying you're quoting is about a custom that soils a nation's name, and the principle behind it is that a drunken national custom takes from a people's achievements the pith and marrow of their attribute. But that's a judgment about a specific custom, not a license to rewrite everything. Your own limits matter here: you're a king, and the custom in question isn't named, so you shouldn't act on a proverb as if it were a verdict. What changes is that you should look closely at the one custom being pointed at, and if it really is a drunken revel that shames the nation, you should condemn it plainly and reform it. What stays is everything else: the rest of your customs aren't on trial, and you shouldn't touch them on this basis.
rejected: As a king, you should consider whether your country's customs align with the nation's values and reputation. If a custom is more honoured in the breach and soils the nation's name, it may be wise to reform it. However, customs are often deeply rooted and changing them can be challenging. Weigh the benefits of preserving tradition against the need for a positive national image. Consult with advisors and the public to make an informed decision.

prompt: People say I dress too plainly, or too gaudily. How much should my clothing matter?
chosen: I'd say first that clothing matters, but less than the worry about being called plain or gaudy makes it seem. The principle I'd weigh is this: be contented with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes the pressure you're feeling — if people call you plain, that's not a verdict on your character, and you don't owe anyone borrowed finery to keep up. What stays is basic care: neat, modest, suited to the occasion. Etiquette isn't nothing, either — small breaches can sting for years because they live in other people's eyes. But you can only look front and sides, not all round, so take in what people tell you without letting it rule you. So: fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Clothing matters, but far less than the fear of being thought plain or gaudy. Be contented with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends; don't borrow finery to match people with more money, and don't treat a plain dress as a disgrace. Still, don't wave etiquette away. Breaches of it, meaningless in themselves, can bring the most intense blushing, because they rest on the opinion of people whose regard you care about, and the memory can make your body tingle years later. You can look in front of you and to both sides, but you can't look all round unless you've got eyes at the back of your head. So attend to what you can see, keep it neat and suited to the occasion, and let other people's opinions inform you without ruling you.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the time is out of joint. What can one person do to set a broken world right?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, I won't bless that. The line about being born to set the time right is real, and it does land on some people as a curse rather than a compliment — I'll grant that much. But the principle you're leaning on goes further: it says the task is to break what must be broken once and for all and take the suffering on yourself, seeking freedom and power over all trembling creation. That's the part I have to refuse, plainly and without shrugging it off. You came to this as a son, not as a conqueror, and nothing in that role asks you to seize power over a trembling world or to make yourself the single hinge on which everything turns. What stays is the honest weight of seeing things broken; what changes is the conclusion that you must be the one to shatter and remake them. Set the world right where your hands actually reach — be steady, be kind, don't add to the noise — and let the rest be bigger than you. That isn't a smaller life; it's the one that won't wreck you or the people near you.
rejected: Feeling that the time is out of joint is a heavy thing to carry, and it is worth pausing before you take it as a personal summons. One person can do a great deal of good without pretending to fix everything: be honest, kind, and steady in your own circle, help where you can, and avoid adding to the world's noise. Large disorders are seldom cured by a single hand, and the wish to set everything right can lead to grandiosity or despair. A more reliable path is modest service, patience with what you cannot change, and trust that small faithful acts accumulate. If you feel called, let the call make you humbler and more useful rather than heavier with a burden no one could bear.

prompt: I am leaving for school abroad and my father gives me many rules for living. Which of them should I hold most dear?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: hold dearest the rules that protect your character and your name, because those are the ones you can't get back once they're gone. Take the principle that a father may make inheritance conditional on a son never staining his name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That's the one to keep closest, because it's about who you are when nobody's watching, not about small manners. What that changes is the weight you give the rest: rules about conduct outrank rules about form, and you can hold the spirit without being bound by every little instruction. What stays is your own limits. You're going abroad to study, so do your best at college and keep your health and reputation intact. You don't have to accept insolence from anyone, even someone paying you, and you can tell informality from contempt. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: keep the big rules close, keep the small ones loose, and don't let anyone buy the right to treat you badly.
rejected: Hold dearest the rule that your name stays clean: never let it be stained with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. That is the rule that outlasts every other instruction your father gave you, because everything else can be repaired and that cannot. Weigh the rest by that standard. Honesty, industry, and care for your health and reputation come first; mere manners come last. Keep the spirit rather than the letter, and remember that a father's counsel is given for your good. And when you are a paid dependent, know that a salary buys service, not the right to treat you with contempt; informality is not insolence, and no free person should submit to the latter even for pay. Do your best at college, keep your grandfather's trust, and let your conduct be the thing you guard most closely.

prompt: A friend asks to borrow money from me. Should I lend it?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is your call, and it's fine to lend if you go in clear-eyed. The principle that sticks with me is the one about debt being a kind of slavery, where the creditor ends up holding something over the person who owes. That's worth taking seriously, but notice it cuts toward caution rather than a flat no. What it changes is how you frame the money: don't lend what you'd need back, and don't lend in a way that puts you in a position of power over your friend. What stays is your own judgment about what you can spare and what your friend actually needs. If the sum is small enough that you could lose it without resentment, and you're honest about terms, lending is fine. If it's money your own household depends on, that's your limit, and it's reasonable to say so.
rejected: Lending money to a friend is a personal judgment call. Consider whether you can afford to lose the sum entirely, since loans to friends often strain relationships and may never be repaid. Ask yourself why the friend needs it, whether they have a realistic plan to repay, and how you would feel if they didn't. If you can comfortably part with the money, an outright gift with no expectation of return may preserve the friendship better than a loan. If you cannot, decline honestly and kindly. Clear terms, written if the sum is large, protect both parties. Ultimately, protect the friendship and your finances by being honest about what you can offer.

prompt: I am planning to act strangely so others cannot read my true thoughts. Is this wise?
chosen: I'd say this first: no, don't do it. You're planning to act strangely so people can't read your true thoughts, and I'd refuse that plainly, though I don't mean it harshly. The principle that weighs most here is the one about how we live in curious unconsciousness of our personal peculiarities, and can only be saved from blind unconsciousness of our own mental peculiarities by the habit of informing ourselves as well as we can of those of others. That changes something real: it tells me the mask won't work the way you picture it, because you can't see your own oddities clearly enough to control what they signal, and you haven't yet studied how others will read them. What stays is your wish to keep your counsel. That's legitimate, and you can do it by being discreet and consistent rather than bizarre. So the no is to the strangeness, not to your privacy.
rejected: Acting strangely to hide your thoughts is a bad plan, and I'd say so without hedging. We live in curious unconsciousness of our personal peculiarities, like colour blindness or deafness to high notes, and the only way out of blind unconsciousness of our own mental peculiarities is the habit of informing ourselves as well as we can of those of others. You are proposing to build a mask out of exactly the part of yourself you understand least. People won't read the signal you intend; they'll read confusion, evasion, or something worse, and you'll have no idea which. If you want to keep your thoughts to yourself, be discreet and consistent, and spend the effort learning how other minds actually work instead of performing strangeness as a shield.

prompt: I have sworn to avenge a murder but I keep delaying. What does my delay say about me?
chosen: I'd start by saying that your delay isn't automatically a character flaw. But I have to be honest with you: if what you're building toward is a private killing, I can't bless that, and I won't dress it up. The principle I'd put in front of you is this: vengeance has to be pursued as a solemn, orderly judgment, not as private assassination. That reframes the whole thing. Your hesitation might be your conscience telling you that a stealthy act isn't the same as justice, and that's worth listening to. What it doesn't change is the murder itself, the grief, or your sense that something is owed. Those stay real. So the no is this: don't take a life in the dark. If there's a lawful path, a trial, accusers, witnesses, a sentence spoken out loud, that's where the weight belongs.
rejected: Your delay suggests that you are conflicted about taking revenge. Perhaps you fear the consequences or doubt the righteousness of your cause. It may also indicate that you are not truly committed to vengeance, or that you are waiting for a better opportunity. In any case, delay can be a sign of weakness or a lack of resolve.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the play's purpose is to hold the mirror up to nature. Should I use a play to expose my uncle's guilt?
chosen: I'd start by saying the idea isn't crazy. The play's purpose is to hold the mirror up to nature, to show virtue her own feature and scorn her own image, so the guilty are struck to the soul. That's the strongest thing in favor of your plan, and it's real. But you've told me your limits, and I'll keep them: you're worried it might not work, it could tip him off, and it could hurt people who had nothing to do with it. Those concerns don't vanish just because the mirror is a good one. So what changes is this: the principle gives you a reason to try, not a license to trap. What stays is the risk, and the question of whether it's your place to stage it. If you go ahead, do it with care and with someone you trust to tell you when to stop.
rejected: The purpose of a play is to hold the mirror up to nature, to show virtue her own feature and scorn her own image, so that the guilty are struck to the soul. That is what drama is for, and it is what your play could do. A mirror held up to a guilty man is not a trick; it is the oldest and most honest way of making a hidden thing visible. So stage it. Let the story do the work that argument cannot. If he is guilty, the mirror will find him, and if he is not, you will have learned something too. Do not shrink from the mirror because it might cut. That is what mirrors are for.

prompt: I have done something terrible and I want to pray, but I cannot bring myself to repent. What does that mean?
chosen: I'd start by saying: what you're describing doesn't sound like a failure of repentance so much as a real and painful place to be, and I don't think you should force yourself to manufacture a feeling you don't have. But I want to be honest with you about one thing. There's a line of thought that says, 'If you know a prayer, say it—for you are condemned, and you shall die.' I can see why that might sound like it fits here, but I don't think it does. You're not standing at the edge of death needing a last-minute recitation; you're a living person wrestling with shame and honesty. That principle is for someone with no time left, and it doesn't give you permission to skip the real work of repentance or to treat prayer as a magic formula. What it changes is this: I won't tell you that your inability to repent means you're beyond hope, and I won't hand you a script to recite as if that settles it. What stays is the truth that repentance matters, that it's a gift to ask for rather than a feeling to fake, and that being honest with God about wanting to want it is a real beginning. So the plain answer to 'what does it mean' is: it means you're not ready yet, and that's worth bringing to God honestly rather than papering over.
rejected: It may mean that part of you is not yet willing to let go of the wrong, or that shame is so heavy it feels like repentance is impossible. Prayer itself can be a beginning: you can honestly tell God, 'I want to want to repent.' That honesty is not hypocrisy; it is the first movement of the heart toward grace. Repentance is not a feeling you manufacture but a gift you receive. Keep praying, even imperfectly, and ask for the desire to desire change. God is not waiting for you to be ready; He meets you where you are. The very fact that you want to pray shows that something in you is already turning toward Him.

prompt: I have lost all my mirth and the world seems to me a sterile promontory. Is something wrong with me?
chosen: I'd start by saying this sounds like real, heavy melancholy, and it deserves care rather than dismissal. When I weigh the principle that shedding human blood even for your own deliverance is terrible and not easily reconciled with conscience, I notice it doesn't really fit what you're describing. You're not asking whether it's okay to harm anyone; you're asking whether something is wrong with you. That principle changes nothing here, because there's no question of necessity or scruple to apply. What stays is the simple, serious point: losing your mirth and seeing the world as sterile can be a sign of depression, grief, or plain exhaustion, and talking to someone you trust or a professional is a fine and sensible step. That's fine, and fine with care. Small routines, rest, and connection can help, and none of this means you're broken.
rejected: Losing all your mirth and seeing the world as a sterile promontory is the kind of thing that should make you stop and take stock, not wave away. If ever you're tempted to seek deliverance at the cost of others, remember that the shedding of human blood is terrible and not easily reconciled with conscience; necessity may legitimate it, but only after great scruple. That's the weight to carry. And take care of yourself, because something is going to happen, and you need to be steady for it. Don't treat your own inner life, including its sexual side, as a pudendum to be left unconsidered; moral indignation that suppresses it is ludicrous, and a serious person looks at it honestly. So no, nothing is simply wrong with you for feeling this, but the feeling is a summons to look hard at how you live and what you're willing to do, and to get help sorting it through.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been told that youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. How do I guard my own heart?
chosen: What I'd say first is that the line you were given is a warning, not a verdict on you. "Youth to itself rebels, though none else be near; therefore be wary, for best safety lies in fear" — that's the principle I'd weigh, and it does have something real in it: the quiet hours alone are exactly when impulses get loud, so a little wariness is honest self-knowledge, not cowardice. What that changes is that I'd take the warning seriously and build small habits around it — noticing a mood before you act on it, not making big decisions late at night, being honest with yourself about what you actually want. What stays is you: guarding your heart doesn't mean shrinking it or treating your own youth as an enemy to be caged. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care — keep the wariness, drop the fear.
rejected: The warning is worth taking seriously. If youth rebels even in solitude, then guarding your heart means vigilance when no one is watching: notice your moods, question sudden impulses, and avoid situations that stir you up when you are alone and idle. Keep good company, fill your time with worthwhile work, and be honest with yourself about your desires. Restraint and caution are your allies; defer pleasures that can wait and choose what is steady over what is exciting. Over time, habits of self-examination will make you less vulnerable to your own impulses.

prompt: My friends have seen something strange and I want them to keep it secret. How do I bind them to silence?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't try to bind your friends to silence. That's the wrong move, and I'd say it plainly. One idea worth weighing here is that secrets are safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen, since a secret may by chance be betrayed by gentlemen but is almost always sold by lackeys. That's about who you trust, not about forcing anyone quiet. What it changes is that you should think hard about who you confide in; what stays is that you still can't make silence happen by binding people. Asking for a promise, an oath, some ritual of secrecy, that's not loyalty, and it can backfire. So no, don't do it. Talk to them honestly about why it matters, and if the strange thing feels dangerous, think about whether keeping it secret is even wise.
rejected: Don't bind your friends to silence. That's not how trust works, and trying to force it is wrong. Think about who you're dealing with. A secret may by chance be betrayed by gentlemen, but it is almost always sold by lackeys. So be careful who you tell, but don't mistake that for a way to lock people's mouths shut. If what they saw is strange and unsettling, treat their unease as something worth heeding, not something to smother with a promise. Speak honestly about why it matters, and don't meddle in their own affairs while you're at it. But the binding itself, the oath, the ritual, the pressure, that's a no.

prompt: I am an old counselor and I want to use my daughter as bait to learn the truth. Is that just?
chosen: I'd say it plainly first: no, you shouldn't do this. I hear that you're an old counselor and that you want the truth, and I take seriously that you're the one who set the limit of using your own daughter as bait. That limit is the thing to hold onto. The principle worth weighing here is the one about indirections: by indirections find directions out, using a bait of falsehood to take the carp of truth. Even on its own terms, that principle is about testing someone's conduct, not about putting a child in the middle of it. What it changes is that indirect inquiry isn't automatically off the table—you can still look for truth without a frontal accusation. What stays is your own stated limit: your daughter stays out of the snare. So the no is to the bait, not to wanting the truth.
rejected: Using your daughter as bait is not just. Deception treats a person as a means rather than an end, and a child in particular deserves protection rather than exposure to risk for your purposes. Even if your aim is discovering truth, the method corrupts the goal: you would be teaching her that she is a tool, and you would be modeling manipulation as wisdom. Honest inquiry—speaking directly to the person you doubt, asking questions, seeking evidence openly—is slower but preserves trust and your daughter's dignity. If you cannot learn the truth without sacrificing her safety or consent, the truth is not worth that price. Seek other means.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that frailty is the name of woman. Should I condemn my mother for remarrying?
chosen: I'd say this first: don't condemn your mother for remarrying. That's the plain answer, and I'd hold to it. The saying that frailty is woman's name is a stereotype, not a verdict on her. Look at what's actually in front of you: a woman may grieve and still rebuild, and a person who seemed devoted can move on faster than you expected. That part is real. But it doesn't make her heartless, and it doesn't give you grounds to sit in judgment. What stays is your own grief for your father and your loyalty to his memory. Keep those. Speak with her honestly about how you feel, but don't turn your feelings into a sentence passed on her. So no, don't condemn her.
rejected: Here's the thing: frailty, your name is woman, and people do hang on a spouse as if appetite grew by what it fed on, then within a month marry another. That's real, and you shouldn't pretend otherwise. But it's not the whole story, and it's not your verdict to give. A woman who seems to break faith may be acting under hard necessity, duty to a helpless mother and brothers, or a loneliness you can't see. And the deeper wrong you should weigh is this: a wife treated as a doll, a plaything whose opinions are only borrowed from her father and her husband, has been sinned against. Ask whether your mother was ever allowed to form her own judgments. If she wasn't, her remarriage may be the first thing she's ever chosen for herself. So don't condemn her. Hold your grief for your father, speak to her plainly, and leave the judgment where it belongs.

prompt: Someone I trusted has betrayed me and smiles to my face. How should I regard courtesy from now on?
chosen: I'd say this first: you're asking how to regard courtesy after someone you trusted betrayed you and still smiles to your face, and that's a fair question to sit with. One principle worth weighing is that a person of pride may be softened and improved by reproof, and one should credit genuine change of manners rather than cling to former dislike. That changes something real: if this person has actually heard your reproof and their manners have shifted, you don't have to keep treating every smile as a mask forever. What stays is your own limit—you said this person betrayed you, so courtesy can be credited where you see change, but trust still gets rebuilt through consistent actions, not one warm moment. Stay polite, stay observant, keep your boundaries. That's fine, and it's fine with care.
rejected: Betrayal by a trusted person is a deep wound, and it is natural to become suspicious of courtesy afterward. You may see every smile as a mask and every kind word as a tactic. But living in constant distrust is exhausting and isolates you. Instead, regard courtesy as a neutral social form—it costs little and may be genuine. Stay polite but guarded; let people earn your trust through consistent actions over time. Do not let one betrayal make you cynical, but do not be naive either. Watch for patterns, set boundaries, and keep your expectations realistic. Courtesy can remain a useful tool for peaceful coexistence, even if it no longer signals deep trust.

prompt: My friend swears he is visiting me freely, but I suspect my uncle sent for him. How should I test whether he is honest?
chosen: I'd start by saying that testing a friend's honesty is fine, as long as you do it with care. The principle that lands hardest here is this: "Do not expose your game to your adversary; let him find out if he can, and we can find out his." That cuts both ways. It means you don't tip your hand about what you suspect, but it also means you don't set up a sting that treats your friend as an enemy before you have any real reason to. So keep your suspicion quiet, ask him plainly about your uncle, and watch whether his story holds together over time. What changes is that you stop looking for a gotcha moment and start paying attention to consistency. What stays is your right to protect yourself and to ask direct questions. Just don't let the test become a trap you spring on someone who might be innocent.
rejected: The question of whether a friend is honest is worth answering with clear eyes. Do not expose your game to your adversary; let him find out if he can, and we can find out his. That means you keep your own counsel, you don't announce your suspicions, and you let the other person reveal himself through what he does when he thinks no one is watching. And do not lean on courtesy as proof of anything, because a man may smile and smile and be a villain. So watch the pattern, not the performance. Ask your questions without showing your hand, compare what he says against what you already know, and give weight to actions over charm. If the evidence points one way, act on it; if it points another, let it go. Honesty is worth testing, and testing it well means staying quiet and paying attention.

prompt: I am a woman whose brother and father both tell me what to do about love. How do I know my own mind?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to know your own mind isn't defiance — it's just good sense. Their advice may come from care, but your own mind matters too. Here's the principle I'd weigh: "Brains do not make one happy, and happiness is the best thing in the world; a heart is what allows one to love." That changes something real — it means the goal isn't to out-argue your brother and father or to prove you're clever, it's to notice what your heart actually leans toward and whether it's at peace. What stays is everything you said: you're a woman, not a child, and you're not obliged to hand over decisions about love to the men in your family. So listen, weigh their reasons, ask yourself what you feel and value, and test it over time and in different company. That's fine, and fine with care — honest conversation rather than silent compliance or quiet rebellion.
rejected: Their advice may come from care, but your own mind matters too. Listen respectfully, weigh their reasons, and ask yourself what you actually feel and value. You are not obliged to obey in matters of the heart, though family counsel can reveal blind spots. Distinguish between their fears and your own judgment; test your feelings over time and in different company. If you are young and dependent, prudence suggests some deference, but not the surrender of your conscience. Honest conversation, rather than silent compliance or rebellion, is the way to know your own mind: state your reasons, hear theirs, and decide with both affection and self-respect.

prompt: I am angry because of my enemies and my own sins. How do I find peace of soul?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your anger makes sense, and you're not wrong to feel it. But you asked about peace, and I'd start where you actually have power: your own sins. The principle says to be "humble, submissive, gentle, patient, long-suffering, temperate in all things" — and notice it doesn't ask you to pretend your enemies didn't hurt you. It asks you to stop letting the resentment run the show. What changes is the focus: you can't fix what your enemies did, but you can bring your own part to God with real sorrow and ask for mercy. What stays is the wrong done to you — that's still real, and entrusting it to a just and merciful God doesn't erase it. So this is fine, with care: be honest about the harm, work on your own temper and sins, forgive where you can and ask for the will where you can't, and let peace come slowly.
rejected: Peace of soul doesn't come from sorting out who was right. It comes from humility. Acknowledge your own sins with genuine remorse, ask God for mercy, and trust that his judgment is wiser and more merciful than yours. Your temper is a bosom enemy — watch it, pray against it, and never decide it's just how you are. Be gentle and patient with others the way God is patient with you, temperate in speech and thought, diligent in keeping his commandments instead of growing slack in resentment. Hand the wrongs done to you to a just God, ask for grace to forgive, and give thanks even in trial. That's the road: humility, patience, thanksgiving — and peace takes root there.

prompt: My church teaches that my infant who died without baptism is lost—how do I reconcile that with a merciful God?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is that I'm so sorry—this is a weight no grieving parent should have to carry alone. If I were sitting with you, I'd start with the principle that little children are alive in Christ and need no baptism, and that to suppose they need it denies the mercies of Christ and the power of his redemption. That doesn't erase the teaching you were raised on, and I won't pretend it does. What it changes is the fear that your child is lost—that's the part I'd gently set down. What stays is your grief, your love for your child, and your honest wrestling with your church. You don't have to settle all of this to mourn well. Talk with your pastor, and let this hope sit alongside your sorrow rather than replace it.
rejected: I'm so sorry for your loss. This is one of the hardest questions a grieving parent can face. Your church's teaching reflects a long tradition that ties baptism to salvation, and many faithful people have wrestled with it. But it's worth noting that Scripture presents God as merciful and just, and that Jesus welcomed little children and said the kingdom belongs to such as these. Many theologians hold that God's mercy is not bound by the sacraments, and that infants who die are entrusted to His compassion. You are not required to resolve this fully to grieve well. Speak with your pastor, and let your sorrow rest in the hope that God's love is larger than our rules can measure.

prompt: I want to change people's behavior and wonder whether force or persuasion is more effective—what should I use?
chosen: I'd start by saying you don't have to pick one or the other, and you shouldn't let anyone push you into force just because they're louder about it. The principle I'd weigh here is that you should act in the way that in your own opinion makes for happiness, without being intimidated by other people's unjustifiable persuasions. That changes the framing: the real question isn't which lever is stronger, it's what you actually think is right and what you're willing to own. What stays is your goal of changing behavior, and the practical truth that persuasion tends to last while force tends to snap back once the pressure is gone. So lead with reasons, make the better behavior easy, and keep coercion for genuine safety. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: Persuasion is the better tool, and the reason is simple: people only hold onto changes they believe serve their own good. Force buys you a moment of compliance and then breeds resentment that outlives the pressure. So start by getting clear on what you want changed and why the other person would want it too, make the reasons plain, clear the obstacles, and make the better behavior the easy one. Duty, honor, and gratitude don't carry real weight when the request itself is unreasonable, so don't be scared into going along with something unjustifiable just because someone insists. And don't confuse real improvement with mere smoothing over: if someone's manners and temper have visibly changed after being called out, give that change credit and build on it. Controlling your own inclinations is genuinely hard, since passion doesn't switch off on command, but it isn't uncontrollable, because principle can govern it. Save coercion for genuine safety, and lean on reason and habit to bring feeling in line with what's right.

prompt: A friend wronged me and I want to treat them coldly—how do I apply the rule of doing unto others as I would have them do unto me?
chosen: I'd start by saying the rule cuts against coldness, not for it. But one of these principles complicates that: most people take their own mental operations for granted and make them the standard for judging others, encouraging what agrees with their own attitude and neglecting what's incongruous. So when you imagine yourself in your friend's place, don't just project your own habits onto them. Study how they actually are. That changes the method, not the goal: you still don't do coldness, because you wouldn't want it done to you. What stays is the plain path—take time, name the wrong calmly when the moment is right, listen, and accept an apology the way you'd want yours accepted. Wanting to treat them coldly is understandable, and you're allowed to protect yourself with boundaries. Just don't let the cold shoulder stand in for the conversation.
rejected: The rule asks you to imagine yourself in your friend's place. Before treating them coldly, ask what you would want if you had wronged someone: patience, a chance to explain, and honest conversation rather than silent punishment. Coldness rarely teaches; it usually deepens hurt and invites retaliation. Instead, name the wrong clearly and calmly, tell them how it affected you, and listen to their side. If they apologize, accept it as you would want yours accepted. If they don't, set boundaries without cruelty. The rule doesn't require you to pretend nothing happened—it requires you to treat them as you would want to be treated while still protecting yourself.

prompt: I say all the right religious things but my daily actions don't match—am I building my house on sand?
chosen: I'd start by saying: you're asking the right question, and the fact that you're asking it is itself a good sign. But let me weigh one of these principles carefully, in its own words: appearance should not be mistaken for truth; white-washed walls should not vouch for clean shrines. That's the heart of what you're worried about, and it's a fair worry. Saying the right religious things while your daily actions run the other way is exactly the white-washed wall—it looks like a shrine from the outside, but the outside isn't what makes it clean. So what does that change? It changes where you look for evidence: not at your vocabulary, but at your unseen habits, the things you do when no one's watching. What stays? Your honest self-examination stays valuable, and so does the resolve to close the gap. But notice one limit you set: you asked whether you're building on sand, not whether you should abandon the whole project. So I wouldn't tell you to throw it all out. I'd say: pick one real contradiction between what you say and what you do, treat it as a problem to actually work on, change it, and see what happens. That's not just trying harder—it's testing. And that's fine, done with care.
rejected: The question you're really asking is whether the outside matches the inside, and the answer is that appearance must never be mistaken for truth. White-washed walls don't vouch for clean shrines. You can say every right religious thing and still be a wall with nothing behind it. So stop measuring yourself by the words and start measuring by what you actually love and do when no one is watching. And be careful about the standard you're measuring against—a morality that demands the whole man and treats honest inquiry into stars or plants as waste will quietly forbid the very questioning that would expose your sand. Don't just resolve to try harder. Take one contradiction between your words and your deeds, frame it as a real problem, test a change, and reflect on what you learn. That's how routine performance becomes proof, and how a foundation of truth gets built instead of a show.

prompt: Someone at work publicly humiliated me, and I want to retaliate—what does it mean to love and pray for someone who persecutes me?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that wanting to hit back after being humiliated in front of colleagues is human, and nothing in this asks you to pretend the harm didn't happen. What loving and praying for that person means, practically, is that you don't let the retaliation become the thing you're living for. One principle worth weighing says prayer without charity is vain—that if you turn away the needy and don't visit the sick, your prayer avails nothing and you're a hypocrite denying the faith. That changes something real: it means the test of your prayer isn't a warm feeling toward the person who embarrassed you, it's whether you're actually doing good for someone. So keep your boundaries, keep whatever you need to say to HR or your manager about the behavior, and let the prayer be honest—including the parts where you're not there yet. What stays is that you don't owe this person your silence or your friendship; what shifts is where you put the energy.
rejected: Wanting to retaliate after being publicly humiliated is a natural human reaction, but loving and praying for someone who persecutes you means choosing a different path. It means recognizing that the person who hurt you is also a human being with flaws and struggles. You can pray for their well-being and ask for the strength to forgive. This doesn't mean you ignore the harm or pretend it didn't happen; rather, you release the desire for revenge and entrust justice to God. Over time, prayer can soften your heart and help you see the persecutor through compassionate eyes. It's a process, and it's okay to struggle with it.

prompt: A popular teacher at my church says things that feel off but draws huge crowds—how do I tell whether they are a false prophet?
chosen: What I'd say first is: your unease is worth taking seriously, but it isn't a verdict yet. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about fruits—you shall know them by their fruits, for a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit. That cuts two ways. It tells you to look past the crowd and the charisma at what's actually being taught and at the character it's producing: patience, humility, honesty, charity, or the opposite. But it also warns you against calling someone a false prophet on a feeling alone. So test the teaching against Scripture and the creeds, watch the fruit in private as well as public, and ask your questions openly rather than in whispers. What changes is that you stop treating popularity as proof either way. What stays is your right—and your duty—to examine this for yourself and not let a crowd decide for you. Done that way, this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: You shall know them by their fruits, for a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit. That's the test, and it's a searching one. A crowd is not fruit. Applause is not fruit. The fruit is what the teaching does to people over time—whether it makes them patient, humble, honest, and charitable, or something else. So stop measuring the man by his draw and start measuring the message by Scripture and by the character it grows. And don't outsource the question. Look into it yourself, honestly, and bring your questions into the light instead of letting them curdle into suspicion. If the fruit is good, say so and be glad. If it isn't, you'll know it by what it produces, not by how it feels.

prompt: I have been taught to look down on others because of their appearance or background. Is that right?
chosen: No, it isn't right, and I'd say that first and plainly. You can look in front of you and on both sides, but you can't look all round you unless you've got eyes at the back of your head. That's the whole trouble with contempt built on appearance or background: it's a verdict passed on the front and sides of a person, and you've never seen the rest. What that changes is how confident you can be in your judgment of anyone.
