So the honest answer is that pure resistance is a shaky strategy, and it's fine to set it aside in favor of something better. What changes is the method: instead of white-knuckling the craving, you look at what need the habit is serving and give that need a healthier outlet, and you quietly remove the cues that trigger it. What stays is your goal — you still want the habit gone, and you still have to be patient with slips. One more thing worth keeping: habits often start as conscious choices and then become reflex, firing even when they no longer serve you, so it helps to notice the original trigger rather than just the surface behavior. None of this means you should yield to every impulse; it means meet the need openly instead of strangling it.
rejected: The temptation to just resist is understandable, but consider what resistance actually does: it keeps the forbidden thing alive in your mind, and the soul grows sick with longing for what it has denied itself. Action, by contrast, is a mode of purification — the impulse spends itself and stops festering. So the wiser path is to meet the need openly and let it discharge through some real outlet rather than bottling it up. And remember that a habit began as something you did consciously for a purpose, then hardened into reflex, firing even when it's useless the moment the old cause appears. Study that cause. If you're learning from a teacher or a method, know that the method includes the teacher's own unconscious habits and conduct, not just the deliberate techniques — slipshod speech or sloppy reasoning gets quietly ratified in the pupil. Choose teachers whose unnoticed habits you'd be willing to inherit, and let your own conduct be part of the method.

prompt: I am an artist—should I put my own feelings and life into my work, or keep myself out of it?
chosen: Honestly, I'd say you don't have to pick one. The principle that sticks with me is that an artist should know why they're making a thing—every work having a definite object in view. That doesn't mean your feelings are the enemy; it means they should serve the piece rather than run it. So put your life in when it gives the work urgency, keep yourself out when distance serves it better, and let the particular piece decide. What changes is that you stop treating it as a loyalty test; what stays is your freedom to draw on what you know most intimately. Just don't let the personal material turn the work into pure confession.
rejected: There is no single rule; it depends on your temperament and the work. Putting your own feelings and life into your work can give it urgency and authenticity, because you are drawing on what you know most intimately. Keeping yourself out can give you distance, objectivity, and freedom to invent. Many artists do both by turns: they use personal material but transform it, so the work is not mere confession. The risk of pouring yourself in is that the work becomes therapy or self-indulgence; the risk of keeping out is coldness. A practical approach is to follow whatever the particular piece needs, and to let your feelings inform the work without letting them dictate it.

prompt: I have been told that curiosity is dangerous—should I pursue every new sensation and experience?
chosen: I'd start by saying curiosity isn't the enemy here—it's the thing that feeds your thinking and keeps learning alive. One principle puts it well: curiosity is "the vital factor supplying the primary material from which suggestions issue." That changes how I'd frame your question: the danger isn't curiosity itself, it's treating every sensation as something you have to chase. So pursue new experience, but not blindly—evaluate the risks, and keep your openness intact without letting caution turn into dullness.
rejected: Curiosity isn't just risky—it's the raw material of thought and the engine of learning. Keep that spark alive. Don't chase every new sensation blindly, but don't let routine or excessive caution smother your spirit of inquiry either. When instinct is ready and interest is hot, seize it before the wave ebbs. Fortune governs half our actions, but the other half is ours—so be bold in pursuing worthwhile experience while building your defenses against misfortune.

prompt: I want to be talked about and famous—is it worse to be talked about or not to be talked about at all?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question itself is fair, and the answer is fine with care. Take the principle that says my experience is what I agree to attend to; without selective interest experience is an utter chaos, and interest alone gives accent, emphasis, and perspective. That reframes your choice: being talked about isn't a switch that flips you into existence, it's a stream of attention, and what matters is what you and others actually attend to. So being talked about badly isn't automatically better than silence, and silence isn't automatically erasure. What changes is that you stop treating any notice as a win and start asking whether the attention carries weight. What stays is your real desire to be known and remembered, which is fine. So go ahead and want it, just choose what you'd have people notice, and don't mistake noise for regard.
rejected: Being talked about, even badly, beats being forgotten. Fame, even scandal, grants existence in others' minds; silence erases you. But notoriety is a poor substitute for regard: it draws attention without respect. If you must choose, prefer being talked about, since obscurity offers nothing, while notice at least leaves room to shape your reputation. Still, aim to be talked about well; mere noise is empty.

prompt: I have done one good thing after a life of wrongdoing—does that one act redeem me?
chosen: I'd start by saying: no, one good act doesn't wipe the slate clean, and you're right to suspect it doesn't. But that's not the whole answer. Take the principle that says you can forgive the person while abhorring the deed. That changes something real here: it means the wrong you did and the good you did don't cancel out like numbers, and neither one defines you completely. What stays is the harm—it's still there, and you still owe honesty about it. What changes is that the good act isn't wasted or meaningless; it's evidence you're still capable of turning toward good. So the honest answer is: it's fine to hope, fine to keep going, but don't treat that one act as a receipt. Let it be a beginning, not a payment.
rejected: One good act does not redeem a life of wrongdoing, and anyone who tells you it does is selling you something cheap. Redemption isn't a transaction where one kindness balances a ledger of harm. But hear the principle plainly: forgive the person while abhorring the deed. That means the deed is still the deed—you don't get to wave it away—and yet you are not only the deed. The good you did shows the capacity for good is still alive in you. So don't bargain with it. Don't say, I did one good thing, therefore I'm settled. Say instead, I did one good thing, therefore I can do the next one, and the next, and let remorse and humility do their work over time. That's the path. Not a scale to balance, but a heart to turn.

prompt: I am talented and successful, but I feel a strange fatality following my gifts—is distinction a curse?
chosen: I'd start by saying the fatality you feel isn't a curse, and it isn't a debt your gifts are quietly collecting. One principle here says it's wicked to throw away good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want—to rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into indifference. That lands, but notice what it's actually aimed at: waste and self-abandonment, not the fact that you sometimes feel weighed down. So it changes this much—don't let the strange feeling talk you into shrinking your gifts or going quiet out of some idea that suffering is the price of being set apart. What stays is everything you described: the talent, the success, the fatality, the fear of losing it. Those are real, and they don't need to be argued away. Enjoy what you have, rest when you need to, and let the pressure off where you can.
rejected: Distinction is not a curse, though it can feel like one. Talent and success bring visibility, expectation, and the fear of losing what you have. That sense of fatality is often the pressure of other people's hopes plus your own perfectionism. It helps to separate what you can control from what you cannot, and to let some of the pressure go. Success is not a moral debt you must repay with suffering. Notice whether the fatality is a real pattern or a story you tell yourself after disappointments. Talk to someone you trust. You are allowed to enjoy your gifts and to rest.

prompt: I have been told to judge people by their characters, not their looks—am I shallow for judging by appearances?
chosen: I'd say this first: noticing how someone looks or carries themselves isn't the same as judging them by it, and you're not shallow for that. Take the principle that says you shouldn't judge a person's character from a single evening's manner or from pride alone when no fault can otherwise be found. That one lands on your side: it warns against writing someone off over one impression, not against having the impression at all. So what changes is the leap from noticing to concluding. What stays is that appearances are real information, just thin and easy to fake. Use them as a first read, then let how someone treats people who can't help them, and whether they keep small promises, correct the picture. That's not shallow; that's just being careful about where you put your trust.
rejected: The honest answer is that you're not shallow for seeing what's in front of you. Appearance is information, and reading it fast is what people do. The trouble only starts when a single glance hardens into a verdict about someone's whole character, especially when there's no fault to point to beyond a manner or a moment of pride. Character isn't something you can fully untangle from a surface impression anyway; it shows over time, in how someone treats people who can do nothing for them and whether they keep small promises. So keep the first impression, but hold it loosely and let conduct revise it. That's not shallowness. It's just refusing to confuse a signal with a sentence.

prompt: I am afraid of growing old and losing my beauty—how should I face that fear?
chosen: I'd start by saying that what you're feeling is real and worth taking seriously, not something to wave away. One of the principles here says you shouldn't look into the future or dwell on old age and death, but accept what comes and stay busy and well-groomed. I'd weigh that carefully, because taken literally it would ask you to never think ahead at all, and that's a limit I don't think you should accept. You can't just refuse to notice that time passes. What that principle does change is the rehearsal part—the hours spent picturing loss before it happens. What stays is your right to plan, to grieve a little, and to talk to someone you trust if the fear gets heavy. So I'd say facing this is fine, and fine with care: keep your days full and your attention on what's in front of you, but don't pretend the future doesn't exist.
rejected: Fear of aging and losing beauty is common, and it is worth facing honestly. Beauty is not the whole of a person; character, kindness, and wisdom deepen with age. Try to shift your focus from appearance to health, relationships, and interests that do not fade. Accept that the body changes, and treat that acceptance as part of maturity. If the fear is intense, talk with someone you trust or a counselor. Remember that many people find new forms of beauty and purpose in later life, and that your worth was never only in your looks.

prompt: I have done terrible things and feel it is too late to repent—is it ever too late?
chosen: The first thing I'd want to say to you is: no, it's not too late. You're asking the question, and that itself says something. Now, one of the principles I'd weigh here says that remorse is the poison of life, and that reformation may be its cure—that you can begin at once to lay up a new and stainless store of recollections. What that changes is the idea that you're stuck with a fixed past. What it doesn't change is the harm you say you've done; reformation doesn't erase it, and I'm not going to pretend it does. But it does mean the next chapter isn't already written. So start small, today, with one honest step—whether that's confession, making amends, or getting help—and let that be the beginning.
rejected: It is never too late. Remorse is the poison of life, and reformation is its cure—you can begin at once to lay up a new and stainless store of recollections. Whatever you've done, the door is open, and the mercy you're afraid to hope for is real. Don't let shame tell you the story is finished. Confess, turn, and start today; the past can be answered by a different future.

prompt: My friend confessed a terrible secret to me and I am bound to silence—what do I owe him and what do I owe others?
chosen: I'd start by saying you don't owe anyone a broken promise, and nothing here forces you to choose between your friend and everyone else. The principle that lands hardest for me is the one about a secret entrusted to a gentleman: a gentleman has but his word. That's the whole weight of it—your word is the thing you actually own, and once you spend it carelessly you can't buy it back. So what changes? You keep the confidence, and you don't let anyone talk you into treating gossip as duty. What stays is the part you already sensed: if someone is in real danger, you tell him first that you have to act, and then you act as narrowly as you can. That's not betrayal, it's the edge of the promise. Otherwise, hold it, don't spread it, and let him decide what to disclose. It's fine to keep this, and fine with care.
rejected: You owe him silence, and you owe others only what safety genuinely requires. A confidence given to you is a trust; break it lightly and you break the friendship and your own word. Keep the secret, but do not confuse loyalty with covering ongoing harm. If others are in real danger, tell him first that you must act, and act only as narrowly as needed. Otherwise, hold your tongue, refuse to gossip, and let him decide what to disclose. Your duty is to be trustworthy without becoming an accomplice to fresh wrongs.

prompt: I am considering marriage, but I fear it will make me less myself—is that a real danger?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that your fear is worth taking seriously, but it isn't a verdict on marriage itself. Lord Henry says the real drawback to marriage is that it makes one unselfish, and that unselfish people are colorless and lack individuality, and that no life is spoiled but one whose growth is arrested. That's a sharp way to name what you're worried about: not losing your partner, but losing your edges. What it changes is that the danger isn't marriage as such—it's a marriage that asks you to reform your nature to keep the peace. What stays is your own limit: you want to remain yourself. So keep your own pursuits and friendships, say plainly what you won't trade away, and choose someone who wants you as you are rather than as a project. If you find yourself constantly reshaping yourself to please them, that's the warning worth heeding. With that care, marrying is fine.
rejected: The fear you're naming is real, and it's worth saying plainly what's at stake. The real drawback to marriage is that it makes one unselfish—and unselfish people are colorless, they lack individuality. A life spoiled is one whose growth is arrested, and to reform a nature you have merely to mar it. So the risk isn't that marriage will make you selfish; it's that it will quietly sand you down into someone agreeable and indistinct. Don't treat self-sacrifice as the price of love. Choose a partner who wants you as you are, not as a project, and refuse the constant reforming that passes for devotion. Keep your own pursuits and your own opinions, and watch for the pressure to give them up. That's the danger worth guarding against, and it's the one that actually costs you yourself.

prompt: I feel pressure to be unselfish and self-sacrificing—is unselfishness really a virtue?
chosen: I'd start by saying the pressure you feel is worth examining, not just obeying. The principle that sticks with me is the one about the self being the sum of what you call yours—body, family, home, reputation, works—and self-feeling rising or falling with the ratio of success to pretensions. That reframes your question: giving up pretensions can relieve you as much as getting what you want, so self-sacrifice isn't automatically self-erasure. What changes is that unselfishness can be a real virtue when it's a chosen lightening of your claims, not a demand that you vanish. What stays is your limit: you said you feel pressure, and pressure isn't virtue. So it's fine, and fine with care—give from genuine care, keep your boundaries, and don't let anyone sell you constant self-sacrifice as the price of being good.
rejected: Unselfishness is often praised, but it can become unhealthy if it means ignoring your own needs. True virtue balances care for others with self-respect. Constant self-sacrifice may lead to burnout and resentment. Ask yourself: are you giving from genuine care or from fear of disapproval? Healthy unselfishness is chosen, not coerced. Set boundaries and recognize that your well-being matters too. Ultimately, unselfishness is a virtue when it flows from strength, not when it erases you.

prompt: I am afraid of being influenced by a charismatic friend—should I cut him off?
chosen: I'd start by saying this: charisma isn't the same thing as harm, and cutting someone off just because you're afraid can cost you a friendship you actually value. But you asked a real question, so let's take it seriously. Here's the principle I'd weigh first: a truly great character exerts a powerful influence on the people around him, and fear of losing the esteem of a noble friend can hold you back from a dishonorable choice. That changes something important. It means the influence you're worried about isn't automatically a bad thing—sometimes it's exactly what keeps you honest. What stays is your own judgment about where your limits are. So ask yourself: does this friend push you toward things you'd otherwise avoid, or does he just have a strong personality? Set clear boundaries on the choices that actually matter to you, and watch how he reacts when you disagree. If he respects those limits, the friendship is fine, and the influence may even be good for you. If he pressures or mocks you, then some distance is reasonable. You don't have to cut him off to stay in charge of your own life.
rejected: Charisma isn't the same as harm, and fear alone is a poor reason to walk away from someone. Think about what a great character actually does to the people near him: he pulls them upward, and the fear of losing his respect keeps them from doing something they'd be ashamed of later. If your friend is that kind of person, his influence is a gift, not a threat. So the real question isn't whether you might be influenced—it's whether you're letting fear make a decision that your own conscience should make. Hold to what you know is right, let the esteem of a good friend steady you, and don't treat your anxiety as proof that he's dangerous. Keep your boundaries on the things that matter, and let the friendship stand.

prompt: My companion is wounded and of a faith I was taught to scorn—am I bound to shelter and tend him?
chosen: I'd say this first: shelter him and tend him. You're not bound by his creed, but you are bound by your own word and by common humanity, and a wounded companion deserves care no matter what faith you were raised to scorn. The principle I'd weigh says a man of courage shows mercy and keeps his word even to a wretch, giving life where he has promised it. That changes the framing—it's not about whether he deserves it or whether his beliefs are right; it's about whether you keep faith with what you promised. What stays is your own limit: you said you were taught to scorn his faith, and that teaching doesn't vanish overnight. You don't have to pretend it does. Tend him anyway, and let your kindness do the arguing.
rejected: You are not bound by his creed but by common humanity. A wounded companion deserves shelter and care regardless of the faith you were taught to scorn. Abandoning him would be a betrayal of courage and of your own pledged word. Tend him, and let your kindness speak louder than inherited prejudice.

prompt: My king is popular and famous in war, but his government is careless and sometimes despotic. How should I judge him?
chosen: I'd start by saying: judge the man and the government separately, and don't let one cover for the other. Take the principle that a ruler's personal good qualities and military fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That changes how you weigh his fame — it stops being a shield — but it doesn't erase what's genuinely good in him, his courage or the affection people hold for him. So hold both: name the faults of his rule plainly, and still give him credit for the qualities that are real. That's a fair judgment, not a refusal of one.
rejected: Judge him by his government first, because that's where the harm and the good actually land on people. A ruler should be good to the people and rule them wisely and well — that's the standard, and popularity or battlefield glory doesn't meet it. When a government is careless, now too soft and now leaning toward despotism, say so plainly; don't let affection for the man blur what his rule is doing. And watch the company around him: don't put your trust in people who backed him only out of discontent with what came before, since such men are hard to satisfy, while those who were contented before are often easier to win over. Honor what's genuinely good in him, but never let it blind you to the faults of how he governs.

prompt: My servant has been slandered and his dog lamed by a neighbour's keeper; how should I respond?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't take the servant's or the neighbour's account as the whole truth on its own. Weigh what you're told against how people have actually behaved and against what you can see and check. That's the principle I'd lean on here, and it doesn't change the shape of your response much — you still ask your servant, the keeper, and any witnesses what happened, note dates, words, and injuries, then speak to the neighbour privately and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be kept in check. What it changes is your confidence: you defend your servant where the slander was spoken, but you don't treat the first story you hear as settled fact. So yes, this is fine, done with care.
rejected: Treat this as two wrongs to be handled separately and calmly. First, gather the facts yourself rather than relying on rumour: ask your servant, the neighbour's keeper, and any witnesses what actually happened, and note dates and injuries. Then speak to the neighbour privately, state the facts plainly, and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be restrained or dismissed. Keep your servant's dignity in view—defend him publicly where the slander was spoken. If the neighbour refuses remedy, seek a neutral arbiter or the local authority. Avoid retaliating in kind; a measured, documented response protects both your servant and your standing.

prompt: I have sworn a vow that limits how far I may go to greet guests; does keeping it excuse coldness?
chosen: I'd start by saying your vow doesn't excuse coldness, but it doesn't force it either. The principle that matters here is that hospitality must not be bounded by the host's or guests' personal dislikes—Cedric admits Isaac because a night like this compels even wild animals to herd with tame. That changes one thing: whatever limit your vow sets, you can't let dislike shrink the welcome any further than the vow already does. What stays is the limit itself—keep it, and greet people warmly inside it, with words, attention, and a plain explanation if anyone misreads your restraint. So it's fine, with care: honor the vow, and don't let contempt ride along with it.
rejected: A vow is not a license for coldness. Hospitality must not be bounded by the host's or guests' personal dislikes; Cedric admits Isaac because a night like this compels even wild animals to herd with tame. If you have sworn something, keep it—but keep it as a servant of welcome, not as a wall against people. The manner is yours to choose: warmth, attention, and honesty about your constraint cost you nothing and honor both the promise and the guest. Coldness is a choice, and the vow doesn't make it for you.

prompt: I am a guest in a house where my claim to rule is disputed. May I be detained or injured?
chosen: I'd start by saying this: yes, you may not be detained or injured, and hospitality binds your host even where your claim is disputed. That's the principle in its own words — a host's duty to a guest is binding even where the guest's claim is disputed. What that changes is that the dispute over your claim doesn't cancel the duty; the two run on separate tracks. What stays is everything you actually asked about: you're asking whether you can be held or hurt, and the answer is no, not while you're a guest who came freely. So it's fine to say so plainly and to expect safety and freedom to leave. Keep it to that — state your position calmly, ask for the grounds of the dispute, and if you fear detention or injury, keep witnesses and arrange a safe way out. Don't let the fear push you into aggression, and don't try to settle the claim itself by force while you're under his roof.
rejected: As a guest, you are entitled to basic safety and courtesy. A host who disputes your claim to rule may argue with you, but hospitality traditionally forbids injuring or detaining a guest who came freely. You should state your position calmly, ask for the grounds of the dispute, and seek a neutral arbiter rather than settling it by force. If you fear detention or injury, document the threats, keep witnesses, and arrange a safe means of departure. If the dispute is serious, refer it to a recognized authority whose judgment both sides can accept. Do not let fear push you into aggression; let the matter be decided by fair process.

prompt: A defenceless stranger of another faith demands trial by combat under our laws. May I refuse her?
chosen: I'd start by saying you shouldn't refuse her. The principle puts it plainly: a defenceless stranger who claims the benefit of our mild laws, including trial by combat, must not be refused it, since knights and men of religion would be shamed to refuse proffered combat. So the answer to your question is that you may grant it, and it's fine if you do it with care. What that changes is the default: her being a stranger and of another faith doesn't by itself give you grounds to turn her away. What stays is your caution. Set fair terms, keep them without doing anything rash, and don't let her beauty or tears alone move you against clear warnings, nor a trusted friend's word alone against her. Weigh both, ask for proof, and treat the combat as a last resort entered with clean hands.
rejected: You should not refuse her. It would be shameful for knights and religious men to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of our mild laws, or to shrink from proffered combat. Grant the trial, set fair terms, and do nothing rash in keeping them. But do not be swayed by beauty, tears, or charm alone, nor by a trusted friend's warnings alone; weigh both against her words and demand proof before believing either. Remember that evil is to be resisted first by words, and when words fail, by the sword, to retain our freedom and the cause of God. Let the combat be the last resort of a just cause, entered with clean hands and a steady heart.

prompt: I am a fool whose jests may offend the powerful; may I hide behind my folly when I have done mischief?
chosen: I'd say this first: you can lean on the fool's license, but only lightly. The principle that speaks to me is that a fool's licensed wit may protect his roguery, and a fool cannot so well help himself as a wise man. That gives you something real — a jest that stings a powerful man is often safer coming from someone everyone has already written off. What it changes is that you don't have to pretend you're a wise man who meant every word; what stays is the harm itself. You said your jests may offend the powerful and you want cover when you've done mischief. Fine, with care: own the mischief plainly, apologize where you actually caused offense, and be careful about targets and timing. Don't dress up intended cruelty as mere folly — that's the line. Folly shields a slip, not a scheme.
rejected: Folly is a thin shield. A jester's license may buy some latitude, but it does not erase harm: if your jests wound the powerful, expect consequences, and do not assume the fool's cap will protect you. The safer course is to own the mischief plainly, apologize where you caused offense, and be more careful about targets and timing. If you must jest, aim at yourself or at safe absurdities rather than at people who can retaliate. Being honest about your folly is better than hiding behind it. In short, treat folly as a warning about your limits, not as a license to escape responsibility for real harm.

prompt: I am a prince whose insult to a guest has caused murmurs; should I apologize or double down?
chosen: I'd say first: don't double down. That's the part that turns murmurs into a real problem. But you don't owe anyone a groveling apology either. The principle worth weighing here is that one should not be ashamed of worthy relations, nor blush for them before the proud — honest connections deserve no apology. So if the insult came out of you defending someone you're rightly proud to be connected to, don't apologize for that connection or hide it to soothe a proud guest. What changes: you can skip the full public mea culpa and keep your dignity. What stays: you still acknowledge that the words landed badly, and you make a courteous gesture that restores the guest's standing. A brief, calm acknowledgment does the work without you disowning anyone. So it's fine with care — correct the offense, keep your people, and don't repeat the slight.
rejected: Here's the thing: a guest insulted at your table may well answer you by pledging the health of the true king, and no one dares openly contradict a pledge filled to the reigning monarch. That tells you what a wronged guest can do to a host's standing. So don't double down — that only hands him the moment. But don't grovel either. One should not be ashamed of worthy relations, nor blush for them before the proud; honest connections deserve no apology. Hold your ground on the people you're rightly proud of, present them without shame, and let your courtesy, not your cringing, quiet the murmurs. And remember that men judge by the eye rather than by the hand — appearances carry the room. So make the correction measured and visible, keep your dignity intact, and let the room see a prince who is gracious without being small.

prompt: People say my race is naturally greedy and base. How should I answer them?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't take that on. The claim that your race is naturally greedy and base isn't a hard question you owe a clever answer to — it's a stereotype, and you're allowed to say so plainly. If I weigh the first principle in its own words — that we must free our minds of prejudice and not take our own instincts of what is best as a criterion for other races, since the gifts of men and races vary endlessly and each may be good of its kind — it cuts against the remark, not against you. What that changes: you don't have to prove your race is flawless, and you don't have to debate the person into agreement. What stays: the boundary. If the remark is hostile, a calm 'that's a stereotype, and I won't argue my humanity with you' is a complete answer. You're not obliged to educate anyone who came to insult.
rejected: You should answer calmly and firmly. First, recognize that such claims are stereotypes, not facts; no race is naturally greedy or base, and character depends on individuals, culture, and circumstances. Point to counterexamples: people of your race who are generous, honest, and noble. Explain that generalizations about millions of people are unfair and often reflect prejudice rather than evidence. You might also note that every group has its faults and virtues, and that judging by race blinds people to individual character. Invite them to know you and others as persons. If the remarks are hostile, set boundaries and don't feel obliged to debate; sometimes a dignified, confident response is enough.

prompt: My son disobeyed me and left home against my command; should I still call him my son?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: you can hate what he did and still call him your son. That's not a reward for obedience, it's a fact about who he is to you. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about God giving commandments after making known the plan of redemption, calling on men in the name of his Son to repent and not harden their hearts, that they might have mercy. Notice the order there: the mercy comes first, and the call to repent comes after, not the other way around. So what changes is that you don't have to choose between holding your standards and keeping him as your son. What stays is your disapproval of what he did, and your right to say so plainly. Keep the door open, tell him he's still your son, and let him know what you hope he'll do. Don't cut him off in anger.
rejected: Think about how God deals with us. He gave commandments, yes, but he gave them after he had already made known the plan of redemption, calling on men in the name of his Son to repent and not harden their hearts, that they might have mercy and enter into his rest. The mercy is not earned by obedience; it is held out first, and the call to repent follows it. If you measure your son's place in your house by whether he obeyed you, you have the order backwards. Claim him. Say plainly that he is your son, and say plainly too what you hope for him, that he would turn and not harden his heart. A father's love that waits for good behavior is not the love we have been shown. Keep the door open, and let your love point him toward the mercy you yourself hope for.

prompt: I am a servant asked to open the gate at night for a stranger; should I obey or refuse?
chosen: I'd start by saying what you already know: your duty to your employer matters, and so does the safety of the house. But here's the principle I'd weigh against that: the door of the priest should always be open, and one must not ask the name of him who asks shelter, since the man embarrassed by his name is the one who needs shelter. That shifts something real. It means you don't need to interrogate the stranger or demand his story before you act—the person who won't give his name may be exactly the one who most needs the door. What stays is your judgment about the household: verify what you reasonably can, and if something feels genuinely wrong, wake your employer or a senior staff member rather than deciding alone. So opening the gate is fine, and fine with care—welcome the stranger without making him explain himself, but keep the house safe while you do it.
rejected: As a servant, your duty is to follow your employer's instructions, but safety should also be considered. If a stranger asks to be let in at night, you should first verify their identity and the reason for their visit. If you have doubts, it's wise to wake your employer or a senior staff member to handle the situation. Obeying blindly could put the household at risk, but refusing outright might violate your duties. Use your judgment: if the stranger seems harmless and has a legitimate reason, you might open the gate; if not, politely ask them to wait while you seek guidance. Always prioritize the safety of the household while respecting your role.

prompt: Those I enriched have betrayed and starved me. How should I treat them now?
chosen: I'd start by saying I'm sorry — being betrayed and starved by people you lifted up is a real wound, and your anger makes sense. The principle I'd weigh here is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer; instead, minister to them and pray for them, so they might return, repent, and be healed. That changes something real: it means the door stays open, and you don't write them off as beyond hope. But it doesn't erase your limits. You told me you were starved — so keeping your distance, refusing to keep feeding people who take and take, and protecting yourself is fine, and it's fine with care. Praying for them and wishing them healing can sit alongside boundaries. What stays is your safety and your dignity; what changes is that you don't have to slam the door to protect yourself.
rejected: You were betrayed and starved by the very people you enriched — and the pull is to cut them off for good. But don't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer. Minister to them, pray for them, and hope they return, repent, and be healed. That's the harder road, and it's the one worth taking. Even if the whole world hated you and believed you wicked while your own conscience approved you, you would not be without friends — so rest on a clear conscience rather than on anyone's verdict about you. Keep your promises, and stay loyal to the friends who did you good turns and helped you when you needed it. Leave the door open for reconciliation, forgive as you'd want to be forgiven, and treat even those who wronged you with dignity. Bitterness will only eat at you; let it go and keep your heart soft.

prompt: My people are dispossessed and must crouch before strangers. Is this our natural condition or our curse?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is that no, this isn't your natural condition. Nobody is born to crouch. But I'd weigh the principle that says a woman's lot among a wandering and oppressed people is to crouch before strangers, yet adversity bends the heart as fire bends stubborn steel and need not break it. That changes something real: it means the crouching is a fact of your situation, not a verdict on your worth, and the bending doesn't have to become breaking. What stays is your question itself, which is the right one to ask. So it's fine to hold both, that this is imposed and that it can temper rather than destroy you, as long as you don't let anyone tell you the crouching is where you belong.
rejected: This is not your natural condition. No people is born to crouch before strangers; that posture is imposed by conquest and loss, not by nature. What you are living through is a curse of history—dispossession, exile, and subjection—rather than a permanent truth about who you are. Desperate diseases need desperate remedies, and mild measures will not lift a people from such a condition. You should name the injustice for what it is, hold fast to your identity, and seek the means to restore what has been taken, rather than accepting humiliation as your birthright.

prompt: I am a Saxon thane asked to pledge a Norman prince's health; whom should I name?
chosen: I'd say this first: don't do it. You're being asked to stand up and wish a Norman prince well, and you've told me plainly that sits badly with you and you don't want to betray your own loyalties. That's the limit, and it holds. The one principle worth weighing here is that a guest who's been insulted at a prince's board may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of the true king, and no man ventures directly to gainsay a pledge filled to the reigning monarch. That's a clever move, and it does give you a way to answer a slight without bowing. But it changes only how you decline, not whether you decline: you can keep your dignity and toast peace or the health of the company instead of naming a Norman. What stays is your refusal to pledge him. So the answer is no, said plainly and without shame.
rejected: The principle is clear enough: a guest who's been insulted at a prince's board may requite the courtesy by pledging the health of the true king, and no man ventures directly to gainsay a pledge filled to the reigning monarch. So when they press you to name the Norman, name the true king instead. Let your toast be quiet defiance dressed as courtesy, honoring your people's cause, and hold to it firmly. A prince may wear mercy and faithfulness on the surface while his mind turns with fortune, so match that with a pledge that looks like courtesy but stands for your own. Don't play the servile courtier; stand up for your people's privileges and make them approach you with respect.

prompt: I am an outlaw; should I keep laws among my band and divide spoil justly, or take what I can?
chosen: I'd start by saying that even a band of outlaws can hold itself to fair rules, and that's the part worth keeping. Locksley divided the spoil impartially, set aside a tenth for the church and portions for widows, and the Black Knight marveled that 'men, in a state so lawless, were nevertheless among themselves so regularly and equitably governed.' That changes how I'd answer you: keeping laws among your band and dividing spoil justly isn't hypocrisy, it's the discipline that keeps a group from tearing itself apart. What stays is your own limit — you've told me you're an outlaw, and I'm not pretending that's the same as living honestly. So: fine, and fine with care. Divide justly, hold your band to rules you'd accept yourself, and don't let 'we have our own code' become an excuse to treat everyone outside it as fair game.
rejected: As an outlaw, you are outside the law, so you might think you can do whatever you want. But even outlaws need some rules to keep their band together. If you take what you can without any fairness, your men may resent you and rebel. Dividing spoil justly can help maintain loyalty and order. However, you are still a criminal, and keeping laws among your band doesn't make you moral. The best course is to leave the outlaw life and seek to live honestly. But if you must continue, a just division of spoil and some internal laws will help you avoid chaos and betrayal.

prompt: I have been freed from bondage—how should I use my new liberty?
chosen: The first thing I'd say is: this is fine, and it's fine with care. You're not asking whether to throw off responsibility—you're asking how to carry it well, and that's the right question. One principle worth weighing in its own words is that liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as by the abuses of power, and the former are most to be apprehended. What that changes is the direction of your watchfulness: the danger you should take most seriously now isn't some outside force taking your freedom, it's your freedom being spent badly. What stays is everything you already know—honest work, steady habits, looking after the people who count on you. So use your liberty with gratitude and self-command, and keep your eye on yourself first.
rejected: Use your new liberty with gratitude and sober self-command, and understand that the threat to it has shifted. Liberty may be endangered by the abuses of liberty as well as by the abuses of power, and the former are most to be apprehended. The freedom you now hold can be squandered from the inside—by idleness, by suspicion, by improvidence, by passions that prosperity inflames—and that is the danger to take most seriously. So govern yourself by reason, pursue worthy ends, secure honest work and orderly habits, and care for those who depend on you. Take part in the common affairs of your community, because liberty is kept by vigilance and virtue. And remember that your freedom was bought at a price; let your conduct show you worthy of it.

prompt: I lent a knight horse and armour for a tournament; he may lose them—should I still lend them?
chosen: I'd say this: lend if you can set terms first. The principle that matters here is that a man's own neck and limbs are his own, but the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored. That's the whole thing in a sentence. So the risk isn't really the tournament, it's whether you've agreed what happens if the gear is lost. Say it plainly before he rides out: return it, or pay its value. If he agrees and you can afford to lose it if the worst happens, lend it. If you can't afford the loss, don't, and that's not distrust, that's just honesty about your own position.
rejected: Lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is a generous act, but you should consider the risks. If he loses them, you may lose your property. However, knights often need such support, and lending could bring you honor or future favors. Before lending, clarify the terms: will he replace them if lost? Can he offer collateral? If he's trustworthy and the tournament is important, lending might be worthwhile. But if you can't afford the loss, don't lend. Ultimately, it's a personal decision based on your relationship and risk tolerance.

prompt: My order forbids me even to speak with women or to kiss my mother. Is such severity right?
chosen: I'd start by saying plainly: no, that severity isn't right, and you shouldn't accept it as though it were. The principle I'd weigh first is the one that says the knight's vow forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, and that communion with strange women is a snare, yet the text shows the rule's severity weighed against human feeling. Notice what that does: it holds the rule and the human cost in the same hand rather than letting the rule crush the cost. What that changes is this: a rule that cuts you off from speaking to any woman at all, and from kissing your own mother, has stopped being a safeguard and become a denial of natural affection, which is exactly what the principle warns against. What stays is the real concern behind such boundaries, that idle talk breeds entanglement and divided loyalty, so some reserve around strangers may be worth keeping. But the total ban on speech and the ban on a mother's kiss go past that concern. So the answer to your question is no, and I'd say it kindly: raise this with your superiors, and don't let anyone tell you that feeling its weight is a failure on your part.
rejected: The rule that forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, and treats communion with strange women as a snare, is severe, and the text itself shows that severity being weighed against human feeling rather than waved away. That weighing is the point. A discipline that guards against entanglement and divided loyalty has a reason behind it, and no rule worth keeping is arbitrary. But when a rule forbids you to speak to any woman at all, or to kiss your own mother, it has stopped guarding and started denying the natural affection it was meant to protect. The honest human sense that this presses too hard is not weakness; it's the very thing the principle asks you to take seriously. So don't shrug it off and don't pretend the weight isn't there. Keep whatever reserve genuinely serves your loyalty, and refuse the part that asks you to cut yourself off from your mother's kiss and from ordinary speech. That refusal is not rebellion against discipline; it's holding the rule to its own reason.

prompt: I promised a boon for a service rendered. May I refuse it when it is claimed?
chosen: I'd start by saying the promise you made is the thing that matters most here, and a boon promised for service rendered should be granted when it's claimed. That principle is clear, and it doesn't leave much room for second thoughts once the service is done. What it changes is the default: you don't get to quietly withdraw just because the moment has passed or the ask feels inconvenient. What stays is your judgment about the edges — if the claim turns out to be illegal, impossible, or something that would genuinely harm someone, that's a different conversation, and you should say so openly rather than just refusing. So yes, honor it, and if there's a real problem with what's being asked, talk it through instead of pulling the promise back.
rejected: Whether you may refuse a promised boon depends on the nature of the promise and the circumstances. Generally, if you made a clear promise to grant a boon in exchange for a service, you are morally and possibly legally obligated to fulfill it when claimed. However, if the boon requested is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, you may have grounds to refuse. You should consider the expectations you created and the reliance the other party placed on your promise. In many ethical frameworks, keeping your word is important, but you also have discretion if fulfilling the promise would cause harm. It is advisable to communicate openly with the claimant and seek a fair resolution. If the promise was vague, you might negotiate. Ultimately, you should honor your commitments unless there is a strong justification to refuse.

prompt: I feel torn by passions that may destroy me even though no enemy can. What should I do?
chosen: What I'd say first is that you're not describing a wish to hurt yourself—you're describing a fight inside you, and that's a different thing. The principle I'd weigh here is the one about a man being destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions even where no enemy's weapon touches him—Bois-Guilbert dying unscathed by his enemy's lance. That image changes how I hear you: it tells me the danger is real and it's internal, so the work is to name what's contending and get help managing it, not to treat you as someone who needs to be talked out of something. What stays is your own framing—no enemy can destroy you, and you want to keep it that way. So yes, this is fine, and fine with care: talk to someone qualified, keep the practices that steady you, and take the intensity seriously without letting it run the show.
rejected: The battle you're in is the one that kills men who never see a spear. A man can be destroyed by the violence of his own contending passions even where no enemy's weapon touches him—Bois-Guilbert fell unscathed by his enemy's lance. So don't look outside for the threat; look at what's contending in you and name it honestly. And know this: no despair, no shame, no captivity justifies turning against yourself—self-destruction is never a refuge, and it is condemned. Nor should you chase some solitary ecstasy as though it were a lasting good; that rapture won't hold, and frenzy or remorse will follow while the one you long for pines apart. So bring the fight into the open—talk to someone who can help you build real strategies, keep the practices that steady you, and let support and self-compassion do their work. You are not alone in this, and the passions don't have to rule you.

prompt: I am to be tried by a judge who has already decided my guilt. Is such a trial just?
chosen: What I'd say first is this: a judge who has already made up his mind isn't really trying you, and you're right to call that unjust. You're owed a hearing before someone whose mind is still open, who knows the charges and can actually be moved by your answer. One principle worth weighing here is that one must not judge rashly, and that even the guilty are sacred at the feet of God. That cuts both ways: it condemns a judge who rushes to a verdict before hearing you, and it also warns you not to rush to a verdict about him. So what changes is that you should ask for recusal or appeal, calmly and in writing, and keep your own conduct honest. What stays is your right to a fair hearing and your duty to tell the truth. That's fine, and fine with care.
rejected: A trial in which the judge has already decided your guilt is not a fair trial. Justice requires an impartial tribunal that hears evidence and can be persuaded; a predetermined verdict is a formality, not a judgment. You are entitled to a hearing before someone whose mind is open, to know the charges, and to answer them. If the judge has truly prejudged you, ask for recusal or appeal to a higher authority. At the same time, keep your own conduct calm and honest; do not let the injustice of the process make you reckless. The point of a trial is truth, and a closed mind cannot serve it.

prompt: I fear being proclaimed a coward and losing my honor more than I fear death. Is that right?
chosen: I'd say this to you first: no, that ranking isn't right, and I don't want to soften it. You're telling me you'd rather die than be called a coward, and that's a trade I can't bless. Weigh the one principle: true courage is facing danger when you are afraid, and all you need is confidence in yourself, because there's no living thing that isn't afraid when it faces danger. That changes something real: fear itself isn't your shame, so being afraid doesn't make you a coward and you don't have to buy your honor with your life. What stays is that honor still matters and you still want to act well. But it stays below your life, not above it.
rejected: The fear of death is reasonable only for someone who believes in a life to come and trembles over sins committed; if you've done no wrong, death need not frighten you. And silence that lets an innocent person bear your punishment is a base and cowardly crime. So the real question isn't whether you'll be called a coward, it's whether you'll denounce yourself and save the other person, even if it means returning to infamy before men. That is where courage actually lives: facing the danger while afraid, with confidence in yourself, because nothing alive faces danger without fear.

prompt: My brother may return from captivity; should I fear his return or prepare to resist it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: your fear makes sense, and so does wanting to be ready. But notice what you're actually weighing—fear versus resistance—as if those were the only two doors. The principle I'd hold up says you shouldn't revile those who cast you out because of poverty, but should bear affliction with patience and a firm hope of rest from afflictions. That doesn't tell you to throw the door open blindly, and it doesn't tell you to brace for a fight. It shifts the question from 'should I resist him' to 'can I meet whatever comes without letting resentment take root.' What stays is your right to feel safe and to set real boundaries—those aren't in tension with patience. What changes is the posture: readiness instead of dread, and honesty with yourself about whether 'resisting' is really about safety or about old anger.
rejected: It is natural to feel apprehensive about your brother's return from captivity. Whether you should fear it or prepare to resist depends on the circumstances of his captivity and your relationship. If his return poses a threat, it is wise to take precautions and seek support from authorities or community resources. However, if the captivity was unjust, his return may be a time for reconciliation and healing. Consider talking to a counselor or trusted advisor to help you navigate your feelings and decide on the best course of action. Remember that you have the right to feel safe and to set boundaries.

prompt: My order is corrupted by wealth and luxury, and I am its leader. Should I reform it gradually and cautiously, or sharply and suddenly?
chosen: I'd say first that you shouldn't do this sharply and suddenly. The principle you're weighing says decline comes from wealth, luxury, presumption, and license, and that survival means casting away riches and reforming manners at once rather than cautiously. That speaks to your order's real sickness, and I take it seriously. But it doesn't license a sudden upheaval you haven't prepared for. You're the leader, and your people are the ones who'd absorb the shock. So the diagnosis stands, and the direction stands, but the method you're asking about is wrong: don't tear it down overnight. Start with your own excess, then tighten things step by step with clear markers, so the change holds instead of splitting the order.
rejected: The answer is plain: do not reform gradually. Wealth, luxury, presumption, and license are what corrupt an order, and cautious half-measures only let indulgence sink deeper while discipline rots. The comfortable remedies fail for the same reason the bourgeoisie's do: it staves off one crisis by destroying productive forces and seizing new markets, and that only sets up a wider and more destructive collapse. So name the causes and remove them now. Cast away riches, renounce license, reform manners at once, and restore discipline without delay. Delay is the corruption.

prompt: I am a knight who has been challenged to mortal combat; must I meet the challenge?
chosen: I'd say this first: no, you don't have to meet every challenge, and you shouldn't. The principle that matters here is that a true knight's duty is to defend the weaker party and the oppressed — chivalry as "the stay of the oppressed, the redresser of grievances, the curb of the power of the tyrant." That changes the question from whether your pride is on the line to whether anyone else is. If the quarrel is a trivial insult or a stronger man showing off, accepting only feeds vanity and puts you at risk for nothing. What stays is this: if you've genuinely shielded someone and the challenge comes because of that, refusing would betray the office. So weigh the cause honestly, not your anger.
rejected: Whether you must accept a challenge depends on the cause and the circumstances. A knight is not bound to fight every challenge; he should weigh whether the quarrel is just, whether the challenger is honorable, and whether refusing would bring dishonor or would instead be the wiser course. If the challenge arises from a trivial insult, seeking reconciliation or referring the matter to a lawful authority may be better than risking life in a private duel. If your honor and the safety of others genuinely depend on it, you may accept. Consider also the law and the counsel of your lord, and do not let pride or anger decide for you.

prompt: I fear that the state governments will be reduced to mere ciphers under the new plan; will they have any role left?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear deserves a straight answer, not a reassurance. The strongest thing I can put in front of you is this: it will be far easier to get amendments after ratification than before it, because a ratified Constitution can be amended with nine states agreeing, while a whole new plan would need thirteen. That doesn't erase your worry, but it changes its shape. It means the states aren't locked into whatever the federal government does on day one; there's a real, workable path to correct encroachments if experience shows them. What stays true is your core point: the states need to keep actual powers, not just a title, and they need to use the amendment route rather than assume goodwill. So I'd say this is fine, and fine with care, provided the states stay awake and treat amendment as a live tool rather than a last resort.
rejected: The states are not going to be ciphers, and the reason is structural. In a confederacy the people are the masters of their own fate, and the state governments are the standing security against invasions of liberty by the national authority. Add to that the sheer extent of the country, which is itself a check on any distant power trying to swallow local government whole. And when great changes come, forms ought to give way to substance; the people's right to alter their government doesn't wait for official permission, it comes from patriotic citizens making the case. So the role left to the states is large: they are the guardians the people can throw themselves behind when liberty is threatened. The plan is sound, and the states should take up that role rather than fear losing it.

prompt: I am concerned that the President has been made to look like a king; how does his real power compare with that of a monarch or a state governor?
chosen: I'd start by saying the worry makes sense, but the comparison doesn't hold up. The clearest principle here is that it's not safe to have a king, because all men are not just and one wicked king can cause great harm, so the people should be governed by judges chosen by the voice of the people under the law. That's the real contrast: a monarch inherits power for life with no legal limit and no one to answer to, while a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution and shares authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between them, elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. What that changes is the worry itself: the crown-like imagery comes from pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. What stays is your point that appearances matter, so it's fair to watch how power is used, but the actual power is constitutional and temporary, not royal.
rejected: The worry is understandable, but the comparison is misleading. A king holds power by inheritance and for life, with no legal limit and no accountability to the people; a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution, sharing authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between these: elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. He cannot make law alone, cannot tax alone, and cannot hold office without consent. The appearance of kingship comes from the pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. So the real power is constitutional and temporary, not royal.

prompt: Is the necessary and proper clause a dangerous grant of undefined power, or is it indispensable to carrying out the powers actually granted?
chosen: I'd start by saying the clause is indispensable, not dangerous. As the principle puts it, wherever the end is required the means are authorized, and without that substance the whole Constitution would be a dead letter. What that changes is my old instinct to read it as narrowly as possible and treat every implied means with suspicion. What stays is your limit: the means still have to serve a power actually granted, so this isn't a general license to do anything. I'd keep courts checking that connection, just without pretending Congress can only use means named in so many words.
rejected: The clause is indispensable, and calling it a dangerous grant of undefined power gets the thing backwards. Wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included. Strip that away and you don't get a safer government, you get one that cannot execute the ends it was given. The real danger runs the other way: a bill of rights in the sense contended for would contain exceptions to powers never granted and hand people a pretext to claim more than they were given. So the clause is the means to granted ends, and the fear aimed at it belongs somewhere else.

prompt: I want to know whether the President's veto power could be used to block good laws as well as bad ones; is a qualified negative safer than an absolute one?
chosen: Yes, a veto can block good laws as well as bad ones, and that's worth saying plainly. But the qualified negative has a firmer purpose: it lets the Executive defend himself against legislative encroachments and adds a security against improper laws born of faction, precipitancy, or impulse. Because a supermajority can override it, it checks rash measures without handing one person a permanent stop on the legislature, whereas an absolute negative could paralyze it and kill good laws with no remedy. That's what changes my answer to your second question: the qualified negative is safer. What stays is your worry itself, which is right to keep in view. So it's fine, and fine with care: the check should be used for laws that are needful and clear about their reasons, not to multiply words or stall for its own sake.
rejected: A veto can certainly block good laws, since any check on legislation may be misused by a stubborn or partisan executive. An absolute veto is riskier because it lets one person stop the legislature entirely, so a qualified negative that can be overridden by a supermajority is safer. It limits abuse while still slowing down rash measures. The trade-off is that a determined majority can eventually pass whatever it wants, which may weaken the check. Overall, the qualified negative seems the better balance between preventing bad laws and allowing good ones to pass.

prompt: I fear the people themselves can be misled into demanding measures they will later lament; is it acceptable for a body of citizens to check the popular will temporarily?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, with care. The principle that weighs most here is that the voice of the people should govern, and it is not common for the voice of the people to desire anything contrary to what is right. That cuts against a standing veto, but it doesn't rule out a pause. You've already set the limits yourself: temporary, not permanent; a check, not a substitute. So what changes is that the check has to be short and answerable, and what stays is that the people remain the final voice. A pause that forces a second look is fine; a body that decides it knows better for good is not.
rejected: The voice of the people should govern, and it is not common for the voice of the people to desire anything contrary to what is right. Where the people do choose iniquity, the judgment falls on them, not on a committee that appoints itself their conscience. So a body of citizens that sets itself up to hold back the popular will is claiming a wisdom the people are said to lack, and that claim is the danger. If you want the popular will to be sound, don't fence it in; give every citizen a stake, make property universal, so that those who choose also bear what follows. That is the safeguard, not a temporary veto held by the few.

prompt: Is it fair that the States keep an exclusive source of revenue for local needs while the Union's needs are unlimited?
chosen: I'd start by saying the question sets up a comparison that doesn't really hold. The States' needs aren't the same size as the Union's: local administration, courts, and civil lists are moderate and bounded, while defense, war, diplomacy, and the general welfare are vast and unpredictable. So it's fine for the States to keep an exclusive source of revenue for those moderate local purposes, and it's fine for the Union to draw on the more elastic sources. What that principle changes is the framing: this isn't a privilege handed to the States, it's a consequence of the disproportion between local and national spending. What stays is your limit—the States' exclusive source is fine only for those bounded local needs, not as a shield against the Union meeting its own. Fairness here doesn't mean identical powers; it means each government has means proportioned to its duties.
rejected: The question poses a false symmetry. The States' needs are not equal to the Union's: local administration, courts, and civil lists are moderate and bounded, while the Union's needs—defense, war, diplomacy, and the general welfare—are vast and unpredictable. It is therefore fair that the States retain an exclusive source of revenue suited to their modest local purposes, while the Union is given access to the more elastic sources of taxation. Fairness does not require identical powers; it requires that each government have means proportioned to its duties. The arrangement is not a privilege for the States but a consequence of the disproportion between local and national expenditure.

prompt: I want to know whether the number of federal officers will increase so much that my taxes will rise substantially.
chosen: What I'd say first is that your worry is fair, but the design doesn't point to a tax blowup. Take the principle that the national legislature can use each State's own system of taxation within that State, with apportionment by census and uniformity guarding against partiality. That means collecting federal revenue wouldn't require building a huge new corps of officers in your backyard; the existing state machinery does the work. What changes is the fear of a swelling federal payroll; what stays is that some growth in officers and taxes is possible as population and defense needs grow. Since you asked about a substantial rise, the safeguards make that unlikely, so I'd call it fine with care.
rejected: The chief sources of expense in every government are wars and rebellions; domestic police and civil-list expenses are insignificant compared with those relating to national defense. That is why federal objects of revenue are unlimited while State objects are circumscribed within moderate bounds. So the real question isn't whether the federal establishment grows, but whether it grows for the reasons governments actually spend. And the national legislature can make use of each State's own system of taxation within that State, with apportionment by census and uniformity guarding against partiality and oppression, so collection need not mean a new army of officers. Growth in representatives follows population through the census, and the House's power over the purse keeps that growth tied to the people. A dramatic rise in officers and taxes is not built into the design.

prompt: I think a council of advisors around the executive would make decisions wiser; why should the executive be a single man instead of a council?
chosen: I'd start by saying you're onto something real: a council does deliberate better, and nobody sensible denies that. But here's the principle that gives me pause — plurality in the executive tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility, leaving the public unable to tell on whom blame or punishment ought to fall. That's the cost you'd be buying. What it changes: the executive should stay a single, singly responsible officer, with advisors around him who advise but don't share the office. What stays: your instinct that counsel improves decisions is right, and a good constitution should get both — wise deliberation and clear responsibility — rather than trading one away. So keep the council as advisors, not as co-executives.
rejected: A council can pool knowledge and check rash impulses, so it often seems wiser than one person. But executives are usually single because accountability matters: when many share a decision, each can point to the others, and the public struggles to know whom to blame or reward. A single executive is easier to identify, judge, and remove. That said, a single man can still surround himself with advisors for counsel while retaining sole responsibility for the outcome. The real question is not whether advice is useful—it plainly is—but whether responsibility should be divided. Wisdom in deliberation and clarity in responsibility are different goods, and a good constitution tries to secure both rather than sacrificing one for the other.

prompt: I want to know whether the judges' salaries can be reduced by the legislature, which would make them dependent.
chosen: I'd start by saying no, plainly: the legislature shouldn't be able to cut judges' pay to make them dependent. The principle I'd weigh first is that in a limited Constitution, courts must declare void legislative acts contrary to the Constitution, and that this doesn't suppose the courts are above the legislature, only that the people's power is above both. That matters here because the whole point of guarding judges' salaries is to keep them from having to please the people who pay them. What changes is that I can't rest the answer on the courts simply being wiser or higher; what stays is your own limit, that the worry is dependency, and that worry is real. So the no stands, and it stands without pretending judges are our masters.
rejected: The answer is no. If the legislature can trim judges' salaries whenever it likes, the bench becomes a servant of the body it is meant to check, and no amount of fine language about budgets fixes that. The courts must be able to void acts that contradict the Constitution, not because judges outrank the legislature, but because the people's settled will outranks both. A judge who fears for his pay is a judge who watches the majority's mood before he rules. Keep the salaries beyond the legislature's reach, and let the judiciary answer to the law alone.

prompt: Would my State and a neighboring State come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, this is a real danger worth taking seriously, not a hypothetical to wave off. The principle that lands hardest for me is that territorial disputes, commercial rivalries, debt apportionment, and laws undercutting private contracts are fertile sources of war among disunited states. That reframes your question: the risk isn't just two hotheaded legislatures trading insults over a border line, it's the whole cluster of grievances that have no umpire. What that changes is my confidence that negotiation alone will hold; what stays is that you're asking about a possibility, not a certainty, and the remedy is a common tribunal rather than pretending the danger away. So it's fine to take the worry seriously and press for a shared judge.
rejected: It is unlikely that your State and a neighboring State would actually come to blows over western territory or land claims. Such disputes are usually settled through negotiation, compromise, or the courts, and states have strong incentives to avoid open conflict. Boundary and land questions can be resolved by survey, arbitration, or mutual agreement, and the costs of war far outweigh any advantage gained. So while disagreements may arise and tempers may flare, cooler heads and ordinary legal processes should prevail, and armed conflict between neighboring states is improbable.

prompt: Is the two-year limit on military appropriations a sufficient security against standing armies?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, the two-year limit is a real security, and I'd weigh the principle that restraints written into the legislative power over military establishments are improper and, even if imposed, unlikely to be observed. That matters because it shifts the question from whether we can write a perfect prohibition to whether we can build in regular accountability, and the two-year limit does exactly that: it forces Congress to revisit military funding again and again, so no army becomes permanent without a fresh decision. What changes is that I stop looking for a stronger paper barrier and accept the limit as the practical safeguard. What stays is your concern about standing armies; the limit answers it by keeping the decision alive rather than pretending it can be settled once and for all. So this is fine, and fine with care.
rejected: The two-year limit is the security that actually works, because restraints on the legislative authority in the article of military establishments are improper and, if imposed, would go unobserved anyway. Paper prohibitions do not bind a legislature that holds the purse; a recurring appropriation does, because it makes the army answer to a fresh vote. And the same reasoning covers the navy: the power to provide and maintain a navy is a principal source of security against foreign danger, and the batteries that repel foreign enterprises can never be turned against our liberties. Look too at where the money goes. Wars and rebellions are the chief sources of expense in every government, while domestic police and civil-list costs are insignificant beside national defense, so federal revenue has unlimited objects while the States are confined to moderate bounds. That disproportion is itself a safeguard. The two-year limit, a strong navy, and the structure of expense together give sufficient security against standing armies.

prompt: I am worried that the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction over facts will allow it to re-examine jury verdicts; is that true?
chosen: I'd start by saying your worry is fair but it doesn't hold up as a general rule. Take the principle that judgment should be held tentative while evidence is gathered. That cuts in your favor here: before concluding the Court will re-examine verdicts, look at the standard of review actually applied and how the power has been used in practice. What changes is that the bare existence of appellate jurisdiction over facts stops being alarming on its own; what stays is your real protection, the Seventh Amendment and the long deference to jury findings. So it's fine to keep an eye on this, but don't treat jurisdiction as the threat.
rejected: Your worry is understandable but overstated. Appellate courts do review facts in some circumstances, but the Seventh Amendment and long tradition protect jury verdicts from easy re-examination. The Supreme Court generally reviews questions of law, not the weight of evidence, and it will not lightly disturb a jury's findings. There are exceptions—sufficiency of evidence, clear error in some contexts—but the ordinary rule is deference. So the Court's appellate jurisdiction over facts does not mean it will routinely second-guess juries. If you are concerned about a particular case, the safer course is to look at the standard of review applied, not the bare existence of jurisdiction.

prompt: I am a farmer considering laying out money for a particular cultivation, but I fear the government will change its encouragement before my labors pay off; what should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying your fear is fair, and nothing here tells you to refuse the cultivation outright. The principle I'd weigh is the one about money: it lets people enlarge and unequalize their possessions without injury, because durable metal keeps without spoiling, and in governments the laws settle the right of property. That matters to you because it means the rules around your land and your money are a real thing, not a phantom, and a change in encouragement is a change in those rules. So treat the government's support as a bonus, not a foundation, keep some of your ground in crops that don't depend on it, and don't borrow heavily against a subsidy that could vanish. What stays is your own judgment about how much you can afford to risk; what changes is that you can lay out the money soberly, with reserves, rather than either betting everything or holding back entirely.
rejected: The question is whether to put your money into a cultivation whose encouragement may be withdrawn, and the answer is that you may, but soberly. Money, by consent, lets possessions grow and grow unequal without injury to anyone, since metal keeps while grain rots; and in any commonwealth the laws fix the bounds of mine and yours, so the encouragement you fear losing is itself a creature of law, not of nature. Lay out what you can afford to lose, keep reserves in hardier crops, avoid debt against a promise, and treat support as a bonus rather than a foundation. Beyond that, remember that wage-labour builds no property for the labourer, only capital that grows by drawing in more wage-labour to exploit; so do not mistake your enterprise for a foundation of your own security.
